“While we are being led away by this goblin, why do you just watch, father? Surely your heart is like a stone, or like iron strongly bound, to remain so firm while seeing your children's distress.”

2132.

2132.

“Yo no baddhe na jānāsi, brāhmaṇena dhanesinā;

Accāyikena luddena, yo no gāvova sumbhati.

“You do not seem to feel the sorrow of our being bound by this wealth-seeking and cruel brahmin, who beats us like cattle until we bleed. Though I suffer such pain, I shall endure it since it is for your benefit, father.

2133.

2133.

“Idheva acchataṃ kaṇhā, na sā jānāti kismiñci;

Migīva khirasammattā, yūthā hīnā pakandatī”ti.

“But little Kaṇhā has always lived in her parents' embrace and has never known such distress. Like a young doe still dependent on milk who cries out when separated from the herd and unable to find its mother, Kaṇhā will surely wither and die of grief, not seeing our mother.”

Tattha udikkhatīti so pitu santikaṃ gantvā kampamāno oloketi. Vedhanti vedhamāno. Tvañca no tāta, dassasīti tvañca amhe tāya anāgatāya eva brāhmaṇassa dadāsi, evaṃ mā kari, adhivāsehi tvaṃ tāva. Yāva ammaṃ passemu, atha no tāya diṭṭhakāle tvaṃ puna dassasi. Vikkiṇātu hanātu vāti tāta, ammāya āgatakāle esa amhe vikkiṇātu vā hanatu [V 7.0320] vā. Yaṃ icchati, taṃ karotu. Apica kho panesa kakkhaḷo pharuso, aṭṭhārasahi purisadosehi samannāgatoti aṭṭhārasa purisadose kathesi.

Thus Jāali lamented piteously before his father, but the Great Being, restraining his emotions, remained silent. Jāali then said: “This old brahmin is harsh and cruel, endowed with the eighteen flaws of a man—he is not human, but a goblin of the earth.”

Tattha balaṅkapādoti patthaṭapādo. Andhanakhoti pūtinakho. Ovaddhapiṇḍikoti heṭṭhāgalitapiṇḍikamaṃso. Dīghuttaroṭṭhoti mukhaṃ pidahitvā ṭhitena dīghena uttaroṭṭhena samannāgato. Capaloti paggharitalālo. Kaḷāroti sūkaradāṭhāhi viya nikkhantadantehi samannāgato[M 7.0329]. Bhagganāsakoti bhaggāya visamāya nāsāya samannāgato. Lohamassūti tambalohavaṇṇamassu. Haritakesoti suvaṇṇavaṇṇavirūḷhakeso. Valīnanti sarīracammamassa valiggahitaṃ. Tilakāhatoti kāḷatilakehi parikiṇṇo. Piṅgaloti nibbiddhapiṅgalo biḷārakkhisadisehi akkhīhi samannāgato. Vinatoti kaṭiyaṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ khandheti tīsu ṭhānesu vaṅko. Vikaṭoti vikaṭapādo. “Abaddhasandhī”tipi vuttaṃ, “kaṭakaṭā”ti viravantehi aṭṭhisandhīhi samannāgato. Brahāti dīgho. Amanussoti na manusso, manussavesena vicarantopi yakkho esa. Bhayānakoti ativiya bhiṃsanako.

Therein, 'balaṅkapāda' means having splayed feet. 'Andhanakha' means with putrid nails. 'Ovaddhapiṇḍika' means the flesh of the calves has slipped downward. 'Dīghuttaroṭṭha' means having a long upper lip that covers the mouth. 'Capala' means with dripping saliva. 'Kaḷāra' means with protruding teeth like a boar's tusks. 'Bhagganāsaka' means with a broken, uneven nose. 'Lohamassu' means with a coppery-red beard. 'Haritakesa' means with golden-colored hair. 'Valīna' means his body-skin is wrinkled. 'Tilakāhata' means covered with black moles. 'Piṅgala' means with staring, tawny eyes like a cat's. 'Vinata' means bent in three places: the waist, the back, and the neck. 'Vikaṭa' means with deformed feet. It is also said 'abaddhasandhī', meaning having bone-joints that creak and crack. 'Brahā' means tall and large. 'Amanussa' means not a human; though wandering in human guise, he is a yakkha. 'Bhayānaka' means exceedingly frightening.

Manusso udāhu yakkhoti tāta, sace koci imaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ disvā evaṃ puccheyya “manussoyaṃ brāhmaṇo, udāhu yakkho”ti. “Na manusso, atha kho maṃsalohitabhojano yakkho”ti vattuṃ yuttaṃ. Dhanaṃ taṃ tāta yācatīti tāta, esa amhākaṃ maṃsaṃ khāditukāmo tumhe puttadhanaṃ yācati. Udikkhasīti ajjhupekkhasi. Asmā nūna te hadayanti tāta, mātāpitūnaṃ hadayaṃ nāma puttesu mudukaṃ hoti, puttānaṃ dukkhaṃ na sahati, tvaṃ ajānanto viya acchasi, tava pana hadayaṃ pāsāṇo viya maññe, atha vā āyasaṃ daḷhabandhanaṃ. Tena amhākaṃ evarūpe dukkhe uppanne na rujati.

'Manusso udāhu yakkho' means, 'Father, if someone, upon seeing this brahmin, were to ask, "Is this brahmin a human or a yakkha?" it would be proper to say, "He is not a human, but a yakkha who feeds on flesh and blood."' 'Dhanaṃ taṃ tāta yācati' means, 'Father, desiring to eat our flesh, he asks you for your children as wealth.' 'Udikkhasī' means 'you are indifferent.' 'Asmā nūna te hadayaṃ' means, 'Father, the hearts of parents are tender toward their children; they cannot bear the suffering of their children. You, however, sit as if unaware—your heart, I think, is like stone, or perhaps like iron, strongly bound. Therefore, it does not ache when such suffering befalls us.'

Na jānāsīti ajānanto viya acchasi. Accāyikena luddenāti ativiya luddena pamāṇātikkantena. Yo noti brāhmaṇena no amhe kaniṭṭhabhātike baddhe bandhite yo tvaṃ na jānāsi. Sumbhatīti potheti. Idheva acchatanti [P 6.0550] tāta, ayaṃ kaṇhājinā kiñci dukkhaṃ na jānāti. Yathā nāma khīrasammattā migapotikā yūthā parihīnā mātaraṃ apassantī khīratthāya kandati, evaṃ ammaṃ apassantī kanditvā sussitvā marissati, tasmā maṃyeva brāhmaṇassa dehi, ahaṃ gamissāmi, ayaṃ kaṇhājinā idheva hotūti.

'Na jānāsi' means 'you sit as if not knowing.' 'Accāyikena luddena' means 'by the exceedingly cruel one, who has exceeded all measure.' 'Yo no' means, 'You do not recognize us, your younger siblings, bound by the brahmin.' 'Sumbhati' means 'he strikes.' 'Idheva acchataṃ' means, 'Father, this Kaṇhājinā knows no suffering at all. Just as a young doe, intoxicated by milk, separated from the herd and not seeing its mother, cries out for milk, so too will she, not seeing her mother, cry until she withers away and dies. Therefore, give me alone to the brahmin; I will go. Let this Kaṇhājinā stay here.'

Evaṃ [V 7.0321] vuttepi mahāsatto na kiñci katheti. Tato kumāro mātāpitaro ārabbha paridevanto āha –

Even when spoken to thus, the Great Being remained unmoved. Then the boy, lamenting for his parents, spoke:

2134.

2134.

“Na me idaṃ tathā dukkhaṃ, labbhā hi pumunā idaṃ;

Yañca ammaṃ na passāmi, taṃ me dukkhataraṃ ito.

“This suffering of being beaten by the brahmin is not my greatest suffering; such pain is common to all beings in saṃsāra. But that I must be led away without seeing my mother—that is a greater sorrow to me than the brahmin's blows."

2135.

2135.

“Na [M 7.0330] me idaṃ tathā dukkhaṃ, labbhā hi pumunā idaṃ;

Yañca tātaṃ na passāmi, taṃ me dukkhataraṃ ito.

“This suffering is not so great for me, but when my mother and father no longer see little Kaṇhā who belongs in their embrace, they will suffer the pain of grief for long days and nights."

2136.

2136.

“Sā nūna kapaṇā ammā, cirarattāya rucchati;

Kaṇhājinaṃ apassantī, kumāriṃ cārudassaniṃ.

“Surely now my poor mother, at midnight and at dawn, missing Kaṇhājinā, the fair-faced maiden, will wither away like a river that has run dry."

2137.

2137.

“So nūna kapaṇo tāto, cirarattāya rucchati;

Kaṇhājinaṃ apassanto, kumāriṃ cārudassaniṃ.

“Surely my poor father will grieve for a long time, not seeing Kaṇhājinā, the lovely maiden.”

2138.

2138.

“Sā nūna kapaṇā ammā, ciraṃ rucchati assame;

Kaṇhājinaṃ apassantī, kumāriṃ cārudassaniṃ.

"Surely now my poor mother will grieve long in the hermitage, not seeing Kaṇhājinā, the fair-faced maiden."

2139.

2139.

“So nūna kapaṇo tāto, ciraṃ rucchati assame;

Kaṇhājinaṃ apassanto, kumāriṃ cārudassaniṃ.

"Surely now my poor father will grieve long in the hermitage, not seeing Kaṇhājinā, the lovely maiden."

2140.

2140.

“Sā nūna kapaṇā ammā, cirarattāya rucchati;

Aḍḍharatte va ratte vā, nadīva avasucchati.

“Surely my poor mother will grieve for a long time; at midnight or in the small hours of the night, she will waste away like a dried-up river.”

2141.

2141.

“So nūna kapaṇo tāto, cirarattāya rucchati;

Aḍḍharatte va ratte vā, nadīva avasucchati.

"Surely now my poor father will grieve for a long time; at midnight or during the night, he will dry up like a river."

2142.

2142.

“Ime te jambukā rukkhā, vedisā sinduvārakā;

Vividhāni rukkhajātāni, tāni ajja jahāmase.

“These are the rose-apple trees, the water-willow and sinduvāraka trees; various kinds of trees—today we abandon them.”

2143.

2143.

“Assatthā [V 7.0322] panasā ceme, nigrodhā ca kapitthanā;

Vividhāni phalajātāni, tāni ajja jahāmase.

"These are the Bodhi trees, the breadfruit and banyan trees, and wood-apple trees; the various kinds of fruit—today we abandon them."

2144.

2144.

“Ime tiṭṭhanti ārāmā, ayaṃ sītūdakā nadī;

Yatthassu pubbe kīḷāma, tāni ajja jahāmase.

“Here stand these groves, here flows this cool-watered river where we used to play together; today we abandon them.”

2145.

2145.

“Vividhāni pupphajātāni, asmiṃ uparipabbate;

Yānassu pubbe dhārema, tāni ajja jahāmase.

“Various kinds of flowers are on this mountain height; those which we formerly wore, today we abandon them.”

2146.

2146.

“Vividhāni phalajātāni, asmiṃ uparipabbate;

Yānassu pubbe bhuñjāma, tāni ajja jahāmase.

“Various kinds of fruits are on this mountain height; those which we formerly ate, today we abandon them.”

2147.

2147.

“Ime no hatthikā assā, balibaddā ca no ime;

Yehissu pubbe kīḷāma, tāni ajja jahāmase”ti.

“These are our toy elephants, horses, and oxen with which we formerly played; today we abandon them.”

Tattha [P 6.0551][M 7.0331] pumunāti bhave vicarantena purisena. Labbhāti labhitabbaṃ. Taṃ me dukkhataraṃ itoti yaṃ me ammaṃ passituṃ alabhantassa dukkhaṃ, taṃ ito pothanadukkhato sataguṇena sahassaguṇena satasahassaguṇena dukkhataraṃ. Rucchatīti rodissati. Aḍḍharatte va ratte vāti aḍḍharatte vā sakalaratte vā amhe saritvā ciraṃ rodissati. Avasucchatīti appodakā kunnadī avasussati. Yathā sā khippameva sussati, evaṃ aruṇe uggacchanteyeva sussitvā marissatīti adhippāyenevamāha. Vedisāti olambanasākhā. Tānīti yesaṃ no mūlapupphaphalāni gaṇhantehi ciraṃ kīḷitaṃ, tāni ajja ubhopi mayaṃ jahāma. Hatthikāti tātena amhākaṃ kīḷanatthāya katā hatthikā.

Therein, ‘pumunā’ means by a person wandering in existence. ‘Labbhā’ means what is to be obtained. ‘Taṃ me dukkhataraṃ ito’ means the sorrow of not being able to see my mother is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold greater than the pain of being struck. ‘Rucchatī’ means she will weep. ‘Aḍḍharatte vā ratte vā’ means at midnight or throughout the night, she will weep for a long time, remembering us. ‘Avasucchatī’ refers to how a small stream with little water dries up; just as it dries up quickly, so too, as the sun rises, she will waste away and die—this is the intended meaning. ‘Vedisā’ refers to trees with hanging branches. ‘Tāni’ refers to those places with flowers and fruits where we played for a long time while gathering them; today we both abandon them. ‘Hatthikā’ refers to the toy elephants made by our father for our play.

Taṃ evaṃ paridevamānameva saddhiṃ bhaginiyā jūjako āgantvā pothento gahetvā pakkāmi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

While he was thus lamenting with his sister, Jūjaka came and, beating them, seized them and departed. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

2148.

2148.

“Nīyamānā kumārā te, pitaraṃ etadabravuṃ;

Ammaṃ ārogyaṃ vajjāsi, tvañca tāta sukhī bhava.

“As those children were being led away, they said this to their father: ‘Tell mother we are well, and may you, father, be happy.’”

2149.

2149.

“Ime [V 7.0323] no hatthikā assā, balibaddā ca no ime;

Tāni ammāya dajjesi, sokaṃ tehi vinessati.

“‘These are our toy elephants, horses, and oxen; give them to mother, and she will dispel her grief with them.’”

2150.

2150.

“Ime no hatthikā assā, balibaddā ca no ime;

Tāni ammā udikkhantī, sokaṃ paṭivinessatī”ti.

"'These are our toy elephants, horses, and oxen; seeing them, mother will dispel her sorrow.'"

Tadā bodhisattassa putte ārabbha balavasoko uppajji, hadayamaṃsaṃ uṇhaṃ ahosi. So kesarasīhena gahitamattavāraṇo viya rāhumukhaṃ paviṭṭhacando viya ca kampamāno sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ asakkonto assupuṇṇehi nettehi paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā kalunaṃ paridevi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

At that time, intense grief concerning his children arose in the Bodhisatta, and his heart grew hot with anguish. Like a wild elephant in musth seized by a maned lion, or like the full moon entering the mouth of Rāhu, he trembled and, unable to maintain his composure, with eyes full of tears, he entered the leaf-hut and lamented pitifully. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

2151.

2151.

“Tato vessantaro rājā, dānaṃ datvāna khattiyo;

Paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā, kalunaṃ paridevayī”ti.

“Then King Vessantara, the Khattiya, having given the gift, entered the leaf-hut and lamented pitifully.”

Tato parā mahāsattassa vilāpagāthā honti –

Then followed these verses of lamentation by the Great Being:

2152.

2152.

“Kaṃ nvajja chātā tasitā, uparucchanti dārakā;

Sāyaṃ saṃvesanākāle, ko ne dassati bhojanaṃ.

“To whom will the hungry and thirsty children cry today? At the evening mealtime, who will give them food?”

2153.

2153.

“Kaṃ [M 7.0332] nvajja chātā tasitā, uparucchanti dārakā;

Sāyaṃ saṃvesanākāle, ‘ammā chātamha detha no’.

"Whom now will the hungry, thirsty children cry to? In the evening, at bedtime, they will say, 'Mother, we are hungry, give us something.'"

2154.

2154.

“Kathaṃ [P 6.0552] nu pathaṃ gacchanti, pattikā anupāhanā;

Santā sūnehi pādehi, ko ne hatthe gahessati.

“How will they walk the path on foot and without sandals? Exhausted, with swollen feet, who will take them by the hand?”

2155.

2155.

“Kathaṃ nu so na lajjeyya, sammukhā paharaṃ mama;

Adūsakānaṃ puttānaṃ, alajjī vata brāhmaṇo.

“How is that brahmin not ashamed, striking my innocent children in my very presence? Shameless, indeed, is that brahmin!”

2156.

2156.

“Yopi me dāsidāsassa, añño vā pana pesiyo;

Tassāpi suvihīnassa, ko lajjī paharissati.

“Even if it were a slave of my female slave, or any other servant, what person with a sense of shame would strike even one so lowly?”

2157.

2157.

“Vārijasseva [V 7.0324] me sato, baddhassa kumināmukhe;

Akkosati paharati, piye putte apassato”ti.

“Like a fish caught at the mouth of a weir, while I am here, he reviles and strikes my beloved children before my very eyes.”

Tattha kaṃ nvajjāti kaṃ nu ajja. Uparucchantīti saṭṭhiyojanamaggaṃ gantvā uparodissanti. Saṃvesanākāleti mahājanassa parivesanākāle. Kone dassatīti ko nesaṃ bhojanaṃ dassati. Kathaṃ nu pathaṃ gacchantīti kathaṃ nu saṭṭhiyojanamaggaṃ gamissanti. Pattikāti hatthiyānādīhi virahitā. Anupāhanāti upāhanamattenapi viyuttā sukhumālapādā. Gahessatīti kilamathavinodanatthāya ko gaṇhissati. Dāsidāsassāti dāsiyā dāso assa. Añño vā pana pesiyoti tassapi dāso, tassapi dāsoti evaṃ dāsapatidāsaparamparāya “yo mayhaṃ catuttho pesiyo pesanakārako assa, tassa evaṃ suvihīnassapi ayaṃ vessantarassa dāsapatidāso”ti ñatvā. Ko lajjīti ko lajjāsampanno pahareyya, yuttaṃ nu kho tassa nillajjassa mama putte paharitunti. Vārijassevāti kumināmukhe baddhassa macchasseva sato mama. Apassatoti a-kāro nipātamatto, passantasseva piyaputte akkosati ceva paharati ca, aho vata dāruṇoti.

Herein, `kaṃ nvajjā` means `kaṃ nu ajja`. `Uparucchanti` means, having gone a sixty-yojana path, they will lament. `Saṃvesanākāle` means at the time of serving food to the great assembly. `Ko ne dassati` means who will give them food? `Kathaṃ nu pathaṃ gacchanti` means how will they travel the sixty-yojana path? `Pattikā` means being without elephants, vehicles, and the like. `Anupāhanā` means being without even sandals, having delicate feet. `Gahessati` means who will take them for the purpose of relieving their fatigue? `Dāsidāsassa` means he would be the slave of a female slave. `Añño vā pana pesiyo` means his slave too, his slave as well—thus, in the lineage of slaves upon slaves, knowing, 'This is a slave of Vessantara's slave, so utterly destitute, even if he were my fourth messenger.' `Ko lajjī` means what person endowed with shame would strike? Is it indeed fitting for that shameless one to strike my children? `Vārijasseva` means of me, being like a fish bound at the mouth of a fish-trap. `Apassato` means the 'a' is merely a particle; it means even while seeing his beloved children, he reviles and strikes them. Alas, how cruel!

Athassa kumāresu sinehena evaṃ parivitakko udapādi “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo mama putte ativiya viheṭheti, sokaṃ sandhāretuṃ na sakkomi, brāhmaṇaṃ anubandhitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā ānessāmi te kumāre”ti[M 7.0333]. Tato “aṭṭhānametaṃ kumārānaṃ pīḷanaṃ atidukkhanti dānaṃ datvā pacchānutappaṃ nāma sataṃ dhammo na hotī”ti cintesi. Tadatthajotanā imā dve parivitakkagāthā nāma honti –

Then, out of affection for his children, this reflection arose in him: ‘This brahmin torments my children excessively; I cannot bear the sorrow. I shall pursue the brahmin, put him to death, and bring back those children.’ Then he reflected: ‘The suffering of these children is extremely painful. But to regret a gift after having given it is not the way of the good.’ To illuminate this meaning, there are these two verses of reflection:

2158.

2158.

“Adu cāpaṃ gahetvāna, khaggaṃ bandhiya vāmato;

Ānessāmi sake putte, puttānañhi vadho dukho.

Taking up the bow and binding the sword on my left, I will bring back my own children, for the slaying of one's children is painful.

2159.

2159.

“Aṭṭhānametaṃ dukkharūpaṃ, yaṃ kumārā vihaññare;

Satañca dhammamaññāya, ko datvā anutappatī”ti.

It is an impossible and painful thing that the children should be tormented. But knowing the way of the good, who, having given, would then regret?

Tattha satanti pubbabodhisattānaṃ paveṇidhammaṃ.

Herein, `sataṃ` means the traditional way of the previous Bodhisattas.

So kira tasmiṃ khaṇe bodhisattānaṃ paveṇiṃ anussari. Tato “sabbabodhisattānaṃ dhanapariccāgaṃ[V 7.0325], aṅgapariccāgaṃ[P 6.0553], puttapariccāgaṃ, bhariyapariccāgaṃ, jīvitapariccāganti ime pañca mahāpariccāge apariccajitvā buddhabhūtapubbo nāma natthi. Ahampi tesaṃ abbhantaro homi, mayāpi piyaputtadhītaro adatvā na sakkā buddhena bhavitu”nti cintetvā “kiṃ tvaṃ vessantara paresaṃ dāsatthāya dinnaputtānaṃ dukkhabhāvaṃ na jānāsi, yena brāhmaṇaṃ anubandhitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpessāmīti saññaṃ uppādesi, dānaṃ datvā pacchānutappo nāma tava nānurūpo”ti evaṃ attānaṃ paribhāsitvā “sacepi eso kumāre māressati, dinnakālato paṭṭhāya mama na kiñci hotī”ti daḷhasamādānaṃ adhiṭṭhāya paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā paṇṇasāladvāre pāsāṇaphalake kañcanapaṭimā viya nisīdi. Jūjakopi bodhisattassa sammukhe kumāre pothetvā neti. Tato kumāro vilapanto āha –

At that moment, it is said, he recalled the tradition of the Bodhisattas. Then he thought: ‘Without having made these five great relinquishments—the relinquishment of wealth, the relinquishment of limbs, the relinquishment of children, the relinquishment of a wife, and the relinquishment of life—no one has ever attained Buddhahood. I too am among them. Without giving away my beloved son and daughter, it is not possible to become a Buddha.’ Having thought thus, he admonished himself: ‘Vessantara, do you not know the suffering of children given into slavery? Why did you produce the thought, “I will pursue the brahmin and put him to death”? To regret a gift after giving it is not fitting for you.’ Having thus reproached himself, he made a firm resolve: ‘Even if he kills the children, from the moment they were given, they are no longer mine.’ Having made this resolution, he came out of the leaf-hut and sat on a stone slab at the door like a golden statue. Jūjaka, in front of the Bodhisatta, beat the children and led them away. Then the prince, weeping, said:

2160.

2160.

“Saccaṃ kirevamāhaṃsu, narā ekacciyā idha;

Yassa natthi sakā mātā, yathā natthi tatheva so.

“Truly, it is said by some people here: ‘One who has no mother is as if he does not exist at all.’”

2161.

2161.

“Ehi kaṇhe marissāma, natthattho jīvitena no;

Dinnamhāti janindena, brāhmaṇassa dhanesino;

Accāyikassa luddassa, yo no gāvova sumbhati.

“Come, Kaṇhā, let us die; there is no purpose in our living. We have been given by the king to a wealth-seeking brahmin, violent and cruel, who strikes us as if we were cattle.”

2162.

2162.

“Ime te jambukā rukkhā, vedisā sinduvārakā;

Vividhāni rukkhajātāni, tāni kaṇhe jahāmase.

“These rose-apple trees, the water-willow and sinduvāraka trees, various kinds of trees—these, O Kaṇhā, we now abandon.”

2163.

2163.

“Assatthā [M 7.0334] panasā ceme, nigrodhā ca kapitthanā;

Vividhāni phalajātāni, tāni kaṇhe jahāmase.

“These holy fig, jackfruit, banyan, and wood-apple trees, with various kinds of fruits—these, O Kaṇhā, we now abandon.”

2164.

2164.

“Ime tiṭṭhanti ārāmā, ayaṃ sītūdakā nadī;

Yatthassu pubbe kīḷāma, tāni kaṇhe jahāmase.

These groves stand here, this river of cool water where we formerly played—these, O Kaṇhā, we now leave behind.

2165.

2165.

“Vividhāni pupphajātāni, asmiṃ uparipabbate;

Yānassu pubbe dhārema, tāni kaṇhe jahāmase.

The various kinds of flowers upon this mountain peak, which we formerly wore—these, O Kaṇhā, we now leave behind.

2166.

2166.

“Vividhāni [V 7.0326] phalajātāni, asmiṃ uparipabbate;

Yānassu pubbe bhuñjāma, tāni kaṇhe jahāmase.

The various kinds of fruits upon this mountain peak, which we formerly ate—these, O Kaṇhā, we now leave behind.

2167.

2167.

“Ime no hatthikā assā, balibaddā ca no ime;

Yehissu pubbe kīḷāma, tāni kaṇhe jahāmase”ti.

These our toy elephants and horses, and these our oxen, with which we formerly played—these, O Kaṇhā, we now leave behind.

Tattha yassāti yassa santike sakā mātā natthi. Pitā atthi, yathā natthiyeva.

Herein, `yassa` means one in whose presence his own mother is not. The father is present, yet it is just as if he were not.

Puna brāhmaṇo ekasmiṃ visamaṭṭhāne pakkhalitvā pati. Tesaṃ hatthato bandhanavalli muccitvā gatā. Te pahaṭakukkuṭā viya kampantā palāyitvā ekavegeneva pitu santikaṃ āgamiṃsu. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Again, the Brahmin slipped in an uneven place and fell. The vine binding their hands was released and fell away. Trembling like chickens frightened by a stick, they fled and in a single rush came to their father's presence. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

2168.

2168.

“Nīyamānā kumārā te, brāhmaṇassa pamuñciya;

Tena tena padhāviṃsu, jālī kaṇhājinā cubho”ti.

Those children, being led away, having been released from the brahmin, ran in that very direction—both Jāli and Kaṇhājinā.

Tattha [P 6.0554] tena tenāti tena muttakhaṇena yena disābhāgena tesaṃ pitā atthi, tena padhāviṃsu, padhāvitvā pitu santikaññeva āgamiṃsūti attho.

Herein, `tena tena` means: at that very moment of being released, they ran in that direction where their father was. Having run, they came right to their father's presence—this is the meaning.

Jūjako vegenuṭṭhāya vallidaṇḍahattho kappuṭṭhānaggi viya avattharanto āgantvā “ativiya palāyituṃ chekā tumhe”ti hatthe bandhitvā puna nesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Jūjaka, rising swiftly, with the vine and stick in hand, came rushing upon them like the world-destroying fire. 'You are very clever at running and hiding!' he said, and binding their hands tightly with the vine, he led them away again. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

2169.

2169.

“Tato [M 7.0335] so rajjumādāya, daṇḍañcādāya brāhmaṇo;

Ākoṭayanto te neti, sivirājassa pekkhato”ti.

Then that brahmin, taking a rope and also a stick, led them away, beating them, as the king of the Sivis looked on.

Evaṃ nīyamānesu kaṇhājinā nivattitvā olokentī pitarā saddhiṃ sallapi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

As they were thus being led away, Kaṇhājinā, turning back and looking, lamented to her father. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

2170.

2170.

“Taṃ taṃ kaṇhājināvoca, ayaṃ maṃ tāta brāhmaṇo;

Laṭṭhiyā paṭikoṭeti, ghare jātaṃva dāsiyaṃ.

To him Kaṇhājinā said: 'Father, this Brahmin strikes me with a stick like a slave-girl born in his house.'

2171.

2171.

“Na [V 7.0327] cāyaṃ brāhmaṇo tāta, dhammikā honti brāhmaṇā;

Yakkho brāhmaṇavaṇṇena, khādituṃ tāta neti no;

Nīyamāne pisācena, kiṃ nu tāta udikkhasī”ti.

'This is no Brahmin, father; for Brahmins are righteous. This is a yakkha in the guise of a Brahmin who leads us away to devour us, father. While we are being led away by this demon, why, father, do you just look on?'

Tattha tanti taṃ passamānaṃ nisinnaṃ pitaraṃ sivirājānaṃ. Dāsiyanti dāsikaṃ. Khāditunti khādanatthāya ayaṃ no giridvāraṃ asampatteyeva ubhohi cakkhūhi rattalohitabinduṃ paggharantehi khādissāmīti neti, tvañca khādituṃ vā pacituṃ vā nīyamāne kiṃ amhe udikkhasi, sabbadā sukhito hohīti paridevi.

Herein, `taṃ` refers to her father, the king of the Sivis, who sat watching. `Dāsiyaṃ` means a female slave. `Khādituṃ` means for the purpose of eating; he leads us away thinking, 'Before they even reach the mountain pass, I will devour them with both my eyes streaming drops of red blood.' And she lamented, 'While we are being led away to be devoured or to be cooked, why do you look on at us? May you be happy always!'

Daharakumārikāya vilapantiyā kampamānāya gacchantiyā mahāsattassa balavasoko uppajji, hadayavatthu uṇhaṃ ahosi. Nāsikāya appahontiyā mukhena uṇhe assāsapassāse vissajjesi. Assūni lohitabindūni hutvā nettehi nikkhamiṃsu. So “idaṃ evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ sinehadosena jātaṃ, na aññena kāraṇena. Sinehaṃ akatvā majjhatteneva bhavitabba”nti tathārūpaṃ sokaṃ attano ñāṇabalena vinodetvā pakatinisinnākāreneva nisīdi. Giridvāraṃ asampattāyeva kumārikā vilapantī agamāsi.

As the young girl lamented and went along trembling, intense sorrow arose in the Great Being; his heart-base grew hot. Since his nose could not vent the heat, he exhaled hot breaths through his mouth. Tears, like drops of blood, flowed from his eyes. He thought: 'This suffering is born from the fault of affection for my children; it is for no other reason. If I were equanimous, this would not happen.' Having dispelled that grief by the power of his wisdom, he sat in his usual posture. Before reaching the mountain gate, the girl went on lamenting.

2172.

2172.

“Ime no pādakā dukkhā, dīgho caddhā suduggamo;

Nīce colambate sūriyo, brāhmaṇo ca dhāreti no.

“Our little feet are sore, the road is long and hard to travel; the sun hangs low, and the Brahmin drags us on.

2173.

2173.

“Okandāmase [P 6.0555] bhūtāni, pabbatāni vanāni ca;

Sarassa sirasā vandāma, supatitthe ca āpake.

“We appeal to the spirits, the mountains, and the forests. With our heads, we prostrate to the lake and the waters at the good fords.

2174.

2174.

“Tiṇalatāni osadhyo, pabbatāni vanāni ca;

Ammaṃ ārogyaṃ vajjātha, ayaṃ no neti brāhmaṇo.

“Grasses, creepers, and medicinal herbs, mountains and forests—tell our mother we are well, for this Brahmin leads us away.

2175.

2175.

“Vajjantu [M 7.0336] bhonto ammañca, maddiṃ asmāka mātaraṃ;

Sace anupatitukāmāsi, khippaṃ anupatiyāsi no.

“May you sirs tell our mother Maddī: ‘If you wish to follow us, follow quickly.’

2176.

2176.

“Ayaṃ ekapadī eti, ujuṃ gacchati assamaṃ;

Tamevānupateyyāsi, api passesi ne lahuṃ.

“This single path leads straight to the hermitage; you should follow it, and perhaps you will see us soon.”

2177.

2177.

“Aho [V 7.0328] vata re jaṭinī, vanamūlaphalahārike;

Suññaṃ disvāna assamaṃ, taṃ te dukkhaṃ bhavissati.

“Alas, O matted-haired mother, gatherer of forest roots and fruits; upon seeing the empty hermitage, you will suffer great distress.

2178.

2178.

“Ativelaṃ nu ammāya, uñchā laddho anappako;

Yā no baddhe na jānāsi, brāhmaṇena dhanesinā.

“Our mother has spent too much time gathering many roots and fruits; she does not know we are bound by this wealth-seeking Brahmin.

2179.

2179.

“Accāyikena luddena, yo no gāvova sumbhati;

Apajja ammaṃ passemu, sāyaṃ uñchāto āgataṃ.

“By this urgent and cruel man, who beats us like cattle, may we yet see our mother returned in the evening from her gathering.”

2180.

2180.

“Dajjā ammā brāhmaṇassa, phalaṃ khuddena missitaṃ;

Tadāyaṃ asito dhāto, na bāḷhaṃ dhārayeyya no.

“Mother would give the Brahmin fruits mixed with honey; then, having eaten his fill, he would not lead us away so harshly. Now our feet are blistered, and the Brahmin leads us away cruelly.”

2181.

2181.

“Sūnā ca vata no pādā, bāḷhaṃ dhāreti brāhmaṇo;

Iti tattha vilapiṃsu, kumārā mātugiddhino”ti.

“Indeed, our feet are swollen, and the brahmin drags us forcefully; thus lamented the princes, who were longing for their mother.”

Tattha pādakāti khuddakapādā. Okandāmaseti avakandāma, apacitiṃ nīcavuttiṃ dassentā jānāpema. Sarassāti imassa padumasarassa pariggāhakāneva nāgakulāni sirasā vandāma. Supatitthe ca āpaketi supatitthāya nadiyā adhivatthā devatāpi vandāma. Tiṇalatānīti tiṇāni ca olambakalatāyo ca. Osadhyoti osadhiyo. Sabbattha adhivatthā devatā sandhāyevamāha. Anupatitukāmāsīti sacepi sā amhākaṃ padānupadaṃ āgantukāmāsi. Api passesi ne lahunti api nāma etāya ekapadiyā anupatamānā puttake te lahuṃ passeyyāsīti evaṃ taṃ vadeyyāthāti. Jaṭinīti baddhajaṭaṃ ārabbha mātaraṃ parammukhālapanena ālapantī āha. Ativelanti pamāṇātikkantaṃ katvā. Uñchāti uñchācariyāya[M 7.0337]. Phalanti vanamūlaphalāphalaṃ. Khuddena missitanti khuddakamadhunā missitaṃ. Asitoti asitāsano paribhuttaphalo. Dhātoti suhito. Na bāḷhaṃ dhārayeyya noti na no bāḷhaṃ vegena nayeyya. Mātugiddhinoti mātari giddhena samannāgatā balavasinehā evaṃ vilaviṃsūti.

Here, 'pādakā' means small feet. 'Okandāmase' means we call out to; showing reverence and a humble state, we make it known. 'Sarassa' means we bow our heads to the Nāga clans who are the guardians of this lotus lake. 'Supatitthe ca āpake' means we also revere the deities dwelling by the river with good fords. 'Tiṇalatāni' means grasses and hanging creepers. 'Osadhyo' means medicinal herbs. Everywhere, he speaks thus, referring to the resident deities. 'Anupatitukāmāsi' means if she wishes to come following in our footsteps. 'Api passesi ne lahun'ti means 'perhaps, following this single-file path, you might see your sons soon'—thus you should tell her. 'Jaṭinī' means he speaks addressing his mother, who has matted hair, with an indirect address. 'Ativelaṃ' means having exceeded the measure. 'Uñchā' means by the practice of gleaning. 'Phalaṃ' means forest roots and fruits. 'Khuddena missitaṃ' means mixed with a little honey. 'Asito' means having eaten his meal, having consumed the fruit. 'Dhāto' means satisfied. 'Na bāḷhaṃ dhārayeyya no' means he would not lead us away forcefully, with great speed. 'Mātugiddhino' means endowed with longing for their mother, with strong affection, thus they lamented.

Dārakapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the chapter on the children is concluded.

Maddīpabbavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Maddī Chapter

Yaṃ [V 7.0329][P 6.0556] pana taṃ raññā pathaviṃ unnādetvā brāhmaṇassa piyaputtesu dinnesu yāva brahmalokā ekakolāhalaṃ jātaṃ, tenapi bhijjamānahadayā viya himavantavāsino devā tesaṃ brāhmaṇena niyamānānaṃ taṃ vilāpaṃ sutvā mantayiṃsu “sace maddī kālasseva assamaṃ āgamissati, tattha puttake adisvā vessantaraṃ pucchitvā brāhmaṇassa dinnabhāvaṃ sutvā balavasinehena padānupadaṃ dhāvitvā mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhaveyyā”ti. Atha te tayo devaputte “tumhe sīhabyagghadīpivese nimminitvā deviyā āgamanamaggaṃ sannirumbhitvā yāciyamānāpi yāva sūriyatthaṅgamanā maggaṃ adatvā yathā candālokena assamaṃ pavisissati, evamassā sīhādīnampi aviheṭhanatthāya ārakkhaṃ susaṃvihitaṃ kareyyāthā”ti āṇāpesuṃ. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Now, when the King had caused the earth to resound by giving his beloved children to the Brahmin, a great uproar arose reaching as far as the Brahma-world. Hearing the lamentation of the children being led away by the Brahmin, the deities dwelling in the Himavanta, their hearts as if breaking, deliberated: 'If Maddī returns to the hermitage early and, not seeing her children, asks Vessantara and hears they were given to the Brahmin, she will follow their tracks out of intense love. If she reaches the deep forest and meets with danger from wild beasts, she will suffer a great loss alone.' Then they commanded three sons of the gods: 'Taking the forms of a lion, a tiger, and a leopard, block the path of the Queen's return. Even if she begs, do not give way until sunset, so that she may enter the hermitage by moonlight. Also, provide well-arranged protection so that she is not harmed by other lions and beasts.' To clarify this, the Teacher said:

2182.

2182.

“Tesaṃ lālappitaṃ sutvā, tayo vāḷā vane migā;

Sīho byaggho ca dīpi ca, idaṃ vacanamabravuṃ.

“Having heard their lamentation, three wild beasts in the forest—a lion, a tiger, and a leopard—spoke this word:

2183.

2183.

“Mā heva no rājaputtī, sāyaṃ uñchāto āgamā;

Mā hevamhāka nibbhoge, heṭhayittha vane migā.

“Let the princess not return from her gleaning in the evening; let no wild beast in the forest harm her in our domain.”

2184.

2184.

“Sīho ce naṃ viheṭheyya, byaggho dīpi ca lakkhaṇaṃ;

Neva jālīkumārassa, kuto kaṇhājinā siyā;

Ubhayeneva jīyetha, patiṃ putte ca lakkhaṇā”ti.

“If a lion, a tiger, or a leopard were to harm her, O auspicious one, then there would be no Jālikumāra for her, much less Kaṇhājinā. She, O auspicious one, would be deprived of both her husband and her children.”

Tattha [M 7.0338] idaṃ vacanamabravunti “tumhe tayo janā sīho ca byaggho ca dīpi cāti evaṃ tayo vāḷā vane migā hothā”ti idaṃ tā devatā tayo devaputte vacanamabravuṃ. Mā heva noti maddī rājaputtī uñchāto sāyaṃ mā āgami, candālokena sāyaṃ āgacchatūti vadanti. Mā hevamhāka nibbhogeti amhākaṃ nibbhoge vijite vanaghaṭāyaṃ mā naṃ kocipi vane vāḷamigo viheṭhesi. Na yathā viheṭheti, evamassā ārakkhaṃ gaṇhathāti vadanti. Sīho ce nanti sace hi taṃ anārakkhaṃ sīhādīsu koci viheṭheyya, athassā jīvitakkhayaṃ pattāya neva jālikumāro assa, kuto kaṇhājinā siyā. Evaṃ sā lakkhaṇasampannā ubhayeneva jīyetha patiṃ putte cāti dvīhi koṭṭhāsehi jīyetheva, tasmā susaṃvihitamassā ārakkhaṃ karothāti.

Here, ‘spoke this word’ means: ‘You three beings—a lion, a tiger, and a leopard—thus, you three shall be wild beasts in the forest.’ This is what the deities said to the three sons of the gods. Regarding ‘Let not’, they say: ‘Let Princess Maddī not come from gleaning in the evening; let her come in the evening by moonlight.’ Regarding ‘in our domain’, they say: ‘Let no wild beast in the forest harm her in our domain, in this forest region.’ They say: “Take up her protection so that she is not harmed.” Regarding ‘If a lion’, they say: ‘If indeed any of the lions or other beasts should harm her while she is unprotected, then, having met with the destruction of her life, there would be no Jālikumāra for her, much less Kaṇhājinā. Thus she, endowed with auspicious marks, would be deprived in two ways—of her husband and her sons. Therefore, arrange well-prepared protection for her.’

Atha [V 7.0330] te tayo devaputtā “sādhū”ti tāsaṃ devatānaṃ taṃ vacanaṃ paṭissuṇitvā sīhabyagghadīpino hutvā āgantvā tassā āgamanamagge paṭipāṭiyā nipajjiṃsu. Maddīpi kho “ajja mayā dussupino [P 6.0557] diṭṭho, kālasseva mūlaphalāphalaṃ gahetvā assamaṃ gamissāmī”ti kampamānā mūlaphalāphalāni upadhāresi. Athassā hatthato khaṇitti pati, tathā aṃsato uggīvañca pati, dakkhiṇakkhica phandati, phalino rukkhā aphalā viya aphalā ca phalino viya khāyiṃsu, dasa disā na paññāyiṃsu. Sā “kiṃ nu kho idaṃ, pubbe abhūtapubbaṃ ajja me hoti, kiṃ bhavissati, mayhaṃ vā antarāyo bhavissati, mama puttānaṃ vā, udāhu vessantarassā”ti cintetvā āha –

Then those three sons of the gods, saying “Excellent” and assenting to the words of those deities, took the forms of a lion, a tiger, and a leopard, and lay down in succession on her path. Maddī thought: “Today I have seen an inauspicious dream and felt uneasy. I will gather roots and fruits and return before sunset.” Trembling, she looked for roots and fruits. Then the digging tool fell from her hand, and the basket and hook fell from her shoulder; her right eye twitched; fruit-bearing trees appeared as if fruitless, and fruitless trees appeared as if fruit-bearing; the ten directions became unclear. She thought: “What is this? This has never happened to me before. Is there danger for me, or for my children, or for King Vessantara?” Reflecting thus, she said:

2185.

2185.

“Khaṇittikaṃ me patitaṃ, dakkhiṇakkhi ca phandati;

Aphalā phalino rukkhā, sabbā muyhanti me disā”ti.

“My digging tool has fallen, and my right eye twitches; fruit-bearing trees appear fruitless, and all directions are confusing to me.”

Evaṃ sā paridevantī pakkāmi.

Lamenting thus, she went on.

2186.

2186.

“Tassā sāyanhakālasmiṃ, assamāgamanaṃ pati;

Atthaṅgatamhi sūriye, vāḷā panthe upaṭṭhahuṃ.

“In the evening, as she was returning to the hermitage, when the sun had set, the wild beasts appeared on the path.”

2187.

2187.

“Nīce colambate sūriyo, dūre ca vata assamo;

Yañca nesaṃ ito hassaṃ, taṃ te bhuñjeyyu bhojanaṃ.

“The sun hangs low, and indeed the hermitage is far. The fruits and roots I brought for them from here, they would have been eating that meal by now.”

2188.

2188.

“So [M 7.0339] nūna khattiyo eko, paṇṇasālāya acchati;

Tosento dārake chāte, mamaṃ disvā anāyatiṃ.

“Surely that prince sits alone in the leaf hut, comforting the hungry children, seeing that I have not returned.”

2189.

2189.

“Te nūna puttakā mayhaṃ, kapaṇāya varākiyā;

Sāyaṃ saṃvesanākāle, khīrapītāva acchare.

“Surely those children of mine, poor and wretched, at the time of evening rest, remain like those longing for milk.”

2190.

2190.

“Te nūna puttakā mayhaṃ, kapaṇāya varākiyā;

Sāyaṃ saṃvesanākāle, vāripītāva acchare.

“Surely those children of me, a poor and wretched woman, remain at evening's bedtime like young ones who have drunk water.”

2191.

2191.

“Te [V 7.0331] nūna puttakā mayhaṃ, kapaṇāya varākiyā;

“Surely those children of me, a poor and wretched woman,”

Paccuggatā maṃ tiṭṭhanti, vacchā bālāva mātaraṃ.

“They would stand to meet me, like young calves meeting their mother.”

2192.

2192.

“Te nūna puttakā mayhaṃ, kapaṇāya varākiyā;

“Surely those children of me, a poor and wretched woman,”

Paccuggatā maṃ tiṭṭhanti, haṃsāvuparipallale.

“Stand to greet me, like swans upon a pond.”

2193.

2193.

“Te nūna puttakā mayhaṃ, kapaṇāya varākiyā;

“Surely those children of me, a poor and wretched woman,”

Paccuggatā maṃ tiṭṭhanti, assamassāvidūrato.

“Stand to greet me, not far from the hermitage.”

2194.

2194.

“Ekāyano ekapatho, sarā sobbhā ca passato;

Aññaṃ maggaṃ na passāmi, yena gaccheyya assamaṃ.

“The path is narrow and single, with lakes and chasms on either side; I see no other path by which I might go to the hermitage.”

2195.

2195.

“Migā namatthu rājāno, kānanasmiṃ mahabbalā;

Dhammena bhātaro hotha, maggaṃ me detha yācitā.

“Homage to you, O kings of beasts, mighty in the forest! Be my brothers in righteousness; grant me the path, I entreat you.”

2196.

2196.

“Avaruddhassāhaṃ bhariyā, rājaputtassa sirīmato;

Taṃ cāhaṃ nātimaññāmi, rāmaṃ sītāvanubbatā.

“I am the wife of the glorious prince who has been exiled; and I do not disregard him, following him as Sītā followed Rāma.”

2197.

2197.

“Tumhe ca putte passatha, sāyaṃ saṃvesanaṃ pati;

Ahañca putte passeyyaṃ, jāliṃ kaṇhājinaṃ cubho.

“You see your own young when they go to rest in the evening; may I also see my children, both Jāli and Kaṇhājina.”

2198.

2198.

“Bahuṃ cidaṃ mūlaphalaṃ, bhakkho cāyaṃ anappako;

Tato upaḍḍhaṃ dassāmi, maggaṃ me detha yācitā.

“Here are many roots and fruits, and this food is not a little; of this I will give you half, grant me the path, I entreat you.”

2199.

2199.

“Rājaputtī [P 6.0558] ca no mātā, rājaputto ca no pitā;

Dhammena bhātaro hotha, maggaṃ me detha yācitā”ti.

“I am a princess by birth and my husband is a prince. Be my brothers in righteousness; grant me the path, I entreat you.”

Tattha [M 7.0340] tassāti tassā mama. Assamāgamanaṃ patīti assamaṃ paṭicca sandhāya āgacchantiyā. Upaṭṭhahunti uṭṭhāya ṭhitā. Te kira paṭhamaṃ paṭipāṭiyā nipajjitvā tāya āgamanakāle uṭṭhāya vijambhitvā maggaṃ rumbhantā paṭipāṭiyā tiriyaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Yañca tesanti ahañca [V 7.0332] yaṃ ito mūlaphalāphalaṃ tesaṃ harissaṃ, tameva vessantaro ca ubho puttakā cāti te tayopi janā bhuñjeyyuṃ, aññaṃ tesaṃ bhojanaṃ natthi. Anāyatinti anāgacchantiṃ maṃ ñatvā ekakova nūna dārake tosento nisinno. Saṃvesanākāleti aññesu divasesu attano khādāpanapivāpanakāle khīrapītāvāti yathā khīrapītā migapotakā khīratthāya kanditvā taṃ alabhitvā kandantāva niddaṃ okkamanti, evaṃ me puttakā phalāphalatthāya kanditvā taṃ alabhitvā kandantāva niddaṃ upagatā bhavissantīti vadati.

Herein, ‘tassā’ refers to ‘of me.’ ‘Assamāgamanaṃ pati’ means ‘of her coming with the hermitage as her destination.’ ‘Upaṭṭhahuṃ’ means ‘they stood up.’ It is said that they first lay down in a row, and at the time of her arrival, they rose, stretched, and, blocking the path, stood sideways in a row. ‘Yañca tesaṃ’ means: ‘And whatever roots and fruits I would bring from here for them, that very thing Vessantara and both children—those three people—would eat; they have no other food.’ ‘Anāyatiṃ’ means: ‘Knowing that I am not coming, he must be sitting alone comforting the children.’ ‘Saṃvesanākāle’ means: ‘On other days, at their time of eating and drinking.’ ‘Khīrapītāva’ means: ‘Just as young deer that are milk-fed cry for milk and, not getting it, fall asleep while crying, so my children, crying for fruits and, not getting them, will have fallen asleep while crying’—so she says.

Vāripītāvāti yathā pipāsitā migapotakā pānīyatthāya kanditvā taṃ alabhitvā kandantāva niddaṃ okkamantīti imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Acchareti acchanti. Paccuggatā maṃ tiṭṭhantīti maṃ paccuggatā hutvā tiṭṭhanti. “Paccuggantunā”tipi pāṭho, paccuggantvāti attho. Ekāyanoti ekasseva ayano ekapadikamaggo. Ekapathoti so ca ekova, dutiyo natthi, okkamitvā gantuṃ na sakkā. Kasmā? Yasmā sarā sobbhā ca passato. Migā namatthūti sā aññaṃ maggaṃ adisvā “ete yācitvā paṭikkamāpessāmī”ti phalapacchiṃ sīsato otāretvā añjaliṃ paggayha namassamānā evamāha. Bhātaroti ahampi manussarājaputtī, tumhīpi migarājaputtā, iti me dhammena bhātaro hotha.

‘Vāripītāvā’—just as thirsty young deer, crying for a drink and, not receiving it, fall asleep still crying—the meaning should be understood in this same way. ‘Acchareti’ means ‘they remain.’ ‘Paccuggatā maṃ tiṭṭhantīti’ means ‘they stand having gone out to meet me.’ There is also the reading ‘paccuggantunā,’ meaning ‘having gone out to meet.’ ‘Ekāyanoti’ means ‘a single way,’ a single-file path. ‘Ekapathoti’ means it is the only one; there is no second, and one cannot step aside to proceed. Why? Because for one passing, there are lakes and chasms. ‘Migā namatthūti’—not seeing another path, she thinks, “Having entreated them, I will make them retreat,” and lowering the fruit basket from her head, she raises her joined hands in reverence and speaks thus. ‘Bhātaroti’ means ‘I too am a daughter of a human king, and you are sons of a deer king; thus, be my brothers in accordance with the Dhamma.’

Avaruddhassāti raṭṭhato pabbājitassa. Rāmaṃ sītāvanubbatāti yathā dasaratharājaputtaṃ rāmaṃ tassa kaniṭṭhabhaginī sītādevī tasseva aggamahesī hutvā taṃ anubbatā patidevatā hutvā appamattā upaṭṭhāsi, tathā ahampi vessantaraṃ upaṭṭhahāmi, nātimaññāmīti vadati. Tumhe cāti tumhe ca mayhaṃ maggaṃ datvā sāyaṃ gocaraggahaṇakāle putte passatha, ahañca attano putte passeyyaṃ, detha me magganthi yācati.

‘Avaruddhassāti’ means ‘of one banished from the kingdom.’ ‘Rāmaṃ sītāvanubbatāti’ means ‘just as Sītādevī, the younger sister of Dasaratha’s son, Rāma, became his chief queen and, devoted to him, regarding her husband as her deity, attended to him diligently, so too do I attend to Vessantara; I do not disrespect him’—so she says. ‘Tumhe cāti’ means ‘And you, having given me the path, may see your young at the evening time of foraging; and may I also see my own children. Give me the path’—thus she begs.

Atha [M 7.0341] te tayo devaputtā velaṃ oloketvā “idānissā maggaṃ dātuṃ velā”ti ñatvā uṭṭhāya apagacchiṃsu. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Then those three deities, observing the time and knowing, ‘Now is the time to open the path for her,’ rose and departed. To explain this matter, the Teacher said:

2200.

2200.

“Tassā lālappamānāya, bahuṃ kāruññasañhitaṃ;

Sutvā nelapatiṃ vācaṃ, vāḷā panthā apakkamu”nti.

“Hearing her lamenting voice, so full of pity, and her faultless words, the wild beasts departed from the path.”

Tattha nelapatinti na elapatiṃ elapātavirahitaṃ visaṭṭhaṃ madhuravācaṃ.

Herein, ‘nelapatiṃ’ means not ‘elapatiṃ’; it means speech that is free from stammering, distinct, and sweet.

Sāpi [V 7.0333] vāḷesu apagatesu assamaṃ agamāsi. Tadā ca puṇṇamuposatho hoti. Sā caṅkamanakoṭiṃ patvā yesu yesu ṭhānesu pubbe putte passati, tesu tesu ṭhānesu apassantī āha –

When the wild beasts had departed, she returned to the hermitage. That day was the full-moon Uposatha day. Reaching the head of the walking path, not seeing the children in those various places where she used to see them, she said:

2201.

2201.

“Imamhi [P 6.0559] naṃ padesamhi, puttakā paṃsukuṇṭhitā;

Paccuggatā maṃ tiṭṭhanti, vacchā bālāva mātaraṃ.

“In this very spot, my children, covered in dust, would stand to greet me, like young calves their mother.”

2202.

2202.

“Imamhi naṃ padesamhi, puttakā paṃsukuṇṭhitā;

Paccuggatā maṃ tiṭṭhanti, haṃsāvuparipallale.

“In this very spot, my children, begrimed with dust, would stand to greet me, like swans upon a pond.”

2203.

2203.

“Imamhi naṃ padesamhi, puttakā paṃsukuṇṭhitā;

Paccuggatā maṃ tiṭṭhanti, assamassāvidūrato.

“In this very spot, my children, begrimed with dust, would stand to greet me, not far from the hermitage.”

2204.

2204.

“Dve migā viya ukkaṇṇā, samantā mabhidhāvino;

Ānandino pamuditā, vaggamānāva kampare;

Tyajja putte na passāmi, jāliṃ kaṇhājinaṃ cubho.

“Like two deer with ears pricked up, running towards me from all sides, joyful and delighted, leaping and gambolling; today I do not see my children, both Jāli and Kaṇhājina.”

2205.

2205.

“Chakalīva migī chāpaṃ, pakkhī muttāva pañjarā;

Ohāya putte nikkhamiṃ, sīhīvāmisagiddhinī;

Tyajja putte na passāmi, jāliṃ kaṇhājinaṃ cubho.

“Like a goat leaving its kid, or a bird its nest, or a lioness seeking meat—I went out leaving my children behind. Today I do not see my children, both Jāli and Kaṇhājina.”

2206.

2206.

“Idaṃ nesaṃ padakkantaṃ, nāgānamiva pabbate;

Citakā parikiṇṇāyo, assamassāvidūrato;

Tyajja putte na passāmi, jāliṃ kaṇhājinaṃ cubho.

“Here are their footprints, like those of elephants on a mountain; their little play-mounds are scattered not far from the hermitage. Today I do not see my children, both Jāli and Kaṇhājina.”

2207.

2207.

“Vālikāyapi [M 7.0342] okiṇṇā, puttakā paṃsukuṇṭhitā;

Samantā abhidhāvanti, te na passāmi dārake.

“Even covered with sand, my children, begrimed with dust, used to run all around; those children I do not see.”

2208.

2208.

“Ye maṃ pure paccuṭṭhenti, araññā dūramāyatiṃ;

Tyajja putte na passāmi, jāliṃ kaṇhājinaṃ cubho.

“Those who used to run to meet me when I came from afar from the forest—today I do not see my children, both Jāli and Kaṇhājina.”

2209.

2209.

“Chakaliṃva [V 7.0334] migiṃ chāpā, paccuggantuna mātaraṃ;

Dūre maṃ pavilokenti, te na passāmi dārake.

“Like kids meeting a goat, or fawns a doe, they would look at me from afar—those children I do not see.”

2210.

2210.

“Idaṃ nesaṃ kīḷanakaṃ, patitaṃ paṇḍubeluvaṃ;

Tyajja putte na passāmi, jāliṃ kaṇhājinaṃ cubho.

“Here is their toy, a fallen yellow beluva fruit. Today I do not see my children, both Jāli and Kaṇhājina.”

2211.

2211.

“Thanā ca mayhime pūrā, uro ca sampadālati;

Tyajja putte na passāmi, jāliṃ kaṇhājinaṃ cubho.

“My breasts are full of milk, and my heart is breaking. Today I do not see my children, both Jāli and Kaṇhājina.”

2212.

2212.

“Ucchaṅgeko vicināti, thanamekāvalambati;

Tyajja putte na passāmi, jāliṃ kaṇhājinaṃ cubho.

One would search in my lap, the other would cling to my breast; today I do not see my children, Jāli and Kaṇhājina, both of them.

2213.

2213.

“Yassu sāyanhasamayaṃ, puttakā paṃsukuṇṭhitā;

Ucchaṅge me vivattanti, te na passāmi dārake.

“In the evening time, my children, begrimed with dust, used to roll about on my lap—those children I do not see.”

2214.

2214.

“Ayaṃ so assamo pubbe, samajjo paṭibhāti maṃ;

Tyajja putte apassantyā, bhamate viya assamo.

“This hermitage used to appear like a festive gathering to me; but today, not seeing my children, the hermitage seems to whirl about.”

2215.

2215.

“Kimidaṃ [P 6.0560] appasaddova, assamo paṭibhāti maṃ;

Kākolāpi na vassanti, matā me nūna dārakā.

“Why does this hermitage seem so silent to me? Even the crows do not cry out; surely my children are dead.”

2216.

2216.

“Kimidaṃ appasaddova, assamo paṭibhāti maṃ;

Sakuṇāpi na vassanti, matā me nūna dārakā”ti.

“Why does this hermitage seem so silent to me? Even the birds do not sing; surely my children are dead.”

Tattha nanti nipātamattaṃ. Paṃsukuṇṭhitāti paṃsumakkhitā. Paccuggatā manti maṃ paccuggatā hutvā. “Paccuggantunā”tipi pāṭho, paccuggantvāicceva attho. Ukkaṇṇāti yathā migapotakā mātaraṃ disvā kaṇṇe ukkhipitvā gīvaṃ pasāretvā mātaraṃ upagantvā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā samantā abhidhāvino. Vaggamānāva [M 7.0343] kamparetivajjamānāyeva mātu hadayamaṃsaṃ kampenti viya evaṃ pubbe mama puttā. Tyajjāti te ajja na passāmi. Chakalīva migī chāpanti yathā chakalī ca migī ca pañjarasaṅkhātā kulāvakā muttā pakkhī ca āmisagiddhinī sīhī ca attano chāpaṃ ohāya [V 7.0335] gocarāya pakkamanti, tathāhampi ohāya putte gocarāya nikkhaminti vadati. Idaṃ nesaṃ padakkantanti vassāratte sānupabbate nāgānaṃ padavalañjaṃ viya idaṃ nesaṃ kīḷanaṭṭhāne ādhāvanaparidhāvanapadakkantaṃ paññāyati. Citakāti sañcitanicitā kavālukapuñjā. Parikiṇṇāyoti vippakiṇṇāyo. Samantā mabhidhāvantīti aññesu divasesu samantā abhidhāvanti.

Here, 'nanti' is merely a particle. 'Paṃsukuṇṭhitā' means 'smeared with dust'. 'Paccuggatā maṃ' means 'having come forth to meet me'. There is also the reading 'paccuggantunā,' which has the same meaning as 'paccuggantvā' (having gone forth). 'Ukkaṇṇā' (with pricked ears) describes how young deer, upon seeing their mother, prick up their ears, stretch out their necks, approach their mother, and, delighted and joyful, run all around. 'Vaggamānāva kampare' (as if shaking with their bleating) means 'as if they were agitating and shaking even the heart-flesh of the mother'; thus were my children formerly. 'Tyajjā' means 'today I do not see them'. 'Chakalīva migī chāpaṃ' (like a doe her fawn) means: just as a chakalī bird and a doe, and a bird freed from its cage-like nest, and a lioness greedy for meat, abandon their young and go forth for food; so too, she says, 'I abandoned my children and went forth for food'. 'Idaṃ nesaṃ padakkantaṃ' (these are their tracks) means: just as the tracks of elephants on a mountain slope in the rainy season are visible, so too in their playground the tracks of their running about and circling are discernible. 'Citakā' means 'heaps of piled-up and accumulated potsherds'. 'Parikiṇṇāyo' means 'scattered about'. 'Samantā mabhidhāvanti' (they run all around me) means on other days they would run all around.

Paccuṭṭhentīti paccuggacchanti. Dūramāyatinti dūrato āgacchantiṃ. Chakaliṃva migiṃ chāpāti attano mātaraṃ chakaliṃ viya migiṃ viya ca chāpā. Idaṃ nesaṃ kīḷanakanti hatthirūpakādīhi kīḷantānaṃ idañca tesaṃ hatthato suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ kīḷanabeluvaṃ parigaḷitvā patitaṃ. Mayhimeti mayhaṃ ime thanā ca khīrassa pūrā. Uro ca sampadālatīti hadayañca phalati. Ucchaṅge me vivattantīti mama ucchaṅge āvattanti vivattanti. Samajjo paṭibhāti manti samajjaṭṭhānaṃ viya mayhaṃ upaṭṭhāti. Tyajjāti te ajja. Apassantyāti apassantiyā mama. Bhamate viyāti kulālacakkaṃ viya bhamati. Kākolāti vanakākā. Matā nūnāti addhā matā vā kenaci nītā vā bhavissanti. Sakuṇāti avasesasakuṇā.

'Paccuṭṭhenti' means 'they go to meet'. 'Dūramāyanti' means 'one coming from afar'. 'Chakaliṃva migiṃ chāpā' (like fawns a doe) means: the fawns are toward their mother as toward a chakalī or a doe. 'Idaṃ nesaṃ kīḷanakaṃ' (this their plaything) means: 'and this golden-colored beluva fruit, their plaything, has slipped and fallen from the hands of those playing with toy elephants and so forth'. 'Mayhime' means 'these breasts of mine are full of milk'. 'Uro ca sampadālati' means 'and my heart splits'. 'Ucchaṅge me vivattanti' means 'they turn and roll about on my lap'. 'Samajjo paṭibhāti maṃ' means 'it appears to me like a festival ground'. 'Tyajjā' means 'they today'. 'Apassantyā' means 'of me not seeing'. 'Bhamate viya' means 'it whirls like a potter’s wheel'. 'Kākolā' means 'forest crows'. 'Matā nūnā' means 'surely they are dead or have been carried off by someone'. 'Sakuṇā' means 'the remaining birds'.

Iti sā vilapantī mahāsattassa santikaṃ gantvā phalapacchiṃ otāretvā mahāsattaṃ tuṇhimāsīnaṃ disvā dārake cassa santike apassantī āha –

Lamenting thus, she went to the Great Being, set down her basket of fruit, and seeing the Great Being sitting in silence and not seeing the children near him, she said:

2217.

2217.

“Kimidaṃ tuṇhibhūtosi, api ratteva me mano;

Kākolāpi na vassanti, matā me nūna dārakā.

“Why are you silent? My mind is in a daze. Even the crows do not cry out; surely my children are dead.”

2218.

2218.

“Kimidaṃ tuṇhibhūtosi, api ratteva me mano;

Sakuṇāpi na vassanti, matā me nūna dārakā.

Why are you silent? Is my mind then in a daze? Even the birds do not cry out; surely my children are dead.

2219.

2219.

“Kacci nu me ayyaputta, migā khādiṃsu dārake;

Araññe iriṇe vivane, kena nītā me dārakā.

“Have wild beasts eaten my children, my lord? In the forest, in the barren wilderness, by whom have my children been taken?”

2220.

2220.

“Adu [P 6.0561][M 7.0344] te pahitā dūtā, adu suttā piyaṃvadā;

Adu bahi no nikkhantā, khiḍḍāsu pasutā nu te.

“Or have you sent them as messengers? Or are they asleep, the sweet-spoken ones? Or have they gone outside, engrossed in their play?”

2221.

2221.

“Nevāsaṃ [V 7.0336] kesā dissanti, hatthapādā ca jālino;

Sakuṇānañca opāto, kena nītā me dārakā”ti.

“I see neither their hair nor the hands and feet of Jāli; have they been snatched by predatory birds? By whom have my children been taken?”

Tattha api ratteva me manoti api balavapaccūse supinaṃ passantiyā viya me mano. Migāti sīhādayo vāḷamigā. Iriṇeti niroje. Vivaneti vivitte. Dūtāti adu jetuttaranagare sivirañño santikaṃ tayā dūtā katvā pesitā. Suttāti antopaṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā sayitā. Adu bahi noti adu te dārakā khiḍḍāpasutā hutvā bahi nikkhantāti pucchati. Nevāsaṃ kesā dissantīti sāmi vessantara, neva tesaṃ kāḷañjanavaṇṇā kesā dissanti. Jālinoti kañcanajālavicittā hatthapādā. Sakuṇānañca opātoti himavantapadese hatthiliṅgasakuṇā nāma atthi, te opatitvā ādāya ākāseneva gacchanti. Tena taṃ pucchāmi “kiṃ tehi sakuṇehi nītā, ito aññesampi kesañci tesaṃ sakuṇānaṃ viya opāto jāto, akkhāhi, kena nītā me dārakā”ti?

Here, 'api ratteva me mano' means 'my mind is as if seeing a dream in the late dawn'. 'Migā' (wild beasts) refers to lions and other fierce animals. 'Iriṇe' (barren) means 'without water'. 'Vivane' (secluded) means 'isolated'. 'Dūtā' (messengers) means: 'or have they been sent by you as envoys to King Sivi in Jetuttara city?'. 'Suttā' (asleep) means 'they entered the leaf-hut and lay down'. 'Adu bahi no' is a question: 'or have those children, engrossed in play, gone outside?'. 'Nevāsaṃ kesā dissanti' (neither is their hair seen) means, 'O lord Vessantara, not even their kohl-colored hair is visible'. 'Jālino' means hands and feet adorned like a golden net. 'Sakuṇānañca opāto' (nor the swoop of birds) refers to birds in the Himalayan region called hatthiliṅga, which swoop down and carry things away through the sky. Therefore, she asks him: 'Were they taken by those birds? Or has a swoop like that of those birds happened to any others here? Tell me, by whom have my children been taken?'

Evaṃ vuttepi mahāsatto na kiñci āha. Atha naṃ sā “deva, kasmā mayā saddhiṃ na kathesi, ko mama doso”ti vatvā āha –

Even when spoken to thus, the Great Being said nothing. Then she said to him, 'Sire, why do you not speak with me? What is my fault?' and spoke thus:

2222.

2222.

“Idaṃ tato dukkhataraṃ, sallaviddho yathā vaṇo;

Tyajja putte na passāmi, jāliṃ kaṇhājinaṃ cubho.

'This (your silence) is more painful than that (the loss of my children), like a wound pierced by a dart; today I do not see my children, Jāli and Kaṇhājina, both of them.'

2223.

2223.

“Idampi dutiyaṃ sallaṃ, kampeti hadayaṃ mama;

Yañca putte na passāmi, tvañca maṃ nābhibhāsasi.

'This second dart, too, shakes my heart: that I do not see my children, and you do not speak to me.'

2224.

2224.

“Ajjeva me imaṃ rattiṃ, rājaputta na saṃsati;

Maññe okkantasantaṃ maṃ, pāto dakkhisi no mata”nti.

'Prince, if you remain silent and do not speak to me this very night, I think I will surely pass away; in the morning you will see only my dead body.'

Tattha idaṃ tato dukkhataranti sāmi vessantara, yaṃ mama raṭṭhā pabbājitāya araññe vasantiyā putte ca apassantiyā dukkhaṃ, idaṃ tava mayā saddhiṃ akathanaṃ mayhaṃ tato dukkhataraṃ. Tvañhi maṃ aggidaḍḍhaṃ paṭidahanto viya [M 7.0345] papātā patitaṃ daṇḍena pothento viya sallena vaṇaṃ vijjhanto viya tuṇhībhāvena kilamesi. Idañhi me hadayaṃ sallaviddho yathā vaṇo tatheva kampati ceva rujati ca. “Sampaviddho”tipi pāṭho, sampatividdhoti attho. Okkantasantaṃ [V 7.0337] manti apagatajīvitaṃ maṃ. Dakkhisi no matanti ettha no-kāro nipātamatto, mataṃ maṃ kālasseva tvaṃ passissasīti attho.

Here, 'idaṃ tato dukkhataraṃ' (this is more painful than that) means: 'O lord Vessantara, the suffering I endure, banished from my kingdom, living in the forest, and not seeing my children—this your not speaking with me is more painful to me than that'. For you, by remaining silent, torment me like one pressing a burn with fire, like one striking with a stick one who has fallen from a precipice, like one piercing a wound with a dart. Indeed, my heart, like a wound pierced by a dart, both trembles and aches. The reading 'sampaviddho' is also found, meaning 'thoroughly pierced'. 'Okkantasantaṃ maṃ' means 'me, whose life has departed'. 'Dakkhisi no mataṃ' (you will see me dead) — here, the particle 'no' is merely a particle; the meaning is, 'you will see me dead in the morning'.

Atha mahāsatto “kakkhaḷakathāya naṃ puttasokaṃ jahāpessāmī”ti cintetvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being, thinking, 'I will make her abandon her grief for her children with harsh words,' spoke this verse:

2225.

2225.

“Nūna [P 6.0562] maddī varārohā, rājaputtī yasassinī;

Pāto gatāsi uñchāya, kimidaṃ sāyamāgatā”ti.

'Surely, Maddī, graceful one, glorious princess, you went out in the morning to gather food; why is it you have returned so late in the evening?'

Tattha kimidaṃ sāyamāgatāti “maddi, tvaṃ abhirūpā pāsādikā, himavante ca nāma bahū vanacarakā tāpasavijjādharādayo vicaranti. Ko jānāti, kiṃ bhavissati, kiñci tayā kataṃ, tvaṃ pātova gantvā kimidaṃ sāyamāgacchasi, daharakumārake ohāya araññagatitthiyo nāma sasāmikitthiyo evarūpā na honti, ‘kā nu kho me dārakānaṃ pavatti, kiṃ vā me sāmiko cintessatī’ti ettakampi te nāhosi. Tvaṃ pātova gantvā candālokena āgacchasi, mama duggatabhāvassevesa doso”ti tajjetvā vañcetvā kathesi.

Here, 'why is it you have returned so late in the evening?' means: 'Maddī, you are endowed with beauty and charm, and in this Himalayan forest, many forest-dwellers, ascetics, and sorcerers roam about. Who knows what might happen? You went out early in the morning, so why do you come back so late? Women who go into the forest, leaving behind young children, especially those with husbands to serve, are not like this. Did it not even occur to you: "What might be happening to my children? What will my husband think?" Being your own master, you went as you pleased and stayed as you pleased, and only now you return by the light of the moon—this is your fault and it causes me great distress.' Thus he spoke, scolding and deceiving her by a clever device to ease her grief over the children by piercing her heart as if with a needle.

Sā tassa kathaṃ sutvā āha –

Having heard his words, she said, 'My Lord, do not be displeased. I shall explain; please listen to me.'

2226.

2226.

“Nanu tvaṃ saddamassosi, ye saraṃ pātumāgatā;

Sīhassapi nadantassa, byagghassa ca nikujjitaṃ.

'Did you not hear the tumultuous sound of those who came to drink at the lake, of the roaring lion, and of the tiger's growl?'

2227.

2227.

“Ahu pubbanimittaṃ me, vicarantyā brahāvane;

Khaṇitto me hatthā patito, uggīvañcāpi aṃsato.

'An ill omen appeared to me at dawn, and with a worried heart, I went into the great forest for roots and fruits. While I was there, my digging tool fell from my hand, and the basket slipped from my shoulder. The earth trembled violently, and the sounds of birds and beasts echoed throughout the forest.'

2228.

2228.

“Tadāhaṃ byathitā bhītā, puthu katvāna añjaliṃ;

Sabbadisā namassissaṃ, api sotthi ito siyā.

'Then I, distressed and fearful, folded my hands in reverence and paid homage to all ten directions, praying: "May my husband and children be safe from lions, tigers, leopards, bears, and hyenas; may they be free from all harm."'

2229.

2229.

“Mā [M 7.0346] heva no rājaputto, hato sīhena dīpinā;

Dārakā vā parāmaṭṭhā, acchakokataracchihi.

'Whenever I heard the unusual sounds of those fierce beasts, I remembered my dream at dawn and wished to return early. Yet, whenever I approached the fruit-bearing trees, they appeared as if they had no fruit, while barren trees appeared as if they were full. Thus, I wandered in confusion and struggled to find food, and then further ill omens appeared to me.'

2230.

2230.

“Sīho [V 7.0338] byaggho ca dīpi ca, tayo vāḷā vane migā;

Te maṃ pariyāvaruṃ maggaṃ, tena sāyamhi āgatā”ti.

'The lion, the tiger, and the leopard—three fierce beasts of the forest—blocked my path. Thus, I was unable to reach the gate of Mount Vaṅka until they moved away. For that reason, I have arrived later than usual. O Prince, do not be displeased with me; please forgive me.'

Tattha ye saraṃ pātumāgatāti ye pānīyaṃ pātuṃ imaṃ saraṃ āgatā. Byagghassa cāti byagghassa ca aññesaṃ hatthiādīnaṃ catuppadānañceva sakuṇasaṅghassa ca nikūjitaṃ ekaninnādasaddaṃ kiṃ tvaṃ na assosīti pucchati. So pana mahāsattena puttānaṃ dinnavelāya saddo ahosi. Ahu pubbanimittaṃ meti deva, imassa me dukkhassa anubhavanatthāya pubbanimittaṃ ahosi. Uggīvanti aṃsakūṭe pacchilagganakaṃ. Puthūti visuṃ visuṃ. Sabbadisā namassissanti sabbā dasa disā namassiṃ. Mā heva noti amhākaṃ rājaputto sīhādīhi hato mā hotu, dārakāpi acchādīhi parāmaṭṭhā mā hontūti patthayantī namassissaṃ. Te maṃ pariyāvaruṃ magganti sāmi vessantara, ahaṃ “imāni ca bhīsanakāni mahantāni, dussupino ca me diṭṭho, ajja sakālasseva gamissāmī”ti kampamānā mūlaphalāphalāni upadhāresiṃ, atha me phalitarukkhāpi aphalā viya aphalā ca phalino viya dissanti, kicchena phalāphalāni gahetvā giridvāraṃ sampāpuṇiṃ. Atha te sīhādayo maṃ disvā maggaṃ paṭipāṭiyā rumbhitvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Tena sāyaṃ āgatāmhi, khamāhi me, sāmīti.

(The sound of forest beasts and birds, more tumultuous than usual, was the same resounding sound that echoed through the entire Himalayan forest when the Great Being gave away his son and daughter.)

Mahāsatto tāya saddhiṃ ettakameva kathaṃ vatvā yāva aruṇuggamanā na kiñci kathesi. Tato paṭṭhāya maddī nānappakārakaṃ vilapantī āha –

The Great Being, having spoken only those initial words, said nothing more to Queen Maddī until the rising of the dawn. From then on, Queen Maddī, distressed in mind, lamented in various ways:

2231.

2231.

“Ahaṃ [P 6.0563] patiñca putte ca, āceramiva māṇavo;

Anuṭṭhitā divārattiṃ, jaṭinī brahmacārinī.

'Like a pupil attending to his teacher, I have served my husband, the King, by rubbing his feet and being diligent day and night. With matted hair and living the holy life, I have avoided the ways of villagers and raised my children well without letting them suffer.'

2232.

2232.

“Ajināni paridahitvā, vanamūlaphalahāriyā;

Vicarāmi divārattiṃ, tumhaṃ kāmā hi puttakā.

'My dear children, where are you? Come to your mother! Fearing that you would be hungry, I wandered day and night searching for roots and fruits. Even when I return from the forest, I do not feel tired for your sake.'

2233.

2233.

“Ahaṃ suvaṇṇahaliddiṃ, ābhataṃ paṇḍubeluvaṃ;

Rukkhapakkāni cāhāsiṃ, ime vo putta kīḷanā.

'I have brought golden turmeric to powder for your bath, and I have brought ripe wood-apples; these are for your toys, my children. Play with these wood-apples.'

2234.

2234.

“Imaṃ [M 7.0347] mūḷālivattakaṃ, sālukaṃ ciñcabhedakaṃ;

Bhuñja khuddehi saṃyuttaṃ, saha puttehi khattiya.

'I have brought coiled lotus stalks, lotus roots, and sweet albizia fruits for you to enjoy. Come, my children, and eat them together with your father.'

2235.

2235.

“Padumaṃ [V 7.0339] jālino dehi, kumudañca kumāriyā;

Māline passa naccante, sivi puttāni avhaya.

'O Lord, sovereign of the Sivi people, please give this red lotus I brought from the lake to Jālī, and this blue water lily to Kaṇhājina. Call them to dance and sing sweet songs while wearing these flowers.'

2236.

2236.

“Tato kaṇhājināyapi, nisāmehi rathesabha;

Mañjussarāya vagguyā, assamaṃ upayantiyā.

'Sire, I wish to see my children. If they are here, please show them to me. Why do you oppress me with such grief that it might end my life?'

2237.

2237.

“Samānasukhadukkhamhā, raṭṭhā pabbājitā ubho;

Api sivi putte passesi, jāliṃ kaṇhājinaṃ cubho.

'Sire, even though we were exiled together and live in this forest with our children, sharing joy and sorrow as a loving husband and wife, it seems as if you are cursing me so that I may never see them again.' Although Maddī lamented so piteously, the Great Being remained silent and did not say a single word in return.

2238.

2238.

“Samaṇe brāhmaṇe nūna, brahmacariyaparāyaṇe;

Ahaṃ loke abhissapiṃ, sīlavante bahussute;

Tyajja putte na passāmi, jāliṃ kaṇhājinaṃ cubho”ti.

"Surely I must have reviled ascetics and brahmins in the world who are devoted to the holy life, the virtuous and learned; for that reason, today I do not see my children, Jālī and Kaṇhājinā, both."

Tattha āceramiva māṇavoti vattasampanno antevāsiko ācariyaṃ viya paṭijaggati. Anuṭṭhitāti pāricariyānuṭṭhānena anuṭṭhitā appamattā hutvā paṭijaggāmi. Tumhaṃ kāmāti tumhākaṃ kāmena tumhe patthayantī. Puttakāti kumāre ālapantī paridevati. Suvaṇṇahaliddinti puttakā ahaṃ tumhākaṃ nhāpanatthāya suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ haliddiṃ ghaṃsitvā ādāya āgatā. Paṇḍubeluvanti kīḷanatthāya ca vo idaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ beluvapakkaṃ mayā ābhataṃ. Rukkhapakkānīti tumhākaṃ kīḷanatthāya aññānipi manāpāni rukkhaphalāni āhāsiṃ. Ime voti puttakā ime vo kīḷanāti vadati. Mūḷālivattakanti mūḷālakuṇḍalakaṃ. Sālukanti idaṃ uppalādisālukampi me bahu ābhataṃ. Ciñcabhedakanti siṅghāṭakaṃ. Bhuñjāti idaṃ sabbaṃ khuddamadhunā saṃyuttaṃ puttehi saddhiṃ bhuñjāhīti paridevati. Sivi puttāni avhayāti sāmi sivirāja, paṇṇasālāya sayāpitaṭṭhānato sīghaṃ puttake pakkosāhi. Api sivi putte passesīti sāmi sivirāja, api putte passasi, sace passasi, mama dassehi, kiṃ maṃ ativiya kilamesi. Abhissapinti tumhākaṃ puttadhītaro mā passitthāti evaṃ nūna akkosinti.

There, 'like a student attending to his teacher' means 'a resident student endowed with good conduct attends to his teacher.' 'Diligent' means 'I attend, having become diligent and heedful in the performance of service.' 'For love of you' means 'desiring you out of love for you.' 'O children' means 'calling out to the boys, she laments.' 'Golden turmeric' means 'O children, for your bathing I have come, having brought ground, golden-colored turmeric.' 'Pale beluva fruit' means 'and for you to play with, this golden-colored ripe beluva fruit has been brought by me.' 'Ripe tree-fruits' means 'for you to play with, I have also brought other delightful tree-fruits.' 'These are yours' means 'she says, "Children, these are your toys."' 'Coiled mūlāla root' means 'a coiled mūlāla root.' 'Lotus root' means 'I have also brought much of this lotus root from water lilies and so on.' 'Water chestnuts' means 'the siṅghāṭaka fruit.' 'Eat' means 'she laments, "Eat all this, mixed with honey from small bees, together with the children."' 'Summon the children of Sivi' means 'Lord Sivirāja, quickly summon the children from their sleeping place in the leaf-hut.' 'Do you see the children of Sivi?' means 'Lord Sivirāja, do you see the children? If you see them, show them to me. Why do you torment me so much?' 'I have reviled' means 'Surely they curse me thus: "May you not see your sons and daughters."'"

Evaṃ [P 6.0564][M 7.0348] vilapamānāyapi tāya saddhiṃ mahāsatto na kiñci kathesi. Sā tasmiṃ akathente kampamānā candālokena putte vicinantī yesu yesu jamburukkhādīsu pubbe kīḷiṃsu, tāni tāni patvā paridevantī āha –

When the Great Being did not speak a single word, Queen Maddī, trembling greatly, left his presence and searched for her children throughout the night by the light of the moon. She went to the places where they used to play and, reaching the foot of various trees, she lamented:

2239.

2239.

“Ime [V 7.0340] te jambukā rukkhā, vedisā sinduvārakā;

Vividhāni rukkhajātāni, te kumārā na dissare.

'This shade of the rose-apple tree is where my children used to play. They are not here at the foot of the vedisa, sinduvāraka, or any of these trees!'

2240.

2240.

“Assatthā panasā ceme, nigrodhā ca kapitthanā;

Vividhāni phalajātāni, te kumārā na dissare.

'My children used to play at the foot of these very trees—the sacred fig, the jackfruit, the banyan, and the wood-apple; but they are not to be seen here.'

2241.

2241.

“Ime tiṭṭhanti ārāmā, ayaṃ sītūdakā nadī;

Yatthassu pubbe kīḷiṃsu, te kumārā na dissare.

She went to the riverbank and lamented, 'This river has cool and clear water where they used to play, but they are not to be seen here now!'

2242.

2242.

“Vividhāni pupphajātāni, asmiṃ uparipabbate;

Yānassu pubbe dhāriṃsu, te kumārā na dissare.

She climbed to the mountaintop and lamented, 'On this mountaintop are various flowers they used to pick and wear, but they are not to be seen here now!'

2243.

2243.

“Vividhāni phalajātāni, asmiṃ uparipabbate;

Yānassu pubbe bhuñjiṃsu, te kumārā na dissare.

'There are various fruits on this mountain that they used to gather and eat, but they are not to be seen at these trees now!'

2244.

2244.

“Ime te hatthikā assā, balibaddā ca te ime;

Yehissu pubbe kīḷiṃsu, te kumārā na dissare”ti.

"These are those toy elephants, horses, and bulls with which they used to play; but those children are not to be seen."

Tattha ime te hatthikāti sā pabbatūpari dārake adisvā paridevamānā tato oruyha puna assamapadaṃ āgantvā tattha te upadhārentī tesaṃ kīḷanabhaṇḍakāni disvā evamāha.

There, 'these are your toy elephants' means: not seeing the children on the mountain, she lamented, and descending from there, she returned to the hermitage grounds. Searching for them there and seeing their playthings, she spoke thus.

Athassā paridevanasaddena ceva padasaddena ca migapakkhino caliṃsu. Sā te disvā āha –

Then, at the sound of her lamentation and her footsteps, the wild animals and birds were startled. Seeing them, she said:

2245.

2245.

“Ime sāmā sasolūkā, bahukā kadalīmigā;

Yehissu pubbe kīḷiṃsu, te kumārā na dissare.

"These sāmā deer, hares, owls, and many kadalī deer, with which they used to play; but those children are not to be seen."

2246.

2246.

“Ime haṃsā ca koñcā ca, mayūrā citrapekhuṇā;

Yehissu pubbe kīḷiṃsu, te kumārā na dissare”ti.

"These swans and cranes, and peacocks with variegated tail-feathers, with which they used to play; but those children are not to be seen."

Tattha sāmāti khuddakā sāmā suvaṇṇamigā. Sasolūkāti sasā ca ulūkā ca.

There, 'sāmā' means small sāmā, golden deer. 'Sasolūkā' means hares and owls.

Sā [V 7.0341][M 7.0349] assamapade piyaputte adisvā nikkhamitvā pupphitavanaghaṭaṃ pavisitvā taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ olokentī āha –

Not seeing her beloved children in the hermitage, she went out and entered a thicket of flowering trees, and looking here and there, she said:

2247.

2247.

“Imā tā vanagumbāyo, pupphitā sabbakālikā;

Yatthassu pubbe kīḷiṃsu, te kumārā na dissare.

"These are those forest thickets, blooming in all seasons, where those children used to play; they are not to be seen."

2248.

2248.

“Imā tā pokkharaṇī rammā, cakkavākūpakūjitā;

Mandālakehi sañchannā, padumuppalakehi ca;

Yatthassu pubbe kīḷiṃsu, te kumārā na dissare”ti.

"These are those lovely lotus ponds, resounding with the calls of ruddy geese, covered with mandālaka flowers, lotuses, and water-lilies, where those children used to play; they are not to be seen."

Tattha [P 6.0565] vanagumbāyoti vanaghaṭāyo.

There, 'vanagumbāyo' means forest thickets.

Sā katthaci piyaputte adisvā puna mahāsattassa santikaṃ āgantvā taṃ dummukhaṃ nisinnaṃ disvā āha –

Not seeing her beloved children anywhere, she returned to the Great Being, and seeing him sitting with a gloomy face, she said:

2249.

2249.

“Na te kaṭṭhāni bhinnāni, na te udakamāhaṭaṃ;

Aggipi te na hāpito, kiṃ nu mandova jhāyasi.

"The firewood is not split, the water is not fetched, and the fire is not kindled. Why do you sit brooding like one who is witless?"

2250.

2250.

“Piyo piyena saṅgamma, samo me byapahaññati;

Tyajja putte na passāmi, jāliṃ kaṇhājinaṃ cubho”ti.

"My weariness is dispelled when I meet my beloved husband; but today I do not see both my children, Jāli and Kaṇhājinā."

Tattha na hāpitoti na jalito. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sāmi, tvaṃ pubbe kaṭṭhāni bhindasi, udakaṃ āharitvā ṭhapesi, aṅgārakapalle aggiṃ karosi, ajja tesu ekampi akatvā kiṃ nu mandova jhāyasi, tava kiriyā mayhaṃ na ruccatīti. Piyo piyenāti vessantaro mayhaṃ piyo, ito me piyataro natthi, iminā me piyena saṅgamma samāgantvā pubbe samo me byapahaññati dukkhaṃ vigacchati, ajja pana me imaṃ passantiyāpi soko na vigacchati, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇanti. Tyajjāti hotu, diṭṭhaṃ me kāraṇaṃ, te ajja putte na passāmi, tena me imaṃ passantiyāpi soko na vigacchatīti.

There, 'na hāpito' means not kindled. This is what is said: "Master, formerly you would split firewood, fetch water and set it down, and make a fire in the charcoal pit. Today, having done none of these things, why do you sit brooding as if you were dull? Your actions do not please me." 'Piyo piyena' means: "Vessantara is beloved to me; there is none more beloved to me than he. Having met and come together with this beloved one, formerly my weariness was dispelled and my suffering vanished. But today, even while seeing him, my sorrow does not vanish. What could be the reason?" 'Tyajja' means: "So be it, I have seen the reason. Today I do not see those sons, and for that reason, even while seeing him, my sorrow does not vanish."

Tāya evaṃ vuttepi mahāsatto tuṇhībhūtova nisīdi. Sā tasmiṃ akathente sokasamappitā [V 7.0342] pahaṭakukkuṭī viya kampamānā puna paṭhamaṃ vicaritaṭṭhānāni vicaritvā mahāsattassa santikaṃ paccāgantvā āha –

Even when she spoke thus, the Great Being sat in silence. As he said nothing, she, overcome with grief and trembling like a struck hen, wandered again through the places she had first searched, and returning to the Great Being, she said:

2251.

2251.

“Na [M 7.0350] kho no deva passāmi, yena te nīhatā matā;

Kākolāpi na vassanti, matā me nūna dārakā.

"Indeed, lord, I do not see who has taken them, or if they are dead; even the crows do not caw; surely my children are dead."

2252.

2252.

“Na kho no deva passāmi, yena te nīhatā matā;

Sakuṇāpi na vassanti, matā me nūna dārakā”ti.

"Indeed, lord, I do not see by whom they were carried off or are dead; even the birds do not cry out; surely my children are dead."

Tattha na kho noti deva, na kho amhākaṃ putte passāmi. Yena te nīhatāti kenaci tesaṃ nīhatabhāvampi na jānāmīti adhippāyenevamāha.

Here, 'na kho no deva' means 'Indeed, lord, I do not see our children.' 'Yena te nīhatā' means 'I do not even know the state of their having been carried off by anyone'—with this intention she spoke thus.

Evaṃ vuttepi mahāsatto na kiñci kathesiyeva. Sā puttasokena phuṭṭhā putte upadhārentī tatiyampi tāni tāni ṭhānāni vātavegena vicari. Tāya ekarattiṃ vicaritaṭṭhānaṃ pariggayhamānaṃ pannarasayojanamattaṃ ahosi. Atha ratti vibhāsi, aruṇodayo jāto. Sā puna gantvā mahāsattassa santike ṭhitā paridevi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Even when this was said, the Great Being said nothing at all. Afflicted by grief for her children, she searched for them, wandering a third time through those same places with the speed of the wind. The distance she travelled in that single night was about fifteen leagues. Then the night faded and dawn broke. She went again and stood near the Great Being, lamenting. The Teacher, explaining this matter, said:

2253.

2253.

“Sā tattha paridevitvā, pabbatāni vanāni ca;

Punadevassamaṃ gantvā, rodi sāmikasantike.

"Having lamented there among the mountains and forests, and having gone back to the hermitage, she wept in her husband’s presence."

2254.

2254.

“Na [P 6.0566] kho no deva passāmi, yena te nīhatā matā;

Kākolāpi na vassanti, matā me nūna dārakā.

"Indeed, lord, I do not see by whom they were carried off or are dead; even the crows do not caw; surely my children are dead.

2255.

2255.

“Na kho no deva passāmi, yena te nīhatā matā;

Sakuṇāpi na vassanti, matā me nūna dārakā.

"Indeed, lord, I do not see by whom they were carried off or are dead; even the birds do not cry out; surely my children are dead.

2256.

2256.

“Nu kho no deva passāmi, yena te nīhatā matā;

Vicarantī rukkhamūlesu, pabbatesu guhāsu ca.

"Now indeed, lord, I do not see by whom they were carried off or are dead, though I wander among the roots of trees, on mountains, and in caves.

2257.

2257.

“Iti [V 7.0343] maddī varārohā, rājaputtī yasassinī;

Bāhā paggayha kanditvā, tattheva patitā chamā”ti.

"Thus the glorious princess Maddī, of excellent form, raising her arms and weeping, fell right there upon the ground."

Tattha sāmikasantiketi bhikkhave, sā maddī tattha vaṅkapabbatakucchiyaṃ sānupabbatāni vanāni ca vicarantī paridevitvā puna gantvā sāmikaṃ nissāya tassa santike ṭhitā puttānaṃ atthāya rodi, “na kho no”tiādīni vadantī [M 7.0351] paridevīti attho. Iti maddī varārohāti bhikkhave, evaṃ sā uttamarūpadharā varārohā maddī rukkhamūlādīsu vicarantī dārake adisvā “nissaṃsayaṃ matā bhavissantī”ti bāhā paggayha kanditvā tattheva vessantarassa pādamūle chinnasuvaṇṇakadalī viya chamāyaṃ pati.

Here, 'in her husband’s presence' means this: monks, that Maddī, having lamented while wandering there in the hollow of Vaṅka Mountain and through the forests with their foothills, went again, and relying on her husband, stood in his presence and wept for the sake of her children, lamenting and saying, 'Indeed, we do not,' and so forth. 'Thus Maddī, of excellent form' means this: monks, in this way, that Maddī, of supreme beauty, of excellent form, wandering at the roots of trees and so forth, not seeing the children, thinking, 'Without a doubt, they must be dead,' raised her arms and wept, and right there at Vessantara’s feet, she fell upon the ground like a golden banana plant that had been cut down.

Atha mahāsatto “matā maddī”ti saññāya kampamāno “aṭṭhāne padese matā maddī. Sace hissā jetuttaranagare kālakiriyā abhavissa, mahanto parivāro abhavissa, dve raṭṭhāni caleyyuṃ. Ahaṃ pana araññe ekakova, kiṃ nu kho karissāmī”ti uppannabalavasokopi satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā “jānissāmi tāvā”ti uṭṭhāya tassā hadaye hatthaṃ ṭhapetvā santāpapavattiṃ ñatvā kamaṇḍalunā udakaṃ āharitvā satta māse kāyasaṃsaggaṃ anāpannapubbopi balavasokena pabbajitabhāvaṃ sallakkhetuṃ asakkonto assupuṇṇehi nettehi tassā sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā ūrūsu ṭhapetvā udakena paripphositvā mukhañca hadayañca parimajjanto nisīdi. Maddīpi kho thokaṃ vītināmetvā satiṃ paṭilabhitvā hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā uṭṭhāya mahāsattaṃ vanditvā “sāmi vessantara, dārakā te kuhiṃ gatā”ti āha. “Devi, ekassa brāhmaṇassa dāsatthāya dinnā”ti. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –
