Then the Great Being, thinking 'Maddī is dead', was deeply shaken: 'Maddī has died in a desolate place. If she had died in the city of Jetuttara, there would have been a great retinue, and the two kingdoms of Ceta and Sivi would have been stirred. But here in the forest, I am all alone; what shall I do?' Though overcome by intense grief, he established mindfulness and thought, 'I shall see if she is really dead.' Rising, he placed his hand on her heart and, perceiving the warmth of her breath, he fetched water in a jar. Though he had not come into physical contact with her for seven months, in his intense grief, he was unable to maintain his composure as a renunciant. With eyes full of tears, he lifted her head with both hands, placed it on his lap, sprinkled her with water, and sat stroking her face and heart. After a short while, Maddī regained consciousness, and feeling bashful, she rose and paid homage to the Great Being, asking, 'Lord Vessantara, where have our children gone?' 'My queen, I have given them to an old brahmin to be his servants.' The Teacher, explaining this, said:

2258.

2258.

“Tamajjhapattaṃ rājaputtiṃ, udakenābhisiñcatha;

Assatthaṃ naṃ viditvāna, atha naṃ etadabravī”ti.

"He sprinkled with water that princess who had been overcome; and knowing her to be revived, he then spoke these words to her."

Tattha [P 6.0567] ajjhapattanti attano santikaṃ pattaṃ, pādamūle patitvā visaññibhūtanti attho. Etadabravīti etaṃ “ekassa me brāhmaṇassa dāsatthāya dinnā”ti vacanaṃ abravi.

Here, 'ajjhapattam' means having reached his presence; the meaning is, having fallen at his feet and become unconscious. 'Etadabravī' means he spoke this statement: 'They were given by me to a certain brahmin for the purpose of slavery.'

Tato tāya “deva, putte brāhmaṇassa datvā mama sabbarattiṃ paridevitvā vicarantiyā kiṃ nācikkhasī”ti vutte mahāsatto āha –

Then, when she said, 'Lord, you gave the children to the brahmin, but why did you not tell me while I was wandering and lamenting all night in search of them?' the Great Being replied:

2259.

2259.

“Ādiyeneva [V 7.0344] te maddi, dukkhaṃ nakkhātumicchisaṃ;

Daliddo yācako vuḍḍho, brāhmaṇo gharamāgato.

"Maddī, I did not want to tell you of this sorrow at first; for women's hearts are soft, and you might have died of a broken heart. A poor, old, mendicant brahmin came to the hermitage."

2260.

2260.

“Tassa [M 7.0352] dinnā mayā puttā, maddi mā bhāyi assasa;

Maṃ passa maddi mā putte, mā bāḷhaṃ paridevasi;

Lacchāma putte jīvantā, arogā ca bhavāmase.

"I have given the children to that old brahmin. Maddī, do not fear, be comforted. Do not look for the children, look at me; do not lament excessively. We shall see our children again, alive and well."

2261.

2261.

“Putte pasuñca dhaññañca, yañca aññaṃ ghare dhanaṃ;

Dajjā sappuriso dānaṃ, disvā yācakamāgataṃ;

Anumodāhi me maddi, puttake dānamuttama”nti.

"A good person, when seeing a mendicant, should give children, cattle, grain, or whatever wealth is in the house. Maddī, rejoice with me in this supreme gift of our children."

Tattha ādiyenevāti ādikeneva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace te ahaṃ āditova tamatthaṃ ācikkhissaṃ, tato tava sokaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkontiyā hadayaṃ phaleyya, tasmā ādikeneva te maddi dukkhaṃ na akkhātuṃ icchissanti. Gharamāgatoti imaṃ amhākaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āgato. Arogā ca bhavāmaseti yathā tathā mayaṃ arogā homa, jīvamānā avassaṃ putte brāhmaṇena nītepi passissāma. Yañca aññanti yañca aññaṃ ghare saviññāṇakaṃ dhanaṃ. Dajjā sappuriso dānanti sappuriso uttamatthaṃ patthento uraṃ bhinditvā hadayamaṃsampi gahetvā dānaṃ dadeyyāti.

Herein, 'ādiyenevāti' means 'from the very beginning.' This is said: 'If I were to explain that matter to you from the very start, your heart would burst, being unable to bear the sorrow. Therefore, Maddī, I did not wish to tell you about the suffering from the beginning.' 'He has come home' means 'he has come to this our dwelling place.' 'May we be free from illness' means 'in whatever way we may be free from illness. As long as we live, we will surely see our sons even if they have been taken by the brahmin.' 'And whatever else' refers to 'whatever other sentient wealth is in the house.' 'A noble person gives gifts' means 'a noble person, desiring the highest attainment, would even tear open his chest, take out the flesh of his heart, and give it as a gift.'

Maddī āha –

Maddī said:

2262.

2262.

“Anumodāmi te deva, puttake dānamuttamaṃ;

Datvā cittaṃ pasādehi, bhiyyo dānaṃ dado bhava.

“I rejoice in your supreme gift of our children, O king. Having given it, gladden your heart; may you continue to give even more gifts.”

2263.

2263.

“Yo tvaṃ maccherabhūtesu, manussesu janādhipa;

Brāhmaṇassa adā dānaṃ, sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhano”ti.

“You, O lord of men, amidst human beings who are full of stinginess, gave a gift to the brahmin, O increaser of the Sivi kingdom.”

Tattha anumodāmi teti dasa māse kucchiyā dhāretvā divasassa dvattikkhattuṃ nhāpetvā pāyetvā bhojetvā ure nipajjāpetvā paṭijaggitaputtakesu bodhisattena dinnesu sayaṃ puttadānaṃ anumodantī evamāha. Iminā kāraṇena jānitabbaṃ “pitāva puttānaṃ sāmiko”ti. Bhiyyo dānaṃ [V 7.0345] dado bhavāti mahārāja, uttaripi punappunaṃ dānaṃ dāyakova hohi, “sudinnaṃ me dāna”nti cittaṃ pasādehi, yo tvaṃ maccherabhūtesu sattesu piyaputte adāsīti.

Herein, 'I rejoice in you' means: she herself, rejoicing in the gift of her sons, spoke thus about the sons she had carried in her womb for ten months, bathed two or three times a day, given drink, fed, laid upon her breast, and cared for, who were given away by the Bodhisatta. By this reason, it should be known: 'The father is indeed the master of his sons.' 'May you be one who gives even more' means: 'O great king, hereafter also, again and again, be a giver of gifts. Gladden your mind with the thought, “My gift is well-given,” for you have given your beloved sons amidst beings who are full of stinginess.'

Evaṃ [M 7.0353] vutte mahāsatto “maddi, kinnāmetaṃ kathesi, sace hi mayā putte datvā cittaṃ pasādetuṃ nābhavissa, imāni pana me acchariyāni na pavatteyyu”nti vatvā sabbāni pathavininnādādīni [P 6.0568] kathesi. Tato maddī tāni acchariyāni kittetvā dānaṃ anumodantī āha –

When she said this, the Great Being replied, "Maddī, why do you say 'gladden your heart'? If I had not been able to gladden my heart after giving the children, these miracles would not have occurred," and he recounted the wonders, such as the earthquake. Then Maddī, praising those marvels and rejoicing in the gift, said:

2264.

2264.

“Ninnāditā te pathavī, saddo te tidivaṅgato;

Samantā vijjutā āguṃ, girīnaṃva patissutā”ti.

“The earth resounded for you, and your fame reached the heavens. Lightning flashed all around, and the whole forest echoed like the crashing of mountains.”

Tattha vijjutā āgunti akālavijjulatā himavantapadese samantā nicchariṃsu. Girīnaṃva patissutāti girīnaṃ patissutasaddā viya viravā uṭṭhahiṃsu.

Herein, 'lightning flashed' means untimely lightning flashes issued forth all around in the region of the Himalayas. 'Like echoes from the mountains' means cries arose like the echoing sounds of mountains.

2265.

2265.

“Tassa te anumodanti, ubho nāradapabbatā;

Indo ca brahmā pajāpati, somo yamo vessavaṇo;

Sabbe devānumodanti, tāvatiṃsā saindakā.

“The deities Nārada and Pabbata, Indra, Brahmā, Pajāpati, Soma, Yama, and Vessavaṇa—all the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, with Indra as their chief, rejoice in your gift.”

2266.

2266.

“Iti maddī varārohā, rājaputtī yasassinī;

Vessantarassa anumodi, puttake dānamuttama”nti.

“Thus the glorious princess Maddī, of excellent form, rejoiced in Vessantara’s supreme gift of his children.”

Tattha ubho nāradapabbatāti imepi dve devanikāyā attano vimānadvāre ṭhitāva “sudinnaṃ te dāna”nti anumodanti. Tāvatiṃsā saindakāti indajeṭṭhakā tāvatiṃsāpi devā te dānaṃ anumodantīti.

Herein, 'both Nārada and Pabbata' means these two groups of deities, standing at the entrances of their celestial mansions, rejoice, saying, 'Well given is your gift.' 'The Tāvatiṃsa with Indra' means the Tāvatiṃsa gods, who have Indra as their chief, also rejoice in your gift.

Evaṃ mahāsattena attano dāne vaṇṇite tamevatthaṃ parivattetvā “mahārāja vessantara, sudinnaṃ nāma te dāna”nti maddīpi tatheva dānaṃ vaṇṇayitvā anumodamānā nisīdi. Tena satthā “iti maddī varārohā”ti gāthamāha.

Thus, when the Great Being had praised his own giving, turning the matter around, Maddī also, praising the gift in the same way and rejoicing, sat down, saying, 'Great King Vessantara, your gift is indeed well given.' Therefore, the Teacher spoke this verse: 'Thus Maddī, the noble lady...'

Maddīpabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Maddī Chapter is concluded.

Sakkapabbavaṇṇanā

The Section on Sakka

Evaṃ [V 7.0346][M 7.0354] tesu aññamaññaṃ sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ kathentesu sakko cintesi “ayaṃ vessantaro rājā hiyyo jūjakassa pathaviṃ unnādetvā dārake adāsi, idāni taṃ koci hīnapuriso upasaṅkamitvā sabbalakkhaṇasampannaṃ maddiṃ yācitvā rājānaṃ ekakaṃ katvā maddiṃ gahetvā gaccheyya, tato esa anātho nippaccayo bhaveyya. Ahaṃ brāhmaṇavaṇṇena naṃ upasaṅkamitvā maddiṃ yācitvā pāramikūṭaṃ gāhāpetvā kassaci avissajjiyaṃ katvā puna naṃ tasseva datvā āgamissāmī”ti. So sūriyuggamanavelāya tassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

While they were thus conversing pleasantly with one another, Sakka thought: “Yesterday, King Vessantara gave his children to the brahmin Jūjaka, causing the earth to resound. Now, if some lowly person were to approach him and ask for Maddī, who is endowed with all auspicious marks, he might give her away, leaving the king all alone. Then he would become helpless and without support. I will approach him in the guise of a brahmin, ask for Maddī, cause him to reach the pinnacle of the perfections, and then, making her a gift that cannot be given away to anyone else, I will return her to him and return to my own place.” At sunrise, he went into his presence. To illuminate this matter, the Teacher said:

2267.

2267.

“Tato ratyā vivasāne, sūriyassuggamanaṃ pati;

Sakko brāhmaṇavaṇṇena, pāto tesaṃ adissathā”ti.

“Then, at the end of the night, toward the rising of the sun, Sakka, in the guise of a brahmin, appeared to them in the morning.”

Tattha [P 6.0569] pāto tesaṃ adissathāti pātova nesaṃ dvinnampi janānaṃ paññāyamānarūpo purato aṭṭhāsi, ṭhatvā ca pana paṭisanthāraṃ karonto āha –

Herein, “appeared to them in the morning” means that at dawn he stood before both of them, his form made visible. And standing there, offering a friendly greeting, he said:

2268.

2268.

“Kacci nu bhoto kusalaṃ, kacci bhoto anāmayaṃ;

Kacci uñchena yāpetha, kacci mūlaphalā bahū.

“Are you well, sir? Are you free from illness? Do you sustain yourselves by gathering fallen fruits? Are roots and fruits plentiful?

2269.

2269.

“Kacci ḍaṃsā makasā ca, appameva sarīsapā;

Vane vāḷamigākiṇṇe, kacci hiṃsā na vijjatī”ti.

“Are gadflies and mosquitoes few, and likewise creeping things? In this forest teeming with beasts of prey, is there no harm?”

Mahāsatto āha –

The Great Being said:

2270.

2270.

“Kusalañceva no brahme, atho brahme anāmayaṃ;

Atho uñchena yāpema, atho mūlaphalā bahū.

“We are well, O brahmin, and also, brahmin, free from illness. We sustain ourselves by gathering fallen fruits, and roots and fruits are plentiful.

2271.

2271.

“Atho ḍaṃsā makasā ca, appameva sarīsapā;

Vane vāḷamigākiṇṇe, hiṃsā mayhaṃ na vijjati.

“Also, gadflies and mosquitoes are few, and likewise creeping things. In this forest teeming with beasts of prey, there is no harm to me.

2272.

2272.

“Satta [V 7.0347] no māse vasataṃ, araññe jīvasokinaṃ;

Idaṃ dutiyaṃ passāma, brāhmaṇaṃ devavaṇṇinaṃ;

Ādāya veḷuvaṃ daṇḍaṃ, dhārentaṃ ajinakkhipaṃ.

“For seven months we have lived in the forest, living in sorrow. This is the second time we have seen a brahmin of divine appearance, carrying a bamboo staff and wearing an antelope-skin cloak.

2273.

2273.

“Svāgataṃ [M 7.0355] te mahābrahme, atho te adurāgataṃ;

Anto pavisa bhaddante, pāde pakkhālayassu te.

“Welcome to you, great brahmin, your arrival is a good one. Please enter, venerable sir, and wash your feet.

2274.

2274.

“Tindukāni piyālāni, madhuke kāsumāriyo;

Phalāni khuddakappāni, bhuñja brahme varaṃ varaṃ.

“Tinduka fruits, piyāla fruits, madhuka and kāsumāriya fruits, and other small fruits—eat whichever you prefer, O brahmin.

2275.

2275.

“Idampi pānīyaṃ sītaṃ, ābhataṃ girigabbharā;

Tato piva mahābrahme, sace tvaṃ abhikaṅkhasī”ti.

“This cool water, too, was brought from a mountain cavern. Drink of it, great brahmin, if you so desire.”

Evaṃ tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā mahāsatto –

Having thus exchanged friendly greetings with him, the Great Being asked:

2276.

2276.

“Atha tvaṃ kena vaṇṇena, kena vā pana hetunā;

Anuppatto brahāraññaṃ, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti. –

“Now, for what reason, on what account, have you come to this great forest? Tell me this, as you are asked.”

Āgamanakāraṇaṃ pucchi. Atha naṃ sakko “mahārāja, ahaṃ mahallako, idhāgacchanto tava bhariyaṃ maddiṃ yācituṃ āgato, taṃ me dehī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

He inquired about the reason for his coming. Then Sakka, saying to him, “Great king, I am an old man. I have come here to ask for your wife Maddī. Give her to me,” spoke this verse:

2277.

2277.

“Yathā vārivaho pūro, sabbakālaṃ na khīyati;

Evaṃ taṃ yācitāgacchiṃ, bhariyaṃ me dehi yācito”ti.

“Just as a full river is never exhausted at any time, so I have come to you to beg. Give me your wife, as you are asked.”

Evaṃ vutte mahāsatto “hiyyo me brāhmaṇassa dārakā dinnā, araññe ekako hutvā kathaṃ te maddiṃ dassāmī”ti avatvā pasāritahatthe sahassatthavikaṃ ṭhapento viya asajjitvā abajjhitvā anolīnamānaso hutvā giriṃ unnādento imaṃ gāthamāha –

When this was said, the Great Being, without saying, “Yesterday I gave my children to a brahmin, and now I am alone in the forest—how can I give you Maddī?” as if placing a purse of a thousand pieces in an outstretched hand, unhesitatingly, unfalteringly, with an unyielding mind, making the mountain resound, spoke this verse:

2278.

2278.

“Dadāmi [P 6.0570] na vikampāmi, yaṃ maṃ yācasi brāhmaṇa;

Santaṃ nappaṭiguyhāmi, dāne me ramatī mano”ti.

“I give without wavering, O brahmin, whatever you ask of me. I do not hide what I have; my mind delights in giving.”

Tattha [V 7.0348] santaṃ nappaṭiguyhāmīti saṃvijjamānaṃ na guyhāmi.

Here, “I do not hide what I have” means I do not hide what is existing.

Evañca pana vatvā sīghameva kamaṇḍalunā udakaṃ āharitvā udakaṃ hatthe pātetvā piyabhariyaṃ brāhmaṇassa adāsi. Taṅkhaṇeyeva heṭṭhā vuttappakārāni sabbāni acchariyāni pāturahesuṃ. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Having said this, he quickly fetched water with the water-pot, poured water into the brahmin's hand, and gave his beloved wife to the brahmin. At that very moment, all the marvelous events mentioned before manifested. To illuminate this matter, the Teacher said:

2279.

2279.

“Maddiṃ [M 7.0356] hatthe gahetvāna, udakassa kamaṇḍaluṃ;

Brāhmaṇassa adā dānaṃ, sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhano.

“Taking Maddī by the hand, with the water-pot, the increaser of the Sivi kingdom gave the gift to the brahmin.”

2280.

2280.

“Tadāsi yaṃ bhiṃsanakaṃ, tadāsi lomahaṃsanaṃ;

Maddiṃ pariccajantassa, medanī sampakampatha.

“Then there was that which was frightening, then there was that which was hair-raising; as he was giving up Maddī, the earth trembled.”

2281.

2281.

“Nevassa maddī bhākuṭi, na sandhīyati na rodati;

Pekkhatevassa tuṇhī sā, eso jānāti yaṃ vara”nti.

“Maddī neither frowned at him, nor was she distressed, nor did she weep; she only looked at him in silence, thinking, ‘He knows what is best.’”

Tattha adā dānanti “ambho brāhmaṇa, maddito me sataguṇena sahassaguṇena satasahassaguṇena sabbaññutaññāṇameva piyataraṃ, idaṃ me dānaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇappaṭivedhassa paccayo hotū”ti vatvā dānaṃ adāsi vuttampi cetaṃ –

Here, “he gave a gift” means: “O brahmin, dearer to me than Maddī by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold is the knowledge of omniscience itself. May this gift of mine be a condition for the realization of the knowledge of omniscience.” Having said this, he gave the gift. And this was also said:

“Jāliṃ kaṇhājinaṃ dhītaṃ, maddiṃ deviṃ patibbataṃ;

Cajamāno na cintesiṃ, bodhiyāyeva kāraṇā.

“Jāli, my daughter Kaṇhājina, and Queen Maddī, the devoted wife; giving them up, I did not hesitate, for the sake of awakening alone.”

“Na me dessā ubho puttā, maddī devī na dessiyā;

Sabbaññutaṃ piyaṃ mayhaṃ, tasmā piye adāsaha”nti. (cariyā. 1.118-119);

“My two sons were not hateful to me, nor was Queen Maddī hateful. Omniscience is dear to me; therefore, I gave those who were dear.” (Cariyāpiṭaka 1.9.56-57)

Tattha sampakampathāti pathavī udakapariyantaṃ katvā kampittha. Nevassa maddī bhākuṭīti bhikkhave, tasmiṃ khaṇe maddī “maṃ mahallakassa brāhmaṇassa rājā detī”ti kodhavasena bhākuṭipi nāhosi. Na sandhīyati na rodatīti neva maṅku ahosi, na akkhīni pūretvā rodati, atha kho tuṇhī sā hutvā “mādisaṃ itthiratanaṃ dadamāno na nikkāraṇā dassati, eso [V 7.0349] yaṃ varaṃ, taṃ jānātī”ti phullapadumavaṇṇaṃ assa mukhaṃ pekkhateva, olokayamānāva ṭhitāti attho.

In the passage, 'trembled' means the earth shook down to its watery limits. 'Maddī neither frowned at him' means, monks, at that moment Maddī did not even frown out of anger, thinking, 'The king is giving me to this old brahmin.' 'Nor was she distressed, nor did she weep' means she was neither sullen nor did she weep with eyes full of tears. Rather, remaining silent, she stood and gazed at his face, which was like a blooming lotus, thinking, 'One who gives a jewel of a woman such as me will not do so without reason; he knows what is best.' This is the meaning.

Atha mahāsatto “kīdisā maddī”ti tassā mukhaṃ olokesi. Sāpi “sāmi kiṃ maṃ olokesī”ti vatvā sīhanādaṃ nadantī imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Great Being looked at her face, wondering, “How is Maddī feeling?” And she, saying, “My lord, why do you look at me?” uttered a lion's roar and spoke this verse:

2282.

2282.

“Komārī yassāhaṃ bhariyā, sāmiko mama issaro;

Yassicche tassa maṃ dajjā, vikkiṇeyya haneyya vā”ti.

“I, who have been his wife since maidenhood—my husband is my lord; to whomever he wishes, he may give me, sell me, or even slay me.”

Tattha [P 6.0571][M 7.0357] komārī yassāhaṃ bhariyāti ahaṃ yassa tava daharikā bhariyā, so tvaññeva mama issaro sāmiko. Yassicche tassāti issaro ca nāma dāsiṃ maṃ yassa dātuṃ iccheyya, tassa dadeyya. Vikkiṇeyya vāti dhanena vā atthe sati vikkiṇeyya, maṃsena vā atthe sati haneyya, tasmā yaṃ vo ruccati, taṃ karotha, nāhaṃ kujjhāmīti.

In the passage, 'I, who have been his wife since maidenhood' means: 'I have been your young wife, and you alone are my lord and master.' 'To whomever he wishes' means that as my lord, if he wished to give me, his slave-woman, he could give me. 'Or he may sell me' means he may sell me if he has need of wealth, or he may kill me if he has need of my flesh. Therefore, do whatever you please; I am not angry.

Sakko tesaṃ paṇītajjhāsayataṃ viditvā thutiṃ akāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Sakka, knowing the excellence of their intention, offered praise. To illuminate this matter, the Teacher said:

2283.

2283.

“Tesaṃ saṅkappamaññāya, devindo etadabravi;

Sabbe jitā te paccūhā, ye dibbā ye ca mānusā.

“Knowing their intention, the king of gods said this: ‘All obstacles are conquered by you, both those that are divine and those that are human.’”

2284.

2284.

“Ninnāditā te pathavī, saddo te tidivaṅgato;

Samantā vijjutā āguṃ, girīnaṃva patissutā.

“The earth was made to resound by you, your sound reached the triple heaven. Lightnings flashed on all sides, like the echoes from the mountains.”

2285.

2285.

“Tassa te anumodanti, ubho nāradapabbatā;

Indo ca brahmā pajāpati, somo yamo vessavaṇo;

Sabbe devānumodanti, dukkarañhi karoti so.

“Both Nārada and Pabbata rejoice in that deed of yours; Indra, Brahmā, Pajāpati, Soma, Yama, and Vessavaṇa—all the gods rejoice, for he does what is difficult to do.”

2286.

2286.

“Duddadaṃ dadamānānaṃ, dukkaraṃ kamma kubbataṃ;

Asanto nānukubbanti, sataṃ dhammo durannayo.

“Giving what is hard to give, doing a deed that is difficult—the unrighteous do not imitate this; the Dhamma of the virtuous is hard to follow.”

2287.

2287.

“Tasmā [V 7.0350] satañca asataṃ, nānā hoti ito gati;

Asanto nirayaṃ yanti, santo saggaparāyaṇā.

“Therefore, for the virtuous and the unvirtuous, the destination after departing from here is different: the unvirtuous go to hell, while the virtuous are bound for heaven.”

2288.

2288.

“Yametaṃ kumāre adā, bhariyaṃ adā vane vasaṃ;

Brahmayānamanokkamma, sagge te taṃ vipaccatū”ti.

“That you gave your children and your wife while dwelling in the forest, not deviating from the Brahmā-vehicle—may that ripen for you in heaven.”

Tattha paccūhāti paccatthikā. Dibbāti dibbasampattipaṭibāhakā. Mānusāti manussasampattipaṭibāhakā. Ke pana teti? Macchariyadhammā. Te sabbe puttadāraṃ dentena mahāsattena jitā. Tenāha “sabbe jitā te paccūhā”ti. Dukkarañhi karoti soti so vessantaro rājā ekakova araññe vasanto bhariyaṃ brāhmaṇassa dento dukkaraṃ [M 7.0358] karotīti evaṃ sabbe devā anumodantīti vadati. “Yameta”nti gāthaṃ anumodanaṃ karonto āha. Vane vasanti vane vasanto. Brahmayānanti seṭṭhayānaṃ. Tividho hi sucaritadhammo evarūpo ca dānadhammo ariyamaggassa paccayo hotīti “brahmayāna”nti vuccati. Tasmā yaṃ taṃ idaṃ ajja dānaṃ dadatopi nipphannaṃ brahmayānaṃ apāyabhūmiṃ anokkamitvā sagge te taṃ vipaccatu, vipākapariyosāne ca sabbaññutaññāṇadāyakaṃ hotūti.

Here, ‘paccūhā’ means adversaries. ‘Dibba’ refers to those who obstruct divine success. ‘Mānusa’ refers to those who obstruct human success. But what are these? The qualities of stinginess. All these were conquered by the Great Being when he gave away his children and wife. Therefore, it is said, ‘All obstacles are conquered by you.’ ‘Dukkarañhi karoti so’ means that King Vessantara, dwelling alone in the forest and giving his wife to a brahmin, performs what is difficult to do; thus, it is said that all the gods rejoice. He spoke the verse beginning ‘Yametaṃ’ while expressing his approval. ‘Vane vasaṃ’ means dwelling in the forest. ‘Brahmayāna’ means the excellent vehicle. For the threefold good conduct and such a practice of giving become a condition for the noble path—thus it is called ‘brahmayāna.’ Therefore, may that ‘brahmayāna,’ accomplished by the giving of this gift today, not descending into the realms of misery, ripen for you in heaven, and at the culmination of its result, may it bestow the knowledge of omniscience.

Evamassa sakko anumodanaṃ katvā “idāni mayā idha papañcaṃ akatvā imaṃ imasseva datvā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā āha –

Thus Sakka, having expressed his approval to him, thought, “Now, without delaying here, it is fitting for me to give her back to him and go,” and so he said:

2289.

2289.

“Dadāmi [P 6.0572] bhoto bhariyaṃ, maddiṃ sabbaṅgasobhanaṃ;

Tvañceva maddiyā channo, maddī ca patinā saha.

“I give you back your wife, Maddī, beautiful in every limb. May you be a fitting match for Maddī, and Maddī for her husband.”

2290.

2290.

“Yathā payo ca saṅkho ca, ubho samānavaṇṇino;

Evaṃ tuvañca maddī ca, samānamanacetasā.

“Just as milk and a conch are both of the same color, so too are you and Maddī, of one mind and heart.”

2291.

2291.

“Avaruddhettha araññasmiṃ, ubho sammatha assame;

Khattiyā gottasampannā, sujātā mātupettito;

Yathā puññāni kayirātha, dadantā aparāpara”nti.

“Confined here in the forest, may you both dwell peacefully in the hermitage. You are Khattiyas, endowed with noble lineage, well-born on both your mother's and father's side. May you perform meritorious deeds, giving again and again.”

Tattha [V 7.0351] channoti anurūpo. Ubho samānavaṇṇinoti samānavaṇṇā ubhopi parisuddhāyeva. Samānamanacetasāti ācārādīhi kammehi samānena manasaṅkhātena cetasā samannāgatā. Avaruddhetthāti raṭṭhato pabbājitā hutvā ettha araññe vasatha. Yathā puññānīti yathā jetuttaranagare vo bahūni puññāni katāni, hiyyo puttānaṃ ajja bhariyāya dānavasenapi katānīti ettakeneva paritosaṃ akatvā ito uttaripi aparāparaṃ dadantā yathānurūpāni puññāni kareyyāthāti.

Here, ‘channo’ means suitable. ‘Both of the same color’ means both are of the same appearance and both are indeed pure. ‘Of one mind and heart’ means endowed with a mind, that is, consciousness, that is alike in conduct and other actions. ‘Confined here’ means having been banished from the kingdom, you dwell here in the forest. ‘May you perform meritorious deeds’ means: just as many meritorious deeds were performed by you in the city of Jetuttara, and yesterday by the giving of your sons, and today your wife, not being satisfied with just this much, but continuing to give again and again, you should perform meritorious deeds as is fitting.

Evañca pana vatvā sakko mahāsattassa maddiṃ paṭicchāpetvā varaṃ dātuṃ attānaṃ ācikkhanto āha –

And having spoken thus, Sakka, having had the Great Being accept Maddī back, revealed himself in order to grant a boon, and said:

2292.

2292.

“Sakkohamasmi devindo, āgatosmi tavantike;

Varaṃ varassu rājisi, vare aṭṭha dadāmi te”ti.

“I am Sakka, lord of the gods; I have come into your presence. Choose a boon, O royal sage; I will grant you eight boons.”

Kathentoyeva [M 7.0359] ca dibbattabhāvena jalanto taruṇasūriyo viya ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Tato bodhisatto varaṃ gaṇhanto āha –

And even as he spoke, blazing with his divine nature like the morning sun, he stood in the sky. Then the Bodhisatta, accepting the boons, said:

2293.

2293.

“Varaṃ ce me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Pitā maṃ anumodeyya, ito pattaṃ sakaṃ gharaṃ;

Āsanena nimanteyya, paṭhametaṃ varaṃ vare.

“O Sakka, lord of all beings, if you would grant me a boon: may my father approve of me and invite me back from here to my own home with a seat—this is the first boon I choose.”

2294.

2294.

“Purisassa vadhaṃ na roceyyaṃ, api kibbisakārakaṃ;

Vajjhaṃ vadhamhā moceyyaṃ, dutiyetaṃ varaṃ vare.

“I would not approve of the killing of a man, even a wrongdoer; I would free the condemned from execution—this is the second boon I choose.”

2295.

2295.

“Ye vuḍḍhā ye ca daharā, ye ca majjhimaporisā;

Mameva upajīveyyuṃ, tatiyetaṃ varaṃ vare.

“May the old, the young, and those of middle age live dependent on me alone—this is the third boon I choose.”

2296.

2296.

“Paradāraṃ na gaccheyyaṃ, sadārapasuto siyaṃ;

Thīnaṃ vasaṃ na gaccheyyaṃ, catutthetaṃ varaṃ vare.

“May I never go to another’s wife, but remain devoted to my own wife; may I never fall under the sway of women—this is the fourth boon I choose.”

2297.

2297.

“Putto [V 7.0352] me sakka jāyetha, so ca dīghāyuko siyā;

Dhammena jine pathaviṃ, pañcametaṃ varaṃ vare.

“O Sakka, may a son be born to me, and may he be long-lived; may he conquer the earth with righteousness—this is the fifth boon I choose.”

2298.

2298.

“Tato ratyā vivasāne, sūriyassuggamanaṃ pati;

Dibbā bhakkhā pātubhaveyyuṃ, chaṭṭhametaṃ varaṃ vare.

“Then, at the end of the night, toward the rising of the sun, may divine foods appear—this is the sixth boon I choose.”

2299.

2299.

“Dadato me na khīyetha, datvā nānutapeyyahaṃ;

Dadaṃ cittaṃ pasādeyyaṃ, sattametaṃ varaṃ vare.

“While I am giving, may my wealth not diminish; having given, may I not regret it; while giving, may I gladden my mind—this is the seventh boon I choose.”

2300.

2300.

“Ito [P 6.0573] vimuccamānāhaṃ, saggagāmī visesagū;

Anivatti tato assaṃ, aṭṭhametaṃ varaṃ vare”ti.

“Being freed from here, may I be a heaven-goer who has attained distinction; may I be a non-returner from there—this is the eighth boon I choose.”

Tattha anumodeyyāti sampaṭiccheyya na kujjheyya. Ito pattanti imamhā araññā sakaṃ gharaṃ anuppattaṃ. Āsanenāti rājāsanena. Rajjaṃ me detūti vadati. Api kibbisakārakanti rājā hutvā rājāparādhikampi vajjhaṃ vadhamhā moceyyaṃ, evarūpassapi me vadho nāma na ruccatu. Mameva upajīveyyunti sabbete maññeva nissāya upajīveyyuṃ. Dhammena jineti dhammena jinātu, dhammena rajjaṃ kāretūti attho. Visesagūti visesagamano hutvā tusitapure nibbatto homīti vadati. Anivatti [M 7.0360] tato assanti tusitabhavanato cavitvā manussattaṃ āgato punabhave anivatti assaṃ, sabbaññutaṃ sampāpuṇeyyanti vadati.

Herein, 'may he approve' means may he accept me and not be angry. 'Having returned from here' means having arrived at my own home from this forest. By 'with a seat' is meant with the royal throne; he is saying, 'May he give me the kingdom.' By 'even a wrongdoer' is meant: being a king, I would free even one who has committed an offense against the king from execution; may killing of such a kind never be agreeable to me. By 'may they live dependent on me alone' means may all these people live depending on me alone. By 'may he conquer with Dhamma' is meant may he conquer with Dhamma and rule the kingdom with Dhamma—this is the meaning. By 'one who has attained distinction' he means: having gone to a special state, may I be reborn in the Tusita heaven. By 'may I be a non-returner from there' he means: having passed away from the Tusita existence and come to the human state, in a future life may I be a non-returner and attain omniscience.

2301.

2301.

“Tassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, devindo etadabravi;

‘Aciraṃ vata te tato, pitā taṃ daṭṭhumessatī’”ti.

Having heard his words, the king of the gods said this: 'Indeed, before long, your father will come to see you, restore the kingdom to you, and lead you to the city of Jetuttara.'

Tattha daṭṭhumessatīti mahārāja, tava mātā ca pitā ca acireneva taṃ passitukāmo hutvā idhāgamissati, āgantvā ca pana setacchattaṃ datvā rajjaṃ niyyādetvā jetuttaranagarameva nessati, sabbe te manorathā matthakaṃ pāpuṇissanti, mā cintayi, appamatto hohi, mahārājāti.

Herein, 'will come to see' means: O great king, your mother and father, desiring to see you, will soon come here. And having come, they will give you the white parasol, hand over the kingdom to you, and take you to the city of Jetuttara itself. All your wishes will be fulfilled. Do not worry, be diligent, O great king.

Evaṃ mahāsattassa ovādaṃ datvā sakko sakaṭṭhānameva gato. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Having thus given advice to the Great Being, Sakka went to his own abode. Revealing that meaning, the Teacher said:

2302.

2302.

“Idaṃ [V 7.0353] vatvāna maghavā, devarājā sujampati;

Vessantare varaṃ datvā, saggakāyaṃ apakkamī”ti.

Having said this, Maghavā, king of the gods, Sujampati, having granted Vessantara the boons, departed to the heavenly host.

Tattha vessantareti vessantarassa. Apakkamīti gato anuppattoyevāti.

Therein, 'Vessantare' means 'to Vessantara'. 'Apakkami' means he has gone, he has indeed arrived.

Sakkapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Section on Sakka is concluded.

Mahārājapabbavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on the Great King

Bodhisatto ca maddī ca sammodamānā sakkadattiye assame vasiṃsu. Jūjakopi kumāre gahetvā saṭṭhiyojanamaggaṃ paṭipajji. Devatā kumārānaṃ ārakkhamakaṃsu. Jūjakopi sūriye atthaṅgate kumāre gacche bandhitvā bhūmiyaṃ nipajjāpetvā sayaṃ caṇḍavāḷamigabhayena rukkhaṃ āruyha viṭapantare sayati. Tasmiṃ khaṇe eko devaputto vessantaravaṇṇena, ekā devadhītā maddivaṇṇena āgantvā kumāre mocetvā hatthapāde sambāhitvā nhāpetvā maṇḍetvā dibbabhojanaṃ bhojetvā dibbasayane sayāpetvā [M 7.0361] aruṇuggamanakāle [P 6.0574] baddhākāreneva nipajjāpetvā antaradhāyi. Evaṃ te devatāsaṅgahena arogā hutvā gacchanti. Jūjakopi devatādhiggahito hutvā “kāliṅgaraṭṭhaṃ gacchāmī”ti gacchanto aḍḍhamāsena jetuttaranagaraṃ patto. Taṃ divasaṃ paccūsakāle sañjayo mahārājā supinaṃ passi. Evarūpo supino ahosi – rañño mahāvinicchaye nisinnassa eko puriso kaṇho dve padumāni āharitvā rañño hatthe ṭhapesi. Rājā tāni dvīsu kaṇṇesu piḷandhi. Tesaṃ reṇu bhassitvā rañño ure patati. So pabujjhitvā pātova brāhmaṇe pucchi. Te “cirapavutthā vo, deva, bandhavā āgamissantī”ti byākariṃsu. So pātova sīsaṃ nhāyitvā nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā alaṅkaritvā vinicchaye nisīdi. Devatā brāhmaṇaṃ dvīhi kumārehi saddhiṃ ānetvā rājaṅgaṇe ṭhapayiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe rājā maggaṃ olokento kumāre disvā āha –

The Bodhisatta and Maddī, rejoicing together, lived in the hermitage given by Sakka. Jūjaka, taking the children, set out on the sixty-yojana journey. The deities protected the children. When the sun had set, Jūjaka bound the children with a vine and made them lie on the ground, while he himself, fearing fierce wild beasts, climbed a tree and slept among the branches. At that moment, a son of the gods in the form of Vessantara and a daughter of the gods in the form of Maddī came, freed the children, massaged their hands and feet, bathed and adorned them, fed them divine food, and made them sleep on a divine bed. At dawn, they placed them back in their bound state and then disappeared. Thus, through the assistance of the deities, they traveled in good health. Jūjaka, influenced by the deities, while traveling and thinking, 'I will go to the Kāliṅga country,' reached the city of Jetuttara in half a month. That day at dawn, King Sañjaya had a dream. The dream was like this: While the king was seated in the great hall of justice, a dark-skinned man brought two lotuses and placed them in the king’s hands. The king placed one on each of his ears. Their pollen fell and scattered on the king’s chest. Upon waking, he asked the brahmins early in the morning. They predicted, 'Your long-lost relatives will return, O king.' Early in the morning, he bathed his head, ate food of various excellent flavors, dressed himself, and sat in the hall of justice. The deities brought the brahmin with the two children and placed them in the royal courtyard. At that moment, the king, looking down the road, saw the children and said:

2303.

2303.

“Kassetaṃ mukhamābhāti, hemaṃ-vuttattamagginā;

Nikkhaṃva jātarūpassa, ukkāmukhapahaṃsitaṃ.

“Whose face is this that shines, like gold refined by fire, like a bullion of pure gold, polished at the mouth of a crucible?

2304.

2304.

“Ubho [V 7.0354] sadisapaccaṅgā, ubho sadisalakkhaṇā;

Jālissa sadiso eko, ekā kaṇhājinā yathā.

“Both have similar limbs, both have similar marks; one is like Jāli, the other is like Kaṇhājinā.

2305.

2305.

“Sīhā bilāva nikkhantā, ubho sampatirūpakā;

Jātarūpamayāyeva, ime dissanti dārakā”ti.

“Like young lions emerging from a cave, both of matching appearance; these children appear as if made of pure gold.”

Tattha hemaṃvuttattamaggināti hemaṃ iva uttattaṃ agginā. Sīhā bilāva nikkhantāti kañcanaguhato nikkhantā sīhā viya.

Therein, 'hemaṃ-vuttattamagginā' means like gold heated by fire. 'Sīhā bilāva nikkhantā' means like lions emerging from a golden cave.

Evaṃ rājā tīhi gāthāhi kumāre vaṇṇetvā ekaṃ amaccaṃ āṇāpesi “gacchetaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ dārakehi saddhiṃ ānehī”ti. So vegena gantvā brāhmaṇaṃ ānesi. Atha rājā brāhmaṇaṃ āha –

Thus, the king, having praised the children with these three verses, ordered a minister, 'Go and bring that brahmin here together with the children.' He swiftly went and brought the brahmin. Then the king said to the brahmin:

2306.

2306.

“Kuto nu bhavaṃ bhāradvāja, ime ānesi dārake;

Ajja raṭṭhaṃ anuppatto, kuhiṃ gacchasi brāhmaṇā”ti.

“From where, venerable Bhāradvāja, have you brought these children? Today you have arrived in the kingdom. Where are you going, brahmin?”

Jūjako [M 7.0362] āha –

Jūjaka said:

2307.

2307.

“Mayhaṃ te dārakā deva, dinnā vittena sañjaya;

Ajja pannarasā ratti, yato laddhā me dārakā”ti.

“To me these children, O king, O Sañjaya, were given with joy. Today is the fifteenth night since the children were obtained by me.”

Tattha vittenāti tuṭṭhena pasannena. Ajja pannarasā rattīti imesaṃ laddhadivasato paṭṭhāya ajja pannarasā rattīti vadati.

Herein, by 'vittena' is meant with a pleased and clear mind. 'Today is the fifteenth night' means he is saying: 'Counting from the day they were received, today is the fifteenth night.'

Rājā [P 6.0575] āha –

The king said:

2308.

2308.

“Kena vā vācapeyyena, sammāñāyena saddahe;

Ko tetaṃ dānamadadā, puttake dānamuttama”nti.

“By what persuasive speech, by what right method should I believe? Who gave you that gift—the supreme gift of children?”

Tattha kena vā vācapeyyenāti brāhmaṇa, kena piyavacanena te tayā laddhā. Sammāñāyena saddaheti [V 7.0355] musāvādaṃ akatvā sammāñāyena kāraṇena amhe saddahāpeyyāsi. Puttaketi attano piyaputtake uttamaṃ dānaṃ katvā ko te etaṃ dānaṃ adadāti.

Herein, 'by what persuasive speech' means: 'Brahmin, by what endearing speech were they obtained by you?' 'By what right method should I believe' means: 'Without speaking falsehood, by what right reason could you make us believe?' By 'who gave you that gift—the supreme gift of children' is meant: 'Who gave you this gift, having made the supreme gift of his own beloved children?'

Jūjako āha –

Jūjaka said:

2309.

2309.

“Yo yācataṃ patiṭṭhāsi, bhūtānaṃ dharaṇīriva;

So me vessantaro rājā, puttedāsi vane vasaṃ.

“He who was the support for those who begged, like the earth for all beings—that King Vessantara gave me his children while dwelling in the forest.

2310.

2310.

“Yo yācataṃ gatī āsi, savantīnaṃva sāgaro;

So me vessantaro rājā, puttedāsi vane vasa”nti.

“He who was the resort for beggars, like the ocean for flowing rivers—that King Vessantara gave me his children while dwelling in the forest.”

Tattha patiṭṭhāsīti patiṭṭhā āsi.

Here, ‘patiṭṭhāsi’ means ‘was a support’.

Taṃ sutvā amaccā vessantaraṃ garahamānā āhaṃsu –

Hearing this, the ministers, reproaching Vessantara, said:

2311.

2311.

“Dukkaṭaṃ vata bho raññā, saddhena gharamesinā;

Kathaṃ nu puttake dajjā, araññe avaruddhako.

“Indeed, a wrong was done by the king, a faithful householder. How could he give away his children while living in exile in the forest?

2312.

2312.

“Imaṃ bhonto nisāmetha, yāvantettha samāgatā;

Kathaṃ vessantaro rājā, puttedāsi vane vasaṃ.

Listen to this, good sirs, all who are gathered here: how King Vessantara gave away his children, dwelling in the forest.

2313.

2313.

“Dāsiṃ dāsañca so dajjā, assaṃ cassatarīrathaṃ;

Hatthiñca kuñjaraṃ dajjā, kathaṃ so dajja dārake”ti.

“He might give a female slave and a male slave, a horse, a mule, and a chariot; he might give an elephant and a great tusker—but how could he give away his children?”

Tattha [M 7.0363] saddhenāti saddhāya sampannenapi satā gharaṃ āvasantena raññā idaṃ dukkaṭaṃ vata, ayuttaṃ vata kataṃ. Avaruddhakoti raṭṭhā pabbājito araññe vasanto. Imaṃ bhontoti bhonto nagaravāsino yāvanto ettha samāgatā, sabbe imaṃ nisāmetha upadhāretha, kathaṃ nāmeso puttake dāse katvā adāsi, kena nāma evarūpaṃ katapubbanti adhippāyenevamāhaṃsu. Dajjāti dāsādīsu yaṃ kiñci dhanaṃ detu. Kathaṃ so dajja dāraketi ime pana dārake kena kāraṇena adāsīti.

Here, ‘saddhena’ means: by the king, though endowed with faith and living at home, this was indeed a wrong deed, an improper deed. ‘Avaruddhako’ means: banished from the kingdom, dwelling in the forest. ‘Imaṃ bhonto’ means: ‘O townsfolk, all who are gathered here, listen to this, consider this: how indeed did he make his children into slaves and give them away? By whom indeed has such a thing been done before?’—with this intention they spoke thus. ‘Dajjā’ means: let him give any wealth such as slaves and so forth. ‘Kathaṃ so dajja dārake’ means: for what reason did he give away these children?

Taṃ [V 7.0356] sutvā kumāro pitu garahaṃ asahanto vātābhihatassa sineruno bāhaṃ oḍḍento viya imaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing this, the prince, unable to bear the reproach of his father, as if stretching out an arm to protect Mount Sineru when struck by the wind, spoke this verse:

2314.

2314.

“Yassa nassa ghare dāso, asso cassatarīratho;

Hatthī ca kuñjaro nāgo, kiṃ so dajjā pitāmahā”ti.

“If one has no slave in his house, no horses, mules, or chariots, no elephants or great tuskers—what could he give, O grandfather?”

Rājā āha –

The king said:

2315.

2315.

“Dānamassa [P 6.0576] pasaṃsāma, na ca nindāma puttakā;

Kathaṃ nu hadayaṃ āsi, tumhe datvā vanibbake”ti.

“We praise his gift, O children, and do not blame it. How indeed was his heart when he gave you to the mendicant?”

Tattha dānamassa pasaṃsāmāti puttakā mayaṃ tava pitu dānaṃ pasaṃsāma na nindāma.

Here, ‘dānamassa pasaṃsāma’ means, ‘O children, we praise your father’s gift, we do not blame it.’

Taṃ sutvā kumāro āha –

Hearing that, the prince said:

2316.

2316.

“Dukkhassa hadayaṃ āsi, atho uṇhampi passasi;

Rohinīheva tambakkhī, pitā assūni vattayī”ti.

“His heart was full of sorrow, and his breath was hot; with eyes red like the star Rohiṇī, my father shed tears.”

Tattha dukkhassa hadayaṃ āsīti pitāmaha kaṇhājināya vuttaṃ etaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā tassa hadayaṃ dukkhaṃ āsi. Rohinīheva tambakkhīti tambavaṇṇehi viya rattaakkhīhi mama pitā tasmiṃ khaṇe assūni pavattayi.

Here, ‘Dukkhassa hadayaṃ āsi’ means, ‘O grandfather, upon hearing these words spoken by Kaṇhājinā, his heart was sorrowful.’ ‘Rohinīheva tambakkhī’ means that at that moment, my father shed tears with eyes reddened like copper.

Idānissā taṃ vacanaṃ dassento āha –

Now, showing her words, he said:

2317.

2317.

“Yaṃ taṃ kaṇhājināvoca, ayaṃ maṃ tāta brāhmaṇo;

Laṭṭhiyā paṭikoṭeti, ghare jātaṃva dāsiyaṃ.

“What Kaṇhājinā said was: ‘This brahmin, dear father, strikes me with a stick as if I were a slave born in his house.’

2318.

2318.

“Na [M 7.0364] cāyaṃ brāhmaṇo tāta, dhammikā honti brāhmaṇā;

Yakkho brāhmaṇavaṇṇena, khādituṃ tāta neti no;

Nīyamāne pisācena, kiṃ nu tāta udikkhasī”ti.

“‘This is no true brahmin, dear father, for brahmins are righteous; he is a yakkha in a brahmin’s guise, dear father, who leads us away to devour us. While we are being led away by a goblin, why do you merely look on, dear father?’”

Atha [V 7.0357] ne kumāre brāhmaṇaṃ amuñcante disvā rājā gāthamāha –

Then, seeing that the brahmin would not release the children, the king spoke this verse:

2319.

2319.

“Rājaputtī ca vo mātā, rājaputto ca vo pitā;

Pubbe me aṅkamāruyha, kiṃ nu tiṭṭhatha ārakā”ti.

“Your mother is a princess, and your father is a prince; formerly you climbed upon my lap, why do you now stand afar?”

Tattha pubbe meti tumhe ito pubbe maṃ disvā vegenāgantvā mama aṅkamāruyha, idāni kiṃ nu ārakā tiṭṭhathāti?

Here, ‘pubbe me’ means, ‘Before, when you saw me, you would rush over and climb onto my lap—why do you now stand at a distance?’

Kumāro āha –

The prince said:

2320.

2320.

“Rājaputtī ca no mātā, rājaputto ca no pitā;

Dāsā mayaṃ brāhmaṇassa, tasmā tiṭṭhāma ārakā”ti.

“Our mother is a princess, and our father is a prince; but we are the brahmin’s slaves, therefore we stand afar.”

Tattha dāsā mayanti idāni pana mayaṃ brāhmaṇassa dāsā bhavāma.

Here, ‘dāsā mayaṃ’ means, ‘but now we have become the Brahmin’s slaves.’

Rājā āha –

The king said:

2321.

2321.

“Mā sammevaṃ avacuttha, ḍayhate hadayaṃ mama;

Citakāyaṃva me kāyo, āsane na sukhaṃ labhe.

“Do not speak thus, my dears! My heart burns; my body is like a funeral pyre, I find no comfort on my seat.”

2322.

2322.

“Mā sammevaṃ avacuttha, bhiyyo sokaṃ janetha maṃ;

Nikkiṇissāmi dabbena, na vo dāsā bhavissatha.

“Do not speak thus, my dears, you increase my sorrow even more; I will ransom you with wealth; you shall not be slaves.”

2323.

2323.

“Kimagghiyañhi [P 6.0577] vo tāta, brāhmaṇassa pitā adā;

Yathābhūtaṃ me akkhātha, paṭipādentu brāhmaṇa”nti.

“At what price indeed, dear children, did your father give you to the brahmin? Tell me truthfully, so that the brahmin may be paid.”

Tattha sammāti piyavacanaṃ. Citakāyaṃva me kāyoti idāni mama kāyo aṅgāracitakāyaṃ āropito viya jāto. Janetha manti janetha me, ayameva vā pāṭho. Nikkiṇissāmi dabbenāti dhanaṃ datvā mocessāmi. Kimagghiyanti kiṃ agghaṃ katvā. Paṭipādentūti dhanaṃ paṭicchāpentu.

Here, ‘samma’ is an affectionate term. ‘Citakāyaṃva me kāyo’ means: ‘Now my body has become as if placed on a pyre of burning coals.’ ‘Janetha maṃ’ means ‘janetha me’, or this is the reading. ‘Nikkiṇissāmi dabbena’ means: ‘I will free you by giving wealth.’ ‘Kimagghiyaṃ’ means: ‘At what price?’ that is, ‘For what value?’ ‘Paṭipādentu’ means: ‘Let them receive,’ that is, ‘Let them accept the wealth.’

Kumāro [V 7.0358][M 7.0365] āha –

The prince said:

2324.

2324.

“Sahassagghañhi maṃ tāta, brāhmaṇassa pitā adā;

Atha kaṇhājinaṃ kaññaṃ, hatthinā ca satena cā”ti.

“Indeed, dear grandfather, my father gave me to the brahmin, valued at a thousand gold pieces; and then Kaṇhājinā the maiden, and a hundred elephants.”

Tattha sahassagghaṃ hīti deva, maṃ pitā tadā nikkhasahassaṃ agghāpetvā adāsi. Atha kaṇhājinanti kaniṭṭhaṃ pana me kaṇhājinaṃ. Hatthinā ca satena cāti hatthīnañca assānañca usabhānañca nikkhānañcāti sabbesaṃ etesaṃ satena antamaso mañcapīṭhapāduke upādāya sabbasatena agghāpesīti.

Herein, ‘sahassagghaṃ hi’ means, ‘O deva, my father then gave me, having valued me at a thousand nikkhas.’ ‘Atha kaṇhājinaṃ’ means, ‘and my younger sister Kaṇhājinā.’ ‘Hatthinā ca satena ca’ means that he valued all of these at a hundred each—elephants, horses, bulls, and nikkhas—and everything down to beds, chairs, and footstools, he valued at a hundred of each.

Rājā kumārānaṃ nikkayaṃ dāpento āha –

The king, causing the ransom to be given for the princes, said:

2325.

2325.

“Uṭṭhehi katte taramāno, brāhmaṇassa avākara;

Dāsisataṃ dāsasataṃ, gavaṃ hatthusabhaṃ sataṃ;

Jātarūpasahassañca, puttānaṃ dehi nikkaya”nti.

“Arise, Katta, make haste; give to the brahmin: a hundred female slaves, a hundred male slaves, a hundred cows, noble elephants, and bulls, and a thousand pieces of gold. Give this as the ransom for the sons.”

Tattha avākarāti dehi.

Herein, ‘avākara’ means ‘give.’

2326.

2326.

“Tato kattā taramāno, brāhmaṇassa avākari;

Dāsisataṃ dāsasataṃ, gavaṃ hatthusabhaṃ sataṃ;

Jātarūpasahassañca, puttānaṃdāsi nikkaya”nti.

“Then Katta, hurrying, gave to the brahmin: a hundred female slaves, a hundred male slaves, a hundred cows, noble elephants, and bulls, and a thousand pieces of gold; he gave this as the ransom for the sons.”

Tattha avākarīti adāsi. Nikkayanti agghassa mūlaṃ.

Herein, ‘avākari’ means ‘he gave.’ ‘Nikkayaṃ’ means the redemption price.

Evaṃ brāhmaṇassa sabbasatañca nikkhasahassañca kumārānaṃ nikkayaṃ adāsi, sattabhūmikañca pāsādaṃ, brāhmaṇassa parivāro mahā ahosi. So dhanaṃ paṭisāmetvā pāsādaṃ abhiruyha sādurasabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā mahāsayane nipajji. Kumāre sīsaṃ nahāpetvā bhojetvā alaṅkaritvā ekaṃ ayyako, ekaṃ ayyikāti dvepi ucchaṅge upavesesuṃ. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Thus, he gave to the brahmin a hundred of each item and a thousand nikkhas as ransom for the princes, and a seven-storied palace. The brahmin’s retinue became vast. Having secured his wealth, he ascended the palace, feasted on delicious food, and lay down on a grand bed. Having had the children bathed, fed, and adorned, they seated both of them on their laps—one by the grandfather, one by the grandmother. The Teacher, making this matter clear, said:

2327.

2327.

“Nikkiṇitvā nahāpetvā, bhojayitvāna dārake;

Samalaṅkaritvā bhaṇḍena, ucchaṅge upavesayuṃ.

“Having ransomed, bathed, and fed the children, and having adorned them with ornaments, they seated them upon their laps.”

2328.

2328.

“Sīsaṃ [V 7.0359][M 7.0366] nhāte [P 6.0578] sucivatthe, sabbābharaṇabhūsite;

Rājā aṅke karitvāna, ayyako paripucchatha.

“With heads bathed, in clean clothes, adorned with all ornaments, the king, the grandfather, having taken them on his lap, asked:”

2329.

2329.

“Kuṇḍale ghusite māle, sabbābharaṇabhūsite;

Rājā aṅke karitvāna, idaṃ vacanamabravi.

“With resounding earrings and garlands, adorned with all ornaments, the king, having taken them on his lap, spoke this word:”

2330.

2330.

“Kacci ubho arogā te, jāli mātāpitā tava;

Kacci uñchena yāpenti, kacci mūlaphalā bahū.

“Are both your parents well, Jāli? Do they sustain themselves by gleaning? Are roots and fruits abundant?”

2331.

2331.

“Kacci ḍaṃsā makasā ca, appameva sarīsapā;

Vane vāḷamigākiṇṇe, kacci hiṃsā na vijjatī”ti.

“Are gadflies and mosquitoes few, and likewise reptiles? In the forest teeming with wild beasts, is there no harm?”

Tattha kuṇḍaleti kuṇḍalāni pilandhāpetvā. Ghusiteti ugghosite manoramaṃ ravaṃ ravante. Māleti pupphāni pilandhāpetvā. Aṅke karitvānāti jālikumāraṃ aṅke nisīdāpetvā.

Herein, ‘kuṇḍale’ means having adorned them with earrings. ‘Ghusite’ means resounding, making a pleasant sound. ‘Māle’ means having adorned them with flowers. ‘Aṅke karitvāna’ means having seated Prince Jāli on his lap.

Kumāro āha –

The prince said:

2332.

2332.

“Atho ubho arogā me, deva mātāpitā mama;

Atho uñchena yāpenti, atho mūlaphalā bahū.

“Indeed, both my parents are healthy, O deva; indeed, they sustain themselves by gleaning; indeed, roots and fruits are abundant.”

2333.

2333.

“Atho ḍaṃsā makasā ca, appameva sarīsapā;

Vane vāḷamigākiṇṇe, hiṃsā nesaṃ na vijjati.

“Indeed, gadflies and mosquitoes, and likewise reptiles, are few; in the forest teeming with wild beasts, there is no harm for them.”

2334.

2334.

“Khaṇantālukalambāni, bilāni takkalāni ca;

Kolaṃ bhallātakaṃ bellaṃ, sā no āhatva posati.

“Digging up ālu and kalamba roots, bilva and takkala fruits, jujube, marking nut, and bael fruit—these she brings and nourishes us.”

2335.

2335.

“Yañceva sā āharati, vanamūlaphalahāriyā;

Taṃ no sabbe samāgantvā, rattiṃ bhuñjāma no divā.

“Whatever she, the gatherer of forest roots and fruits, brings, that we all assemble and eat at night, not by day.”

2336.

2336.

“Ammāva [V 7.0360] no kisā paṇḍu, āharantī dumapphalaṃ;

Vātātapena sukhumālī, padumaṃ hatthagatāmiva.

“Our mother is thin and pale, gathering fruit from the trees; delicate from wind and sun, like a lotus crushed in the hand.”

2337.

2337.

“Ammāya patanū kesā, vicarantyā brahāvane;

Vane vāḷamigākiṇṇe, khaggadīpinisevite.

“Our mother’s hair is thin, as she wanders in the great forest, in a forest teeming with wild beasts, frequented by rhinoceroses and leopards.”

2338.

2338.

“Kesesu [M 7.0367] jaṭaṃ bandhitvā, kacche jallamadhārayi;

Cammavāsī chamā seti, jātavedaṃ namassatī”ti.

“Binding her hair in a matted lock, she wears grime in her armpits; clad in a hide, she sleeps on the ground and pays homage to the sacred fire.”

Tattha khaṇantālukalambānīti khaṇantī ālūni ca kalambāni ca. Iminā mātāpitūnaṃ kicchajīvikaṃ vaṇṇeti. Taṃ noti ettha noti nipātamattaṃ. Padumaṃ hatthagatāmivāti hatthena parimadditaṃ padumaṃ viya jātā. Patanū kesāti deva, ammāya me mahāvane vicarantiyā te bhamarapattavaṇṇā kāḷakesā rukkhasākhādīhi viluttā patanū jātā. Jallamadhārayīti ubhohi kacchehi jallaṃ dhāreti, kiliṭṭhavesena vicaratīti.

Herein, ‘khaṇantālukalambāni’ means ‘digging up ālu and kalamba.’ By this, he describes the difficult livelihood of his parents. In ‘Taṃ no,’ ‘no’ is merely a particle. ‘Padumaṃ hatthagatāmiva’ means she became like a lotus crushed by the hand. ‘Patanū kesā’ means, ‘O deva, as my mother wandered in the great forest, her black hair, the color of a bee’s wing, became thin, ravaged by tree branches and the like.’ ‘Jallamadhārayi’ means she bore grime in both armpits, living in a soiled state.

So evaṃ mātu dukkhitabhāvaṃ kathetvā ayyakaṃ codento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Having thus described his mother’s suffering, he admonished his grandfather, speaking this verse:

2339.

2339.

“Puttā piyā manussānaṃ, lokasmiṃ udapajjisuṃ;

Na hi nūnamhākaṃ ayyassa, putte sneho ajāyathā”ti.

“Sons are dear to people; they are born into the world. Surely for our grandfather, no affection for his son has arisen.”

Tattha [P 6.0579] udapajjisunti uppajjiṃsu.

Herein, ‘udapajjiṃsu’ means ‘they arose.’

Tato rājā attano dosaṃ āvikaronto āha –

Then the king, revealing his own fault, said:

2340.

2340.

“Dukkaṭañca hi no putta, bhūnahaccaṃ kataṃ mayā;

Yohaṃ sivīnaṃ vacanā, pabbājesimadūsakaṃ.

“Indeed, my child, a wrong deed, a terrible crime, has been done by me, who at the word of the Sivis banished the innocent one.”

2341.

2341.

“Yaṃ me kiñci idha atthi, dhanaṃ dhaññañca vijjati;

Etu vessantaro rājā, siviraṭṭhe pasāsatū”ti.

“Whatever wealth and grain I have here, let King Vessantara come and rule over the Sivi kingdom.”

Tattha [V 7.0361] puttāti putta jāli etaṃ amhākaṃ dukkaṭaṃ. Bhūnahaccanti vuḍḍhighātakammaṃ. Yaṃ me kiñcīti tāta, yaṃ me kiñci idha atthi, sabbaṃ te pitu demi. Siviraṭṭhe pasāsatūti imasmiṃ nagare so rājā hutvā pasāsatūti.

Herein, 'putta' means, 'O son Jāli, this is our wrongdoing.' 'Bhūnahaccaṃ' means a deed of killing one who is grown. 'Yaṃ me kiñci' means, 'Dear father, whatever I possess here, I give it all to your father.' 'Siviraṭṭhe pasāsatū' means, 'Let him, having become king, rule in this city.'

Kumāro āha –

The prince said:

2342.

2342.

“Na deva mayhaṃ vacanā, ehiti sivisuttamo;

Sayameva devo gantvā, siñca bhogehi atraja”nti.

“Not by my word, O king, will the foremost of the Sivis come; you yourself, O king, must go and shower your son with possessions.”

Tattha sivisuttamoti siviseṭṭho vessantaro. Siñcāti mahāmegho viya vuṭṭhiyā bhogehi abhisiñca.

Herein, 'sivisuttamo' means Vessantara, the foremost of the Sivis. 'Siñca' means 'anoint with possessions like a great cloud with its rain.'

2343.

2343.

“Tato [M 7.0368] senāpatiṃ rājā, sañjayo ajjhabhāsatha;

Hatthī assā rathā pattī, senā sannāhayantu naṃ;

Negamā ca maṃ anventu, brāhmaṇā ca purohitā.

Then King Sañjaya addressed his commander-in-chief: 'Let elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—the army—be equipped for him. Let the townsfolk follow me, and the brahmins and royal chaplains.'

2344.

2344.

“Tato saṭṭhisahassāni, yodhino cārudassanā;

Khippamāyantu sannaddhā, nānāvaṇṇehilaṅkatā.

“Then let sixty thousand warriors, of pleasing appearance, come swiftly, equipped for battle and adorned in diverse colors.”

2345.

2345.

“Nīlavatthadharā neke, pītāneke nivāsitā;

Aññe lohitauṇhīsā, suddhāneke nivāsitā;

Khippamāyantu sannaddhā, nānāvaṇṇehilaṅkatā.

“Let some be clad in dark blue garments and some in yellow; others with crimson turbans, and some in white. Let them come swiftly, well-equipped and adorned in various colors.”

2346.

2346.

“Himavā yathā gandhadharo, pabbato gandhamādano;

Nānārukkhehi sañchanno, mahābhūtagaṇālayo.

“Just as the fragrant mountain Gandhamādana in the Himālayas, covered with various trees and being a dwelling for hosts of spirits, shines and wafts its scent through the eight directions day and night, so let my capital city, filled with all the ministers and soldiers, shine and waft its scent through the eight directions.”

2347.

2347.

“Osadhehi ca dibbehi, disā bhāti pavāti ca;

Khippamāyantu sannaddhā, disā bhantu pavantu ca.

And with divine herbs, the directions shine and are filled with fragrance; let them come swiftly, equipped, and let them brighten and perfume the quarters.

2348.

2348.

“Tato [V 7.0362] nāgasahassāni, yojayantu catuddasa;

Suvaṇṇakacchā mātaṅgā, hemakappanavāsasā.

“Then let fourteen thousand elephants of the Mātaṅga breed be yoked, with golden girths and golden trappings, and let them assemble together with their riders.”

2349.

2349.

“Ārūḷhā gāmaṇīyehi, tomaraṅkusapāṇibhi;

Khippamāyantu sannaddhā, hatthikkhandhehi dassitā.

Mounted by leaders with pikes and goads in hand, let them come swiftly, equipped, displayed upon the backs of elephants.

2350.

2350.

“Tato assasahassāni, yojayantu catuddasa;

Ājānīyāva jātiyā, sindhavā sīghavāhanā.

“Then let fourteen thousand Sindh horses, thoroughbred by birth and swift as the wind, be yoked and assembled now together with their riders, armed with bows and arrows.”

2351.

2351.

“Ārūḷhā gāmaṇīyehi, illiyācāpadhāribhi;

Khippamāyantu sannaddhā, assapiṭṭhehīlaṅkatā.

Mounted by leaders bearing short swords and bows, let them come swiftly, equipped and adorned on horseback.

2352.

2352.

“Tato [P 6.0580] rathasahassāni, yojayantu catuddasa;

Ayosukatanemiyo, suvaṇṇacitapakkhare.

“Then let fourteen thousand chariots be yoked, well-made with iron rims and side-panels decorated with gold and silver; with banners raised on the chariot fronts, and let the warriors equipped with shields and the expert archers who can hit a hair-tip assemble now,” thus he ordered all the divisions of the army.

2353.

2353.

“Āropentu dhaje tattha, cammāni kavacāni ca;

Vippālentu ca cāpāni, daḷhadhammā pahārino;

Khippamāyantu sannaddhā, rathesu rathajīvino”ti.

Let them raise banners there, along with shields and armor. Let them string their bows, resolute strikers; let the chariot-warriors come swiftly, equipped, in their chariots.

Tattha [M 7.0369] sannāhayantunanti sannayhantu. Saṭṭhisahassānīti mama puttena sahajātā saṭṭhisahassā amaccā. Nīlavatthadharā neketi eke nīlavatthanivāsitā hutvā āyantu. Mahābhūtagaṇālayoti bahuyakkhagaṇānaṃ ālayo. Disā bhantu pavantu cāti vuttappakāro himavā viya ābharaṇavilepanādīhi obhāsentu ceva pavāyantu ca. Hatthikkhandhehīti te hatthigāmaṇino hatthikkhandhehi khippamāyantu. Dassitāti dassitavibhūsanā. Ayosukatanemiyoti ayena suṭṭhu parikkhittanemiyo. Suvaṇṇacitapakkhareti suvaṇṇena khacitapakkhare. Evarūpe cuddasa sahasse rathe yojayantūti vadati. Vippālentūti āropentu.

Herein, 'sannāhayantu' means let them be harnessed. 'Saṭṭhisahassāni' means the sixty thousand ministers born together with my son. 'Nīlavatthadharā neke' means some, having dressed in blue garments, should come. 'Mahābhūtagaṇālayo' means the abode of many hosts of yakkhas. 'Disā bhantu pavantu ca' means, like the aforementioned Himālaya, let them both shine and give off fragrance with ornaments, ointments, and so on. 'Hatthikkhandhehi' means those elephant leaders should come swiftly on the backs of elephants. 'Dassitā' means displaying their adornments. 'Ayosukatanemiyo' means wheels well-encircled with an iron rim. 'Suvaṇṇacitapakkhare' means with side-panels inlaid with gold. Thus, he speaks of yoking fourteen thousand such chariots. 'Vippālentu' means let them mount.

Evaṃ rājā senaṅgaṃ vicāretvā “puttassa me jetuttaranagarato yāva vaṅkapabbatā aṭṭhusabhavitthāraṃ āgamanamaggaṃ samatalaṃ katvā maggālaṅkāratthāya idañcidañca karothā”ti āṇāpento āha –

Thus the king, having arranged the divisions of the army, spoke to his ministers to prepare the road from the city of Jetuttara to the Vaṅka mountain, a distance of sixty yojanas, by clearing and leveling it to a width of eight usabhas: “For my son’s arrival, do this and that for the road's decoration.”

2354.

2354.

“Lājā [V 7.0363] olopiyā pupphā, mālāgandhavilepanā;

Agghiyāni ca tiṭṭhantu, yena maggena ehiti.

“Let parched grain, flowers, garlands, perfumes, and ointments be scattered; let festoons be hung along the path by which he will come. Let the road be cleared of trees and thickets to a width of eight usabhas, leveled, and decorated by the people of the towns and villages with white sand, parched grain, perfumes, plantain trees, sugar-cane, white banners, and many various garlands and gems.”

2355.

2355.

“Gāme gāme sataṃ kumbhā, merayassa surāya ca;

Maggamhi patitiṭṭhantu, yena maggena ehiti.

“In every village and at the city gates, let a hundred pots of wine and liquor be set out; let them be placed along the road by which my son will come.”

2356.

2356.

“Maṃsā pūvā saṅkuliyo, kummāsā macchasaṃyutā;

Maggamhi patitiṭṭhantu, yena maggena ehiti.

“Let meat, cakes, sweetmeats, and barley-gruel mixed with fish be placed in shops on both sides of the road where he will come, for people to buy and eat.”

2357.

2357.

“Sappi telaṃ dadhi khīraṃ, kaṅgubījā bahū surā;

Maggamhi patitiṭṭhantu, yena maggena ehiti.

Let ghee, oil, curds, milk, millet seeds, and much liquor be placed along the road by which he will come.

2358.

2358.

“Āḷārikā ca sūdā ca, naṭanaṭṭakagāyino;

Pāṇissarā kumbhathūṇiyo, mandakā sokajjhāyikā.

“Let there be cooks and bakers, and let festivals capable of dispelling all sorrow be held; let dancers, actors, singers, hand-clappers, pot-drummers, acrobats, pole-climbers, and rope-walkers perform with all kinds of musical instruments.”

2359.

2359.

“Āhaññantu sabbavīṇā, bheriyo dindimāni ca;

Kharamukhāni dhamentu, nadantu ekapokkharā.

“Let those who can sweetly sing various types of songs perform; let those who play flutes, conches, and various drums also play. Let all lutes, drums, and kettledrums be struck; let them blow the horns and let the single-headed drums roar.”

2360.

2360.

“Mudiṅgā paṇavā saṅkhā, godhā parivadentikā;

Dindimāni ca haññantu, kutumpadindimāni cā”ti.

“Let the mṛdaṅgas, small drums, and conches be played, along with crocodile-shaped harps and lutes; let the kettledrums and various other drums be struck with a sweet and harmonious sound following the melody.”

Tattha [M 7.0370] lājā olopiyā pupphāti lājehi saddhiṃ lājapañcamakāni pupphāni okirantānaṃ okiraṇapupphāni paṭiyādethāti āṇāpeti. Mālāgandhavilepanāti maggavitāne olambakamālā [P 6.0581] ceva gandhavilepanāni ca. Agghiyāni cāti pupphaagghiyāni ceva ratanaagghiyāni ca yena maggena mama putto ehiti, tattha tiṭṭhantu. Gāme gāmeti gāmadvāre gāmadvāre. Patitiṭṭhantūti pipāsitānaṃ pivanatthāya paṭiyāditā hutvā surāmerayamajjakumbhā tiṭṭhantu. Macchasaṃyutāti macchehi saṃyuttā. Kaṅgubījāti kaṅgupiṭṭhamayā. Mandakāti mandakagāyino. Sokajjhāyikāti māyākārā, aññepi vā ye keci uppannasokaharaṇasamatthā sokajjhāyikāti vuccanti, socante jane attano vaṃsaghosaparamparānaṃ nacce kate nissoke katvā sayāpakāti attho. Kharamukhānīti sāmuddikamahāmukhasaṅkhā. Saṅkhāti dakkhiṇāvaṭṭā muṭṭhisaṅkhā[V 7.0364], nāḷisaṅkhāti dve saṅkhā. Godhā parivadentikā dindimāni kutumpadindimānīti imānipi cattāri tūriyāneva.

Herein, 'Lājā olopiyā pupphā' means he ordered: 'Prepare flowers for scattering,' meaning that flowers of the fifth kind with parched grain should be scattered. 'Mālāgandhavilepanā' means garlands hanging from the road's canopy, as well as perfumes and ointments. 'Agghiyāni ca' means flower offerings and jewel offerings should be placed along the path by which my son will come. 'Gāme gāme' means at the gate of every village. 'Patitiṭṭhantu' means let pots of liquor, mead, and intoxicants, prepared for the thirsty to drink, be placed. 'Macchasaṃyutā' means prepared with fish. 'Kaṅgubījā' means made from millet flour. 'Mandakā' means singers of mandaka songs. 'Sokajjhāyikā' means illusionists, or any others skilled in dispelling arisen sorrow are called sokajjhāyikā; the meaning is that they make grieving people free from sorrow by performing their traditional lineage dance, causing them to be at ease. 'Kharamukhāni' means large-mouthed ocean conches. 'Saṅkhā' means two kinds of conches: right-turning fist-conches and tube-conches. 'Godhā, parivadentikā, dindimas, and kutumpadindimas'—these four are also musical instruments.

Evaṃ rājā maggālaṅkārāni vicāresi. Jūjakopi pamāṇātikkantaṃ bhuñjitvā jīrāpetuṃ asakkonto tattheva kālamakāsi. Rājā tassa sarīrakiccaṃ kārāpetvā “nagare koci brāhmaṇassa ñātako atthi, idaṃ gaṇhātū”ti bheriṃ carāpesi. Na kañcissa ñātakaṃ passi, dhanaṃ puna raññoyeva ahosi. Atha sattame divase sabbā senā sannipati. Atha rājā mahantena parivārena jāliṃ magganāyakaṃ katvā nikkhami. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Thus King Sañjaya had the road decorated. As for the brahmin Jūjaka, having enjoyed a level of luxury he had never known before and eating beyond measure of the fine food, he was unable to digest it and died of surfeit. King Sañjaya performed his funeral rites and had a drum beaten throughout the city, announcing, 'If there are any relatives of the brahmin Jūjaka, let them take his wealth.' When no relative was found, the wealth reverted to the king as unclaimed property. Then, on the seventh day after the arrival of Jāli, the entire army of twelve akkhobhinīs assembled. Then the king, with a great retinue and with Prince Jāli as the guide, set out from Jetuttara for the Vaṅka mountain. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:

2361.

2361.

“Sā senā mahatī āsi, uyyuttā sivivāhinī;

Jālinā magganāyena, vaṅkaṃ pāyāsi pabbataṃ.

That great army, the Sivi host, set out; with Jāli as their guide, they marched toward the Vaṅka mountain.

2362.

2362.

“Koñcaṃ nadati mātaṅgo, kuñjaro saṭṭhihāyano;

Kacchāya baddhamānāya, koñcaṃ nadati vāraṇo.

The royal elephant Paccaya, which had been returned by the King of Kaliṅga after the rains became favorable, sounded its cry. As its girth was being fastened for the journey to the Vaṅka mountain, the sixty-year-old elephant, joyful at the prospect of seeing its master Vessantara, trumpeted like a crane.

2363.

2363.

“Ājānīyā [M 7.0371] hasiyanti, nemighoso ajāyatha;

Abbhaṃ rajo acchādesi, uyyuttā sivivāhinī.

As King Sañjaya set out, the neighing of noble steeds and the roar of chariot wheels echoed, and dust covered the sky as the Sivi host marched forth.

2364.

2364.

“Sā senā mahatī āsi, uyyuttā hārahārinī;

Jālinā magganāyena, vaṅkaṃ pāyāsi pabbataṃ.

That great army, bearing garlands, set out; with Jāli as their guide, they marched to the Vaṅka mountain.

2365.

2365.

“Te pāviṃsu brahāraññaṃ, bahusākhaṃ mahodakaṃ;

Puppharukkhehi sañchannaṃ, phalarukkhehi cūbhayaṃ.

They entered the great forest, following the path past rivers flowing from mountains and valleys, a place adorned with various land and water flowers and both flowering and fruit-bearing trees.

2366.

2366.

“Tattha bindussarā vaggū, nānāvaṇṇā bahū dijā;

Kūjantamupakūjanti, utusampupphite dume.

There, many sweet-voiced birds of various colors sang and echoed one another in the trees blooming in season, flying in pairs from tree to tree, making the Himālayas a delight to the heart.

2367.

2367.

“Te gantvā dīghamaddhānaṃ, ahorattānamaccaye;

Padesaṃ taṃ upāgacchuṃ, yattha vessantaro ahū”ti.

Having traveled the distance of sixty yojanas from the city of Jetuttara over several days and nights, they approached the vicinity of the hermitage on the Vaṅka mountain where Vessantara was.

Tattha [V 7.0365] mahatīti dvādasaakkhobhaṇisaṅkhātā senā. Uyyuttāti payātā. Koñcaṃ nadatīti tadā kāliṅgaraṭṭhavāsino brāhmaṇā attano raṭṭhe deve vuṭṭhe taṃ nāgaṃ āharitvā sañjayassa adaṃsu. So hatthī “sāmikaṃ vata passituṃ labhissāmī”ti tuṭṭho koñcanādamakāsi. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kacchāyāti suvaṇṇakacchāya baddhamānāyapi tussitvā koñcaṃ nadati. Hasiyantīti hasasaddamakaṃsu[P 6.0582]. Hārahārinīti haritabbaharaṇasamatthā. Pāviṃsūti pavisiṃsu. Bahusākhanti bahurukkhasākhaṃ. Dīghamaddhānanti saṭṭhiyojanamaggaṃ. Upāgacchunti yattha vessantaro ahosi, taṃ padesaṃ upagatāti.

Therein, 'mahatī' means the army, numbered as twelve akkhobhiṇī. 'Uyyuttā' means set out. 'Koñcaṃ nadati' means: at that time, the brahmins of the Kāliṅga country, after the deity had rained upon their land, brought that elephant and gave it to Sañjaya. The elephant, pleased, thinking, 'Oh, I shall get to see my master,' made a trumpeting sound. This was said in reference to that. 'Kacchāyā' means: even while being bound with a golden girth, it trumpets in delight. 'Hasiyanti' means they made sounds of neighing. 'Hārahārinī' means capable of carrying what should be carried. 'Pāviṃsu' means they entered. 'Bahusākhaṃ' means having many tree branches. 'Dīghamaddhānaṃ' means the sixty-yojana journey. 'Upāgacchuṃ' means: they approached that region where Vessantara was.

Mahārājapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Description of the Chapter on the Great King is concluded.

Chakhattiyakammavaṇṇanā

12. The Chapter of the Six Khattiyas

Jālikumāro mucalindasaratīre khandhāvāraṃ nivāsāpetvā cuddasa rathasahassāni āgatamaggābhimukhāneva ṭhapāpetvā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ padese sīhabyagghadīpiādīsu ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahi. Hatthiādīnaṃ saddo mahā ahosi. Atha mahāsatto taṃ saddaṃ sutvā “kiṃ nu kho me paccāmittā [M 7.0372] mama pitaraṃ ghātetvā mamatthāya āgatā”ti maraṇabhayabhīto maddiṃ ādāya pabbataṃ āruyha senaṃ olokesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Prince Jāli established a camp on the shore of Lake Mucalinda, and having stationed fourteen thousand chariots facing the road they had come, he arranged for guards at the junctions where wild beasts like lions and tigers roamed. The sound of the twelve akkhobhinīs of soldiers, elephants, and horses echoed throughout the Himālayas. Then the Great Being, hearing that sound, thought, "Could it be that my enemies, after killing my father, have now come to kill me?" Terrified of death, he took Maddī and climbed the mountain to observe the army. Explaining this matter, the Teacher said:

2368.

2368.

“Tesaṃ sutvāna nigghosaṃ, bhīto vessantaro ahu;

Pabbataṃ abhiruhitvā, bhīto senaṃ udikkhati.

Hearing their uproar, Vessantara was afraid; climbing the mountain, he gazed upon the army in fear.

2369.

2369.

“Iṅgha maddi nisāmehi, nigghoso yādiso vane;

Ājānīyā hasiyanti, dhajaggāni ca dissare.

“Come, Maddī, listen! What an uproar there is in the forest! Noble steeds are neighing, and the tops of banners are seen fluttering.”

2370.

2370.

“Ime nūna araññasmiṃ, migasaṅghāni luddakā;

Vāgurāhi parikkhippa, sobbhaṃ pātetvā tāvade;

Vikkosamānā tibbāhi, hanti nesaṃ varaṃ varaṃ.

“O Maddī, just as hunters and fishermen surround herds of deer with nets and trap them in pits or pools, then kill the best among them with sharp spears, so these soldiers might kill us. O Maddī, look and see if this is our army or an enemy's. Why do they wish to harm us who live in such hardship after being driven from the kingdom?” Thus, fearing death, he lamented.

2371.

2371.

“Yathā mayaṃ adūsakā, araññe avaruddhakā;

Amittahatthattaṃ gatā, passa dubbalaghātaka”nti.

Just so, we who are innocent, confined in the forest, have fallen into the hands of enemies. Behold, the killer of the weak!

Tattha [V 7.0366] iṅghāti codanatthe nipāto. Nisāmehīti sakasenā vā parasenā vāti olokehi upadhārehi. “Ime nūna araññasmi”ntiādīnaṃ aḍḍhateyyagāthānaṃ evamatthasambandho veditabbo “maddi yathā araññamhi migasaṅghāni luddakā vāgurāhi parikkhippa atha vā pana sobbhaṃ pātetvā tāvadeva ‘hanatha, are, duṭṭhamige’ti vikkosamānā tibbāhi migamāraṇasattīhi nesaṃ migānaṃ varaṃ varaṃ thūlaṃ thūlaṃ hananti, ime ca nūna tatheva amhe asabbhāhi vācāhi vikkosamānā tibbāti sattīhi hanissanti, mayañca adūsakā araññe avaruddhakā raṭṭhā pabbājitā vane vasāma, evaṃ santepi amittānaṃ hatthattaṃ gatā, passa dubbalaghātaka”nti. Evaṃ so maraṇabhayena paridevi.

Therein, 'iṅgha' is a particle in the sense of urging. 'Nisāmehi' means: observe, ascertain whether it is our own army or an enemy army. The connection of meaning for the two and a half verses beginning with 'Ime nūna araññasmi' should be understood thus: 'Maddī, just as in the forest hunters, having surrounded herds of deer with nets or else having made them fall into a pit, right then, shouting, “Kill, you wicked deer!” kill the very best and largest of those deer with sharp, deer-killing spears; so too, surely, will these people kill us in the same way, shouting at us with uncivil words and with sharp spears. And we, innocent, confined in the forest, banished from the kingdom, live in the woods; even so, we have fallen into the hands of enemies. Behold, the killer of the weak!' Thus he lamented out of fear of death.

Sā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā senaṃ oloketvā “sakasenāya bhavitabba”nti mahāsattaṃ assāsentī imaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing his words and observing the army, she realized, "It must be our own army," and to reassure the Great Being, she uttered this verse:

2372.

2372.

“Amittā [P 6.0583] nappasāheyyuṃ, aggīva udakaṇṇave;

Tadeva tvaṃ vicintehi, api sotthi ito siyā”ti.

“Great King, enemies cannot harm you, just as a small fire cannot burn the great ocean. Reflect on just this: safety will surely come to us from this.”

Tattha aggīva udakaṇṇaveti yathā tiṇukkādīnaṃ vasena upanīto aggi aṇṇavasaṅkhātāni puthulagambhīrāni udakāni nappasahati, tāpetuṃ na sakkoti[M 7.0373], tathā taṃ amittā nappasaheyyuṃ nābhibhavissanti. Tadevāti yaṃ sakkena tuyhaṃ varaṃ datvā “mahārāja, na cirasseva te pitā ehitī”ti vuttaṃ, tadeva tvaṃ vicintehi, api nāma ito balakāyato amhākaṃ sotthi siyāti mahāsattaṃ assāsesi.

In that verse, 'just as a small fire cannot burn the ocean' means that just as a fire brought by a grass torch cannot overcome or heat the vast and deep waters of the ocean, so too enemies will not overcome you. 'Reflect on that very thing' means: reflect on the eight boons given by Sakka, who said, 'Great King, before long your father will bring you back to the kingdom.' If his words are true, safety and happiness will come to us from this army. Thus she consoled the Great Being.

Atha mahāsatto sokaṃ tanukaṃ katvā tāya saddhiṃ pabbatā oruyha paṇṇasālādvāre nisīdi, itarāpi attano paṇṇasālādvāre nisīdi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Then the Great Being, feeling somewhat relieved, descended the mountain with her and sat calmly like a golden statue on a stone slab at the door of his leaf-hut, while she sat at the door of her own leaf-hut. The Teacher, revealing this meaning, said:

2373.

2373.

“Tato vessantaro rājā, orohitvāna pabbatā;

Nisīdi paṇṇasālāyaṃ, daḷhaṃ katvāna mānasa”nti.

Then King Vessantara, descending from the mountain, sat in the leaf hut, having made his mind firm.

Tattha daḷhaṃ katvāna mānasanti mayaṃ pabbajitā nāma, amhākaṃ ko kiṃ karissatīti thiraṃ hadayaṃ katvā nisīdi.

Therein, 'having made his mind firm' means he sat down with a resolute heart, thinking, "We are renunciants; how could anyone harm us?"

Tasmiṃ [V 7.0367] khaṇe sañjayo rājā deviṃ āmantetvā – “bhadde, phussati amhesu sabbesu ekato gatesu soko mahā bhavissati, paṭhamaṃ tāva ahaṃ gacchāmi, tato ‘idāni sokaṃ vinodetvā nisinnā bhavissantī’ti sallakkhetvā tvaṃ mahantena parivārena āgaccheyyāsi. Atha thokaṃ kālaṃ vītināmetvā jālikaṇhājinā pacchato āgacchantū”ti vatvā rathaṃ nivattāpetvā āgatamaggābhimukhaṃ katvā tattha tattha ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahitvā alaṅkatahatthikkhandhato oruyha puttassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

At that moment, King Sañjaya addressed the queen: "Dear Phusati, if we all go together, great sorrow will arise. First, I shall go. Then, observing that 'they will now be seated, having dispelled their sorrow,' you may come with a large retinue. After allowing some time to pass, let Jāli and Kaṇhājinā follow behind." Having said this, he had the chariot turned back to face the path by which he had come, stationed guards here and there, and descended from the back of the adorned elephant to approach his son. The Teacher, revealing this meaning, said:

2374.

2374.

“Nivattayitvāna rathaṃ, vuṭṭhapetvāna seniyo;

Ekaṃ araññe viharantaṃ, pitā puttaṃ upāgami.

Having turned back the chariot and posted the armies, the father approached his son, who was living alone in the forest.

2375.

2375.

“Hatthikkhandhato oruyha, ekaṃso pañjalīkato;

Parikiṇṇo amaccehi, puttaṃ siñcitumāgami.

Descending from the elephant's back, with one shoulder bared and hands clasped in reverence, surrounded by ministers, he came to anoint his son.

2376.

2376.

“Tatthaddasa kumāraṃ so, rammarūpaṃ samāhitaṃ;

Nisinnaṃ paṇṇasālāyaṃ, jhāyantaṃ akutobhaya”nti.

There he saw the prince, of delightful form and composed, seated in a leaf-hut, meditating, free from fear from any quarter.

Tattha [M 7.0374] vuṭṭhapetvāna seniyoti ārakkhatthāya balakāye ṭhapetvā. Ekaṃsoti ekaṃsakatauttarāsaṅgo. Siñcitumāgamīti rajje abhisiñcituṃ upāgami. Rammarūpanti anañjitaṃ amaṇḍitaṃ.

Therein, 'vuṭṭhapetvāna seniyo' means having stationed the army for protection. 'Ekaṃso' means having the upper robe arranged over one shoulder. 'Siñcitum āgami' means he came to consecrate him for the kingship. 'Rammarūpaṃ' means un-anointed, unadorned.

2377.

2377.

“Tañca [P 6.0584] disvāna āyantaṃ, pitaraṃ puttagiddhinaṃ;

Vessantaro ca maddī ca, paccuggantvā avandisuṃ.

And seeing him, their father, approaching, yearning for his son, both Vessantara and Maddī went out to meet him and paid homage.

2378.

2378.

“Maddī ca sirasā pāde, sasurassābhivādayi;

Maddī ahañhi te deva, pāde vandāmi te suṇhā;

Te su tattha palissajja, pāṇinā parimajjathā”ti.

And Maddī bowed her head to her father-in-law's feet. 'I am Maddī, Your Majesty, your daughter-in-law; I pay homage to your feet.' Then he embraced them both there and stroked them with his hand.

Tattha pāde vandāmi te suṇhāti ahaṃ, deva, tava suṇhā pāde vandāmīti evaṃ vatvā vandi. Te su tatthāti te ubhopi jane tasmiṃ sakkadattiye assame palissajitvā hadaye nipajjāpetvā sīse paricumbitvā mudukena pāṇinā parimajjatha, piṭṭhiyo nesaṃ parimajji.

Therein, 'pāde vandāmi te suṇhā' means: having said, 'I, O King, your daughter-in-law, pay homage to your feet,' she paid homage. 'Te su tattha' means: embracing both those people in that hermitage given by Sakka, making them lie on his heart, kissing their heads, he stroked them with his soft hand; he stroked their backs.

Tato [V 7.0368] roditvā paridevitvā rājā soke parinibbute tehi saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karonto āha –

Then, having wept and lamented, when his sorrow had subsided, the king exchanged friendly greetings with them and said:

2379.

2379.

“Kacci vo kusalaṃ putta, kacci putta anāmayaṃ;

Kacci uñchena yāpetha, kacci mūlaphalā bahū.

Are you well, son? Are you free from illness, son? Do you maintain yourselves by gleaning? Are roots and fruits abundant?

2380.

2380.

“Kacci ḍaṃsā makasā ca, appameva sarīsapā;

Vane vāḷamigākiṇṇe, kacci hiṃsā na vijjatī”ti.

Are gadflies and mosquitoes few, and likewise reptiles? In this forest crowded with beasts of prey, is there no harm?

Pitu vacanaṃ sutvā mahāsatto āha –

Hearing his father's words, the Great Being said:

2381.

2381.

“Atthi no jīvikā deva, sā ca yādisakīdisā;

Kasirā jīvikā homa, uñchācariyāya jīvitaṃ.

We have a livelihood, O deva, such as it is; our livelihood is wretched, life is by gleaning.

2382.

2382.

“Aniddhinaṃ mahārāja, dametassaṃva sārathi;

Tyamhā aniddhikā dantā, asamiddhi dameti no.

O great king, lack of prosperity tames a person as a charioteer tames a horse; therefore we, being without prosperity, are tamed; our lack of prosperity tames us.

2383.

2383.

“Api no kisāni maṃsāni, pitu mātu adassanā;

Avaruddhānaṃ mahārāja, araññe jīvasokina”nti.

Indeed, our flesh is wasted away from not seeing our father and mother; confined, O great king, we live with sorrow in the forest.

Tattha [M 7.0375] yādisakīdisāti yā vā sā vā, lāmakāti attho. Kasirā jīvikā homāti tāta, amhākaṃ uñchācariyāya jīvitaṃ nāma kicchaṃ, dukkhā no jīvikā ahosi. Aniddhinanti mahārāja, aniddhiṃ asamiddhiṃ daliddapurisaṃ nāma sāva aniddhi cheko sārathi assaṃ viya dameti, nibbisevanaṃ karoti, te mayaṃ idha vasantā aniddhikā dantā nibbisevanā katā, asamiddhiyeva no dametīti. “Dametha no”tipi pāṭho, damayittha noti attho. Jīvasokinanti avigatasokānaṃ araññe vasantānaṃ kiṃ nāma amhākaṃ sukhanti vadati.

Herein, 'yādisakīdisā' means 'whatever it may be'; the meaning is 'inferior'. As for 'Kasirā jīvikā homa': 'Dear one, our life by gleaning is indeed difficult; our livelihood was painful.' As for 'Aniddhinaṃ': 'O great king, that very lack of prosperity, like a skilled charioteer taming a horse, tames a poor man who is without prosperity or success; it makes him docile. We, living here, being without prosperity, are tamed, made docile. It is indeed our lack of success that tames us.' There is also the reading 'Dametha no', which means 'you tamed us'. As for 'Jīvasokinaṃ': it means 'for those dwelling in the forest whose sorrow has not departed, what happiness is there for us?' he says.

Evañca pana vatvā puna puttānaṃ pavattiṃ pucchanto āha –

Having said this, he then asked about the welfare of his sons, saying:

2384.

2384.

“Yepi [V 7.0369] te siviseṭṭhassa, dāyādāpattamānasā;

Jālī kaṇhājinā cubho, brāhmaṇassa vasānugā;

Accāyikassa luddassa, yo ne gāvova sumbhati.

And what of those heirs of the best of the Sivis, whose desires are unfulfilled—Jāli and Kaṇhājina, both—who are subject to the will of a brahmin; a cruel one in urgent need, who strikes them like cattle?

2385.

2385.

“Te [P 6.0585] rājaputtiyā putte, yadi jānātha saṃsatha;
