Pariyāpuṇātha no khippaṃ, sappadaṭṭhaṃva māṇava”nti.

If you know those sons of the royal princess, tell us; quickly relieve our minds, as one would a snake-bitten youth.

Tattha dāyādāpattamānasāti mahārāja, yepi te tava siviseṭṭhassa dāyādā apattamānasā asampuṇṇamanorathā hutvā brāhmaṇassa vasānugā jātā, te dve kumāre yo brāhmaṇo gāvova sumbhati paharati, te rājaputtiyā putte yadi diṭṭhavasena vā sutavasena vā jānātha saṃsatha. Sappadaṭṭhaṃva māṇavanti visanimmadanatthāya sappadaṭṭhaṃ māṇavaṃ tikicchantā viya khippaṃ no pariyāpuṇātha kathethāti vadati.

Herein, 'dāyādāpattamānasā' means: O great king, regarding those heirs of yours, the best of the Sivis, who, with unfulfilled desires and wishes unaccomplished, became subject to the brahmin's will; those two princes whom the brahmin strikes like cattle—if you know those sons of the royal princess by sight or by hearing, tell us. 'Sappadaṭṭhaṃva māṇavaṃ' means: 'just as one would treat a snake-bitten youth to remove the venom, so quickly inform us, speak,' he says.

Rājā āha –

The king said:

2386.

2386.

“Ubho kumārā nikkītā, jālī kaṇhājinā cubho;

Brāhmaṇassa dhanaṃ datvā, putta mā bhāyi assasā”ti.

Both princes have been redeemed, Jāli and Kaṇhājina both; having given wealth to the brahmin, son, do not be afraid, be comforted.

Tattha nikkītāti nikkayaṃ datvā gahitā.

Herein, `nikkītā` means taken after giving a price.

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto paṭiladdhassāso pitarā saddhiṃ paṭisanthāramakāsi –

Having heard that, the Great Being, regaining his composure, exchanged friendly greetings with his father:

2387.

2387.

“Kacci [M 7.0376] nu tāta kusalaṃ, kacci tāta anāmayaṃ;

Kacci nu tāta me mātu, cakkhu na parihāyatī”ti.

I hope, father, that you are well? I hope, father, that you are free from illness? I hope, father, that my mother's eyesight has not failed?

Tattha cakkhu na parihāyatīti puttasokena rodantiyā cakkhu na parihāyatīti.

Herein, `cakkhu na parihāyati` means: has her eyesight not failed from weeping out of grief for her son?

Rājā āha –

The king said:

2388.

2388.

“Kusalañceva [V 7.0370] me putta, atho putta anāmayaṃ;

Atho ca putta te mātu, cakkhu na parihāyatī”ti.

It is well with me, son, and, son, I am free from illness. And also, son, your mother's eyesight has not failed.

Bodhisatto āha –

The Bodhisatta said:

2389.

2389.

“Kacci arogaṃ yoggaṃ te, kacci vahati vāhanaṃ;

Kacci phīto janapado, kacci vuṭṭhi na chijjatī”ti.

I hope your draught animals are healthy? I hope your vehicle travels well? I hope the country is prosperous? I hope the rain is not cut off?

Tattha vuṭṭhīti vuṭṭhidhārā.

Herein, `vuṭṭhi` means a stream of rain.

Rājā āha –

The king said:

2390.

2390.

“Atho arogaṃ yoggaṃ me, atho vahati vāhanaṃ;

Atho phīto janapado, atho vuṭṭhi na chijjatī”ti.

And my draught animals are healthy, and my vehicle travels well; and the country is prosperous, and the rain is not cut off.

Evaṃ tesaṃ sallapantānaññeva phussatī devī “idāni sokaṃ tanukaṃ katvā nisinnā bhavissantī”ti sallakkhetvā mahāparivārena saddhiṃ puttassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Tamatthaṃ [P 6.0586] pakāsento satthā āha –

While they were thus conversing, Queen Phussatī, perceiving that 'now they must be sitting with their grief somewhat lessened,' went with a large retinue to her son. The Teacher, revealing that matter, said:

2391.

2391.

“Iccevaṃ mantayantānaṃ, mātā nesaṃ adissatha;

Rājaputtī giridvāre, pattikā anupāhanā.

Thus, while they were conferring, their mother appeared; the princess at the mountain gate, on foot and without sandals.

2392.

2392.

“Tañca disvāna āyantiṃ, mātaraṃ puttagiddhiniṃ;

Vessantaro ca maddī ca, paccuggantvā avandisuṃ.

And seeing her coming, the mother longing for her son, Vessantara and Maddī went forth to meet her and paid homage.

2393.

2393.

“Maddī ca sirasā pāde, sassuyā abhivādayi;

Maddī ahañhi te ayye, pāde vandāmi te suṇhā”ti.

And Maddī, with her head at her mother-in-law's feet, paid homage, saying: 'Noble lady, I am Maddī, your daughter-in-law; I pay homage at your feet.'

Tesaṃ phussatideviṃ vanditvā ṭhitakāle puttakā kumārakumārikāhi parivutā āgamiṃsu. Maddī ca tesaṃ āgamanamaggaṃ olokentīyeva aṭṭhāsi. Sā te sotthinā āgacchante disvā sakabhāvena [V 7.0371] saṇṭhātuṃ [M 7.0377] asakkontī taruṇavacchā viya gāvī paridevamānā tato pāyāsi. Tepi taṃ disvā paridevantā mātarābhimukhāva padhāviṃsu. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

While she stood there, having paid homage to Queen Phussatī, the children approached, surrounded by young boys and girls. Maddī stood watching the path of their arrival. Seeing them coming safely, unable to maintain her composure, she went towards them lamenting like a cow for her young calf. They too, seeing her, ran weeping towards their mother. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

2394.

2394.

“Maddiñca puttakā disvā, dūrato sotthimāgatā;

Kandantā mabhidhāviṃsu, vacchabālāva mātaraṃ.

The children, having come safely from afar, upon seeing Maddī, ran towards her weeping, like young calves towards their mother.

2395.

2395.

“Maddī ca puttake disvā, dūrato sotthimāgate;

Vāruṇīva pavedhentī, thanadhārābhisiñcathā”ti.

And Maddī, seeing her children who had arrived safely from afar, trembling like one possessed, bathed them with streams of milk from her breasts.

Tattha kandantā mabhidhāviṃsūti kandantā abhidhāviṃsu. Vāruṇīvāti yakkhāviṭṭhā ikkhaṇikā viya pavedhamānā thanadhārā abhisiñcathāti.

Herein, `kandantā mabhidhāviṃsu` means 'weeping, they ran towards'. `Vāruṇīva` means 'trembling like a female seer possessed by a yakkha, she bathed them with streams from her breasts'.

Sā kira mahāsaddena paridevitvā kampamānā visaññī hutvā dīghato pathaviyaṃ pati. Kumārāpi vegenāgantvā visaññino hutvā mātu upariyeva patiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe tassā dvīhi thanehi dve khīradhārā nikkhamitvā tesaṃ mukheyeva pavisiṃsu. Sace kira ettako assāso nābhavissa, dve kumārā sukkhahadayā hutvā addhā nassissanti. Vessantaropi piyaputte disvā sokaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto visaññī hutvā tattheva pati. Mātāpitaropissa visaññino hutvā tattheva patiṃsu, tathā sahajātā saṭṭhisahassā amaccā. Taṃ kāruññaṃ passantesu ekopi sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi. Sakalaṃ assamapadaṃ yugantavātena pamadditaṃ viya sālavanaṃ ahosi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe pabbatā nadiṃsu, mahāpathavī kampi, mahāsamuddo saṅkhubhi, sineru girirājā onami. Cha kāmāvacaradevalokā ekakolāhalā ahesuṃ.

She, it is said, wailed with a great cry and, trembling, lost consciousness and fell prostrate upon the ground. The children, rushing swiftly, also lost consciousness and fell right upon their mother. At that moment, two streams of milk flowed from her two breasts and entered their mouths. If there had not been such a solace, the two children would surely have died with parched hearts. Seeing his beloved children, Vessantara, unable to restrain his grief, fell unconscious right there. His parents also lost consciousness and fell in the same place, as did the sixty thousand ministers born at the same time as him. Among those witnessing such a piteous scene, not a single person could maintain their composure. The entire hermitage became like a sāl forest flattened by a world-ending wind. At that moment, the mountains roared, the great earth trembled, the great ocean churned, and Sineru, king of mountains, bowed low. The six heavens of the sense sphere became a single tumultuous uproar.

Sakko devarājā “cha khattiyā saparisā visaññino jātā, tesu ekopi uṭṭhāya kassaci sarīre udakaṃ siñcituṃ samattho nāma natthi, ahaṃ dāni imesaṃ pokkharavassaṃ vassāpessāmī”ti cintetvā chakhattiyasamāgame pokkharavassaṃ vassāpesi. Tattha ye temitukāmā, te tementi, atemitukāmānaṃ upari ekabindumattampi na patati, padumapattato udakaṃ viya nivattitvā gacchati. Iti pokkharavane patitaṃ [M 7.0378] vassaṃ viya taṃ vassaṃ ahosi. Cha khattiyā [P 6.0587] assāsaṃ paṭilabhiṃsu. Mahājano tampi disvā “aho acchariyaṃ, aho abbhutaṃ evarūpe ñātisamāgame pokkharavassaṃ vassi, mahāpathavī kampī”ti acchariyaṃ pavedesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Sakka, the king of the gods, thought: 'Six nobles with their retinues have fallen unconscious. Not one among them is capable of rising to sprinkle water on another's body. Now, I shall cause a pokkhara rain to fall upon them.' Having thus thought, he made a pokkhara rain fall upon the gathering of the six nobles. In that rain, those who wished to be wet were moistened, while not a single drop fell upon those who did not wish to be wet; it rolled off like water from a lotus leaf. Thus, the rain was like a shower fallen in a lotus pond. The six nobles regained consciousness. Seeing this, the great multitude proclaimed the wonder, saying: 'Oh, how marvelous! Oh, how astonishing! At such a gathering of relatives, a pokkhara rain fell, and the great earth trembled!' To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

2396.

2396.

“Samāgatānaṃ [V 7.0372] ñātīnaṃ, mahāghoso ajāyatha;

Pabbatā samanādiṃsu, mahī pakampitā ahu.

When the relatives gathered, a great sound arose; the mountains echoed, and the earth quaked.

2397.

2397.

“Vuṭṭhidhāraṃ pavattento, devo pāvassi tāvade;

Atha vessantaro rājā, ñātīhi samagacchatha.

Causing a stream of rain to fall, the god rained at that very moment; then King Vessantara was reunited with his relatives.

2398.

2398.

“Nattāro suṇisā putto, rājā devī ca ekato;

Yadā samāgatā āsuṃ, tadāsi lomahaṃsanaṃ.

Grandsons, daughter-in-law, son, the king, and the queen together—when they were gathered, it was hair-raising.

2399.

2399.

“Pañjalikā tassa yācanti, rodantā bherave vane;

Vessantarañca maddiñca, sabbe raṭṭhā samāgatā;

Tvaṃ nosi issaro rājā, rajjaṃ kāretha no ubho”ti.

With palms joined in reverence, they plead, weeping in the fearsome forest; all those gathered from the kingdom beg Vessantara and Maddī: 'You are our lord and king; may you both rule the kingdom for us!'

Tattha ghosoti kāruññaghoso. Pañjalikāti sabbe nāgarā ceva negamā ca jānapadā ca paggahitañjalikā hutvā. Tassa yācantīti tassa pādesu patitvā roditvā kanditvā “deva, tvaṃ no sāmi issaro, pitā te idheva abhisiñcitvā nagaraṃ netukāmo, kulasantakaṃ setacchattaṃ paṭicchathā”ti yāciṃsu.

Here, 'sound' means the sound of compassion. 'With palms joined in reverence' means all the city-dwellers, townsfolk, and country-folk had their hands raised in reverence. 'They beg him' means that having fallen at his feet, weeping and wailing, they begged, saying: 'Your Majesty, you are our master and lord. Your father wishes to anoint you right here and take you to the city. Please accept the white umbrella, the family heirloom.'

Chakhattiyakammavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Description of the Affair of the Six Nobles is finished.

Nagarakaṇḍavaṇṇanā

The Description of the Chapter on the Return to the City

Taṃ sutvā mahāsatto pitarā saddhiṃ sallapanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing that, the Great Being, conversing with his father, spoke this verse:

2400.

2400.

“Dhammena rajjaṃ kārentaṃ, raṭṭhā pabbājayittha maṃ;

Tvañca jānapadā ceva, negamā ca samāgatā”ti.

While I was ruling the kingdom according to the Dhamma, you—together with the country-folk and townsfolk—banished me from the realm.'

Tato [M 7.0379] rājā puttaṃ attano dosaṃ khamāpento āha –

Then the king, asking his son to forgive his fault, said:

2401.

2401.

“Dukkaṭañca [V 7.0373] hi no putta, bhūnahaccaṃ kataṃ mayā;

Yohaṃ sivīnaṃ vacanā, pabbājesimadūsaka”nti.

Indeed, my son, a wrong was done, a heinous crime was committed by me; for I, at the word of the Sivis, banished the innocent one.

Imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā attano dukkhaharaṇatthaṃ puttaṃ yācanto itaraṃ gāthamāha –

Having spoken this verse, begging his son for the removal of his own suffering, he spoke another verse:

2402.

2402.

“Yena kenaci vaṇṇena, pitu dukkhaṃ udabbahe;

Mātu bhaginiyā cāpi, api pāṇehi attano”ti.

By whatever means possible, one should remove the suffering of one's father, or of one's mother or sister, even at the cost of one's own life.'

Tattha udabbaheti hareyya. Api pāṇehīti tāta puttena nāma jīvitaṃ pariccajitvāpi mātāpitūnaṃ sokadukkhaṃ haritabbaṃ, tasmā mama dosaṃ hadaye akatvā mama vacanaṃ karohi, imaṃ isiliṅgaṃ hāretvā rājavesaṃ gaṇha tātāti iminā kira naṃ adhippāyenevamāha.

Here, 'one should remove' (udabbahe) means one should take away. 'Even with one's own life' means: 'Dear son, a son should indeed take away the sorrow and suffering of his parents even by sacrificing his own life. Therefore, without taking my fault to heart, do as I ask. Cast off this ascetic's guise and take up the royal attire, dear one.' It was with this intention that he spoke thus.

Bodhisatto [P 6.0588] rajjaṃ kāretukāmopi “ettake pana akathite garukaṃ nāma na hotī”ti kathesi. Mahāsatto “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Athassa adhivāsanaṃ viditvā sahajātā saṭṭhisahassā amaccā “nahānakālo mahārāja, rajojallaṃ pavāhayā”ti vadiṃsu. Atha ne mahāsatto “thokaṃ adhivāsethā”ti vatvā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā isibhaṇḍaṃ omuñcitvā paṭisāmetvā saṅkhavaṇṇasāṭakaṃ nivāsetvā paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā “idaṃ mayā nava māse aḍḍhamāsañca vasantena samaṇadhammassa kataṭṭhānaṃ, pāramīkūṭaṃ gaṇhantena mayā dānaṃ datvā mahāpathaviyā kampāpitaṭṭhāna”nti paṇṇasālaṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Athassa kappakādayo kesamassukammādīni kariṃsu. Tamenaṃ sabbābharaṇabhūsitaṃ devarājānamiva virocamānaṃ rajje abhisiñciṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ –

The Bodhisatta, though wishing to rule the kingdom, thought: 'If I do not speak these words, the matter will not be treated with gravity.' Then the Great Being accepted, saying: 'Good.' Knowing his assent, his sixty thousand ministers, born at the same time as him, said: 'Great king, it is time for a bath; wash away the dust and dirt.' The Great Being replied: 'Wait a little,' and entering the leaf-hut, he took off the ascetic's requisites, put them away, and donned a conch-white cloth. He emerged from the leaf-hut and, reflecting: 'This is the place where I have lived for nine and a half months, fulfilling the duties of a recluse; the place where, reaching the pinnacle of perfections, I gave gifts and caused the great earth to tremble,' he circumambulated the leaf-hut three times. Then, paying homage with the fivefold prostration, he stood there. Then barbers and others attended to his hair and beard. Adorned with all ornaments and shining like the king of the gods, they consecrated him in the kingdom. Therefore, it is said:

2403.

2403.

“Tato vessantaro rājā, rajojallaṃ pavāhayi;

Rajojallaṃ pavāhetvā, saṅkhavaṇṇaṃ adhārayī”ti.

Then King Vessantara washed away the dust and dirt; having washed away the dust and dirt, he put on the conch-white garments.

Tattha pavāhayīti hāresi, hāretvā ca pana rājavesaṃ gaṇhīti attho.

Here, 'washed away' means he had it removed; and having had it removed, he took up the royal attire—that is the meaning.

Athassa yaso mahā ahosi. Olokitaolokitaṭṭhānaṃ kampati, mukhamaṅgalikā mukhamaṅgalāni ghosayiṃsu, sabbatūriyāni paggaṇhiṃsu, mahāsamuddakucchiyaṃ [M 7.0380] meghagajjitaghoso viya tūriyaghoso ahosi. Hatthiratanaṃ alaṅkaritvā upānayiṃsu. So khaggaratanaṃ bandhitvā hatthiratanaṃ [V 7.0374] abhiruhi. Tāvadeva naṃ sahajātā saṭṭhisahassā amaccā sabbālaṅkārappaṭimaṇḍitā parivārayiṃsu, sabbakaññāyo maddidevimpi nahāpetvā alaṅkaritvā abhisiñciṃsu. Sīse ca panassā abhisekaudakaṃ abhisiñcamānā “vessantaro taṃ pāletū”tiādīni maṅgalāni vadiṃsu. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Then his glory was great. Every place he looked upon trembled. Auspicious speakers proclaimed auspicious songs, all musical instruments were struck, and the sound of the instruments was like the sound of thunder in the hollow of the great ocean. They adorned the elephant-jewel and brought it near. He fastened on the sword-jewel and mounted the elephant-jewel. At that very moment, sixty thousand ministers, born at the same time as him, adorned with all ornaments, surrounded him. All the maidens bathed Queen Maddī, adorned her, and consecrated her. And as they poured the consecration water over her head, they spoke auspicious words: 'May Vessantara protect you,' and so forth. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

2404.

2404.

“Sīsaṃ nhāto sucivattho, sabbābharaṇabhūsito;

His head bathed, in clean clothes, adorned with all ornaments;

Paccayaṃ nāgamāruyha, khaggaṃ bandhi parantapaṃ.

Having mounted the elephant Paccaya, the scorcher of foes girded on his sword.

2405.

2405.

“Tato saṭṭhisahassāni, yodhino cārudassanā;

Sahajātā pakiriṃsu, nandayantā rathesabhaṃ.

Then sixty thousand warriors, handsome to behold, born with him, surrounded him, delighting the bull among charioteers.

2406.

2406.

“Tato [P 6.0589] maddimpi nhāpesuṃ, sivikaññā samāgatā;

Vessantaro taṃ pāletu, jālī kaṇhājinā cubho;

Athopi taṃ mahārājā, sañjayo abhirakkhatū”ti.

Then the maidens of Sivi, having gathered, also bathed Maddī. 'May Vessantara protect you, and may both Jālī and Kaṇhājinā; and may the great king Sañjaya also protect you.'

Tattha paccayaṃ nāgamāruyhāti taṃ attano jātadivase uppannaṃ hatthināgaṃ. Parantapanti amittatāpanaṃ. Pakiriṃsūti parivārayiṃsu. Nandayantāti tosentā. Sivikaññāti sivirañño pajāpatiyo sannipatitvā gandhodakena nhāpesuṃ. Jālī kaṇhājinā cubhoti ime te puttāpi mātaraṃ rakkhantūti.

Here, 'having mounted the elephant Paccaya' means that great elephant born on his own birthday. 'Scorcher of foes' means tormentor of enemies. 'Surrounded' means they encircled. 'Delighting' means pleasing. 'Maidens of Sivi' means the wives of the Sivi king assembled and bathed her with fragrant water. 'Jālī and Kaṇhājinā both' means may these your sons also protect their mother.

2407.

2407.

“Idañca paccayaṃ laddhā, pubbe saṃklesamattano;

Ānandiyaṃ ācariṃsu, ramaṇīye giribbaje.

Having obtained this benefit and recalling their own past hardship, they celebrated a festival of joy in the delightful mountain range.

2408.

2408.

“Idañca paccayaṃ laddhā, pubbe saṃklesamattano;

Ānandi vittā sumanā, putte saṅgamma lakkhaṇā.

And having obtained this support, recalling her own past hardship, the one with auspicious signs, having met with her sons, was joyful, glad, and happy.

2409.

2409.

“Idañca paccayaṃ laddhā, pubbe saṃklesamattano;

Ānandi vittā patītā, saha puttehi lakkhaṇā”ti.

And having obtained this support, recalling her own past hardship, the one with auspicious signs, together with her sons, was joyful, glad, and pleased.

Tattha idañca paccayaṃ laddhāti bhikkhave, vessantaro maddī ca idañca paccayaṃ laddhā imaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ [V 7.0375] labhitvā, rajje patiṭṭhahitvāti attho. Pubbeti ito [M 7.0381] pubbe attano vanavāsasaṃklesañca anussaritvā. Ānandiyaṃ ācariṃsu, ramaṇīye giribbajeti ramaṇīye vaṅkagirikucchimhi “vessantarassa rañño āṇā”ti kañcanalatāvinaddhaṃ ānandabheriṃ carāpetvā ānandachaṇaṃ ācariṃsu. Ānandi vittā sumanāti lakkhaṇasampannā maddī putte saṅgamma sampāpuṇitvā vittā sumanā hutvā ativiya nandīti attho. Patītāti somanassā hutvā.

Here, 'and having obtained this benefit' means, monks, that Vessantara and Maddī, having obtained this benefit, having gained this support, having been established in the kingdom—that is the meaning. 'Past' means recalling their own past hardship of dwelling in the forest before this. 'They celebrated a festival of joy in the delightful mountain range' means that in the delightful hollow of Mount Vaṅka, proclaiming, 'By the command of King Vessantara,' they had the joy-drum, entwined with golden vines, beaten as they went about, and celebrated a festival of joy. 'Joyful, glad, and happy' means that Maddī, endowed with auspicious signs, having met and regained her children, became glad and happy and rejoiced exceedingly—that is the meaning. 'Pleased' means having become joyful.

Evaṃ patītā hutvā ca pana putte āha –

And having thus become pleased, she spoke to her children:

2410.

2410.

“Ekabhattā pure āsiṃ, niccaṃ thaṇḍilasāyinī;

Iti metaṃ vataṃ āsi, tumhaṃ kāmā hi puttakā.

“Formerly, I ate but one meal a day and always slept upon the bare ground; this was my vow, for your sake, my children.”

2411.

2411.

“Taṃ me vataṃ samiddhajja, tumhe saṅgamma puttakā;

Mātujampi taṃ pāletu, pitujampi ca puttaka;

Athopi taṃ mahārājā, sañjayo abhirakkhatu.

“That vow of mine is fulfilled today, having been reunited with you, my children; may your mother’s merit protect you, and also your father’s, my child; and may the great king Sañjaya also guard you.”

2412.

2412.

“Yaṃ kiñcitthi kataṃ puññaṃ, mayhañceva pitucca te;

Sabbena tena kusalena, ajaro amaro bhavā”ti.

“Whatever merit has been made by me and also by your father, by all that is wholesome may you be ageless and deathless.”

Tattha tumhaṃ kāmā hi puttakāti puttakā ahaṃ tumhākaṃ kāmā tumhe patthayamānā pure tumhesu brāhmaṇena nītesu ekabhattaṃ bhuñjitvā bhūmiyaṃ sayiṃ, iti me tumhākaṃ kāmā etaṃ vataṃ āsīti vadati. Samiddhajjāti taṃ me vataṃ ajja samiddhaṃ. Mātujampi taṃ pāletu, pitujampi ca puttakāti puttajāli taṃ mātujātaṃ somanassampi pitujātaṃ somanassampi pāletu, mātāpitūnaṃ santakaṃ puññaṃ taṃ pāletūti attho. Tenevāha “yaṃ kiñcitthi kataṃ puñña”nti.

Therein, ‘tumhaṃ kāmā hi puttakā’ means: ‘O children, desiring you, longing for you, formerly when you were led away by the brahmin, I ate one meal and slept on the ground. Thus, this vow was mine because of my desire for you,’ so she says. ‘Samiddhajja’ means ‘that vow of mine is today fulfilled’. ‘Mātujampi taṃ pāletu, pitujampi ca puttaka’ means: ‘O child Jāli, may it protect the happiness born of the mother, and the happiness born of the father; that is, may the merit belonging to the parents protect you.’ Therefore, it is said: ‘Whatever merit has been made...’”

Phussatīpi [P 6.0590] devī “ito paṭṭhāya mama suṇhā imāneva vatthāni nivāsetu, imāni ābharaṇāni dhāretū”ti suvaṇṇasamugge pūretvā pahiṇi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Queen Phussatī also, thinking, 'From now on, let my daughter-in-law wear these clothes and put on these ornaments,' filled golden caskets and sent them. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

2413.

2413.

“Kappāsikañca koseyyaṃ, khomakoṭumbarāni ca;

Sassu suṇhāya pāhesi, yehi maddī asobhatha.

“Cotton and silk fabrics, linen and Kotumbara cloths; the mother-in-law sent these to her daughter-in-law, with which Maddī shone.”

2414.

2414.

“Tato [V 7.0376][M 7.0382] hemañca kāyūraṃ, gīveyyaṃ ratanāmayaṃ;

Sassu suṇhāya pāhesi, yehi maddī asobhatha.

“Then a golden armlet and a jeweled necklace; the mother-in-law sent these to her daughter-in-law, with which Maddī shone.”

2415.

2415.

“Tato hemañca kāyūraṃ, aṅgadaṃ maṇimekhalaṃ;

Sassu suṇhāya pāhesi, yehi maddī asobhatha.

“Then a golden armlet, a bracelet, and a jeweled girdle; the mother-in-law sent these to her daughter-in-law, with which Maddī shone.”

2416.

2416.

“Uṇṇataṃ mukhaphullañca, nānāratte ca māṇike;

Sassu suṇhāya pāhesi, yehi maddī asobhatha.

“A frontlet and a mukhaphulla ornament, and gems of various colors; the mother-in-law sent these to her daughter-in-law, with which Maddī shone.”

2417.

2417.

“Uggatthanaṃ giṅgamakaṃ, mekhalaṃ pāṭipādakaṃ;

Sassu suṇhāya pāhesi, yehi maddī asobhatha.

“A head ornament and a giṅgamaka ornament, a girdle, and foot ornaments; the mother-in-law sent these to her daughter-in-law, with which Maddī shone.”

2418.

2418.

“Suttañca suttavajjañca, upanijjhāya seyyasi;

Asobhatha rājaputtī, devakaññāva nandane.

“Considering the strung and the unstrung ornaments, the princess, most excellent, shone like a divine maiden in the Nandana Grove.”

2419.

2419.

“Sīsaṃ nhātā sucivatthā, sabbālaṅkārabhūsitā;

Asobhatha rājaputtī, tāvatiṃseva accharā.

“With her head bathed, clad in pure garments, adorned with all ornaments, the princess shone like a celestial nymph of Tāvatiṃsa.”

2420.

2420.

“Kadalīva vātacchupitā, jātā cittalatāvane;

Antāvaraṇasampannā, rājaputtī asobhatha.

“Like a plantain tree touched by the wind, grown in the Cittalatā Grove, endowed with fine inner garments, the princess shone.”

2421.

2421.

“Sakuṇī mānusinīva, jātā cittapattā patī;

Nigrodhapakkabimboṭṭhī, rājaputtī asobhathā”ti.

“Like a Mānusinī bird with variegated wings, having taken flight; with lips like a ripe banyan fruit or bimba fruit, the princess shone.”

Tattha hemañca kāyūranti suvaṇṇamayaṃ vanakhajjūriphalasaṇṭhānaṃ gīvāpasādhanameva. Ratanamayanti aparampi ratanamayaṃ gīveyyaṃ. Aṅgadaṃ maṇimekhalanti aṅgadābharaṇañca maṇimayamekhalañca. Uṇṇatanti ekaṃ nalāṭapasādhanaṃ. Mukhaphullanti nalāṭante tilakamālābharaṇaṃ. Nānāratteti nānāvaṇṇe. Māṇiketi maṇimaye. Uggatthanaṃ giṅgamakanti etānipi dve ābharaṇāni. Mekhalanti suvaṇṇarajatamayaṃ mekhalaṃ. Pāṭipādakanti pādapasādhanaṃ. Suttañca suttavajjaṃ cāti suttārūḷhañca asuttārūḷhañca pasādhanaṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “suppañca suppavajjañcā”ti [V 7.0377] likhitaṃ. Upanijjhāya seyyasīti etaṃ suttārūḷhañca asuttārūḷhañca ābharaṇaṃ taṃ taṃ ūnaṭṭhānaṃ oloketvā alaṅkaritvā ṭhitā seyyasī uttamarūpadharā maddī devakaññāva nandane asobhatha. Vātacchupitāti cittalatāvane jātā vātasamphuṭṭhā suvaṇṇakadalī viya taṃ divasaṃ sā vijambhamānā asobhatha[M 7.0383]. Dantāvaraṇasampannāti bimbaphalasadisehi rattadantāvaraṇehi samannāgatā. Sakuṇī mānusinīva, jātā cittapattā patīti yathā mānusiyā sarīrena [P 6.0591] jātā mānusinī nāma sakuṇī cittapattā ākāse uppatamānā pakkhe pasāretvā gacchantī sobhati, evaṃ sā rattoṭṭhatāya nigrodhapakkabimbaphalasadisaoṭṭhehi asobhatha.

Therein, ‘hemañca kāyūraṃ’ means a golden neck ornament shaped like the fruit of the wild date palm. ‘Ratanamayanti’ means another neck ornament made of jewels. ‘Aṅgadaṃ maṇimekhalanti’ refers to an armlet ornament and a gem-studded girdle. ‘Uṇṇataṃ’ means a certain forehead ornament. ‘Mukhaphullaṃ’ means a tilaka garland ornament at the edge of the forehead. ‘Nānāratteti’ means of various colors. ‘Māṇiketi’ means made of jewels. ‘Uggatthanaṃ giṅgamakaṃ’ are also two ornaments. ‘Mekhalaṃ’ means a girdle made of gold and silver. ‘Pāṭipādakaṃ’ means foot ornaments. ‘Suttañca suttavajjaṃ cāti’ means ornaments strung on a thread and those not strung on a thread. In the Pāli text, however, it is written as ‘suppañca suppavajjañca’. ‘Upanijjhāya seyyasīti’ means: having examined this strung and unstrung adornment for any deficient place and having adorned herself, Maddī, possessing supreme beauty, stood and shone like a celestial maiden in Nandana Grove. ‘Vātacchupitāti’ means: like a golden plantain tree born in the Cittalatā grove and touched by the wind, she, expanding in beauty, shone that day. ‘Dantāvaraṇasampannāti’ means endowed with red lips resembling bimba fruits. ‘Sakuṇī mānusinīva, jātā cittapattā patīti’ means: just as a bird called a mānusinī, born with a human body and having beautiful wings, shines as it flies up into the sky spreading its wings, so she shone with her red lips, which resembled ripe nigrodha and bimba fruits.

Saṭṭhisahassā amaccā maddiṃ abhiruhanatthāya sabbālaṅkārappaṭimaṇḍitaṃ nātivaddhaṃ sattisarapahārakkhamaṃ ekaṃ taruṇahatthiṃ upanāmesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ –

Sixty thousand ministers brought forth for Maddī to mount a young elephant, adorned with all ornaments, not too large, and capable of withstanding the blows of spears and arrows. Thus it is said:

2422.

2422.

“Tassā ca nāgamānesuṃ, nātivaddhaṃva kuñjaraṃ;

Sattikkhamaṃ sarakkhamaṃ, īsādantaṃ urūḷhavaṃ.

“And for her they brought an elephant, a tusker not excessively large, capable of enduring spears, capable of enduring arrows, with plough-pole tusks, strongly built.”

2423.

2423.

“Sā maddī nāgamāruhi, nātivaddhaṃva kuñjaraṃ;

Sattikkhamaṃ sarakkhamaṃ, īsādantaṃ urūḷhava”nti.

“That Maddī mounted the elephant, a tusker not excessively large, capable of enduring spears and arrows, with tusks like plough-poles, and strongly built.”

Tattha tassā cāti bhikkhave, tassāpi maddiyā sabbālaṅkārappaṭimaṇḍitaṃ katvā nātivaddhaṃ sattisarapahārakkhamaṃ ekaṃ taruṇahatthiṃ upanesuṃ. Nāgamāruhīti varahatthipiṭṭhiṃ abhiruhi.

Therein, 'and for her' means, monks, that for her, for Maddī, having adorned it with all ornaments, they brought a young elephant, not too large, capable of withstanding the blows of spears and arrows. 'She mounted the elephant' means she mounted the back of an excellent elephant.

Iti te ubhopi mahantena yasena khandhāvāraṃ agamaṃsu. Sañjayarājā dvādasahi akkhobhiṇīhi saddhiṃ māsamattaṃ pabbatakīḷaṃ vanakīḷaṃ kīḷi. Mahāsattassa tejena tāvamahante araññe koci vāḷamigo vā pakkhī vā kañci na viheṭhesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

Thus, they both went to the camp with great splendor. King Sañjaya enjoyed mountain sports and forest sports for about a month with twelve akkhobhiṇīs of troops. Due to the power of the Great Being, no wild beast or bird in that vast forest harmed anyone. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

2424.

2424.

“Sabbamhi taṃ araññamhi, yāvantettha migā ahuṃ;

Vessantarassa tejena, naññamaññaṃ viheṭhayuṃ.

“In that entire forest, however many beasts there were, through Vessantara’s power, they did not harm one another.”

2425.

2425.

“Sabbamhi taṃ araññamhi, yāvantettha dijā ahuṃ;

Vessantarassa tejena, naññamaññaṃ viheṭheyuṃ.

“In that entire forest, however many birds there were, through Vessantara’s power, they did not harm one another.”

2426.

2426.

“Sabbamhi [V 7.0378] taṃ araññamhi, yāvantettha migā ahuṃ;

Ekajjhaṃ sannipātiṃsu, vessantare payātamhi;

Sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhane.

“In that entire forest, however many beasts there were, they gathered together in one place when Vessantara departed, the prosperer of the Sivi kingdom.”

2427.

2427.

“Sabbamhi [M 7.0384] taṃ araññamhi, yāvantettha dijā ahuṃ;

Ekajjhaṃ sannipātiṃsu, vessantare payātamhi;

Sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhane.

“In that entire forest, however many birds there were, they gathered together in one place when Vessantara departed, the prosperer of the Sivi kingdom.”

2428.

2428.

“Sabbamhi taṃ araññamhi, yāvantettha migā ahuṃ;

Nāssu mañjū nikūjiṃsu, vessantare payātamhi;

Sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhane.

“In that entire forest, however many beasts there were, they made no sweet sounds when Vessantara departed, the prosperer of the Sivi kingdom.”

2429.

2429.

“Sabbamhi taṃ araññamhi, yāvantettha dijā ahuṃ;

Nāssu mañjū nikūjiṃsu, vessantare payātamhi;

Sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhane”ti.

“In that entire forest, however many birds there were, they made no sweet sounds when Vessantara departed, the prosperer of the Sivi kingdom.”

Tattha yāvantetthāti yāvanto ettha. Ekajjhaṃ sannipātiṃsūti ekasmiṃ ṭhāne sannipatiṃsu, sannipatitvā ca pana “ito paṭṭhāya idāni amhākaṃ aññamaññaṃ lajjā vā hirottappaṃ vā saṃvaro vā na bhavissatī”ti domanassapattā ahesuṃ. Nāssu mañjū nikūjiṃsūti mahāsattassa viyogadukkhitā madhuraṃ ravaṃ pubbe viya na raviṃsu.

Therein, 'yāvantettha' means 'however many were here'. 'Ekajjhaṃ sannipātiṃsu' means they assembled in one place, and having assembled, they became distressed, thinking, 'From now on, there will be no mutual shame, moral dread, or restraint among us.' 'Nāssu mañjū nikūjiṃsu' means, being pained by the separation from the Great Being, they did not make sweet sounds as they had before.

Sañjayanarindo [P 6.0592] māsamattaṃ pabbatakīḷaṃ, vanakīḷaṃ kīḷitvā senāpatiṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta, ciraṃ no araññe vuttaṃ, kiṃ te mama puttassa gamanamaggo alaṅkato”ti pucchitvā “āma, deva, kālo vo gamanāyā”ti vutte vessantarassa ārocāpetvā senaṃ ādāya nikkhami. Vaṅkagirikucchito yāva jetuttaranagarā saṭṭhiyojanaṃ alaṅkatamaggaṃ mahāsatto mahantena parivārena saddhiṃ paṭipajji. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

King Sañjaya, having enjoyed mountain sports and forest sports for about a month, summoned his general and asked, 'My dear, we have stayed long in the forest. Is the path for my son's journey adorned?' When he was told, 'Yes, Your Majesty, it is time for your departure,' he had it announced to Vessantara and set out with his army. The Great Being, with a great retinue, proceeded along the adorned path stretching sixty yojanas from the slope of Mount Vaṅka to the city of Jetuttara. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:

2430.

2430.

“Paṭiyatto rājamaggo, vicitto pupphasanthato;

Vasi vessantaro yattha, yāvatāva jetuttarā.

“The royal road was prepared, decorated, and strewn with flowers, from where Vessantara resided all the way to Jetuttara.

2431.

2431.

“Tato [V 7.0379] saṭṭhisahassāni, yodhino cārudassanā;

Samantā parikiriṃsu, vessantare payātamhi;

Sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhane.

Then sixty thousand warriors, handsome to behold, surrounded Vessantara on all sides as he departed, the prosperer of the Sivi kingdom.

2432.

2432.

“Orodhā [M 7.0385] ca kumārā ca, vesiyānā ca brāhmaṇā;

Samantā parikiriṃsu, vessantare payātamhi;

Sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhane.

The royal ladies and princes, merchants and brahmins, surrounded Vessantara on all sides as he departed, the prosperer of the Sivi kingdom.

2433.

2433.

“Hatthārohā anīkaṭṭhā, rathikā pattikārakā;

Samantā parikiriṃsu, vessantare payātamhi;

Sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhane.

Elephant riders, troop leaders, charioteers, and foot soldiers surrounded Vessantara on all sides as he departed, the prosperer of the Sivi kingdom.

2434.

2434.

“Samāgatā jānapadā, negamā ca samāgatā;

Samantā parikiriṃsu, vessantare payātamhi;

Sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhane.

The country folk gathered, and the townsfolk assembled; they surrounded Vessantara on all sides as he departed, the prosperer of the Sivi kingdom.

2435.

2435.

“Karoṭiyā cammadharā, illīhatthā suvammino;

Purato paṭipajjiṃsu, vessantare payātamhi;

Sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhane”ti.

“Helmeted, clad in hides, sword in hand, and well-armored, they marched ahead of Vessantara as he departed, the prosperer of the Sivi kingdom.”

Tattha paṭiyattoti visākhāpuṇṇamapūjākāle viya alaṅkato. Vicittoti kadalipuṇṇaghaṭadhajapaṭākādīhi vicitto. Pupphasanthatoti lājāpañcamakehi pupphehi santhato. Yatthāti yasmiṃ vaṅkapabbate vessantaro vasati, tato paṭṭhāya yāva jetuttaranagarā nirantaraṃ alaṅkatappaṭiyattova. Karoṭiyāti sīsakaroṭīti laddhanāmāya sīse paṭimukkakaroṭikā yodhā. Cammadharāti kaṇḍavāraṇacammadharā. Suvamminoti vicitrāhi jālikāhi suṭṭhu vammikā. Purato paṭipajjiṃsūti mattahatthīsupi āgacchantesu anivattino sūrayodhā rañño vessantarassa purato paṭipajjiṃsu.

In that context, ‘prepared’ means adorned, as during the Visākha full-moon worship. ‘Decorated’ means adorned with such items as banana trees, full water-pots, banners, and flags. ‘Strewn with flowers’ means strewn with the five kinds of flowers, including parched grain. ‘Where’ refers to the Vaṅka mountain where Vessantara dwelled; from there all the way to the city of Jetuttara, the path was continuously adorned and prepared. ‘Helmeted’ refers to warriors with helmets (karoṭikā) fastened on their heads, so named from the word for skull-cap (sīsakaroṭī). ‘Clad in hides’ means those carrying shields and armor made of hide. ‘Well-armored’ refers to those who are excellently armored with various kinds of chain-mail. ‘Marched ahead’ means that even as intoxicated elephants advanced, these unretreating, heroic warriors proceeded before King Vessantara.

Rājā saṭṭhiyojanamaggaṃ dvīhi māsehi atikkamma jetuttaranagaraṃ patto alaṅkatappaṭiyattanagaraṃ pavisitvā pāsādaṃ abhiruhi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

The king, having traversed the sixty-yojana road in two months, arrived at the city of Jetuttara and, entering the adorned and prepared city, ascended the palace. To illuminate this matter, the Teacher said:

2436.

2436.

“Te [V 7.0380] pāvisuṃ puraṃ rammaṃ, mahāpākāratoraṇaṃ;

Upetaṃ annapānehi, naccagītehi cūbhayaṃ.

“They entered the delightful city, with its great ramparts and gateways, replete with food and drink, and with both dance and song.

2437.

2437.

“Vittā [M 7.0386] jānapadā āsuṃ, negamā ca samāgatā;

Anuppatte kumāramhi, sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhane.

“The country folk were joyful, and the townsfolk gathered together, upon the arrival of the prince, the prosperer of the Sivi kingdom.

2438.

2438.

“Celukkhepo avattittha, āgate dhanadāyake;

Nandiṃ pavesi nagare, bandhanā mokkho aghosathā”ti.

“The tossing of garments took place when the giver of wealth arrived; joy entered the city, and release from bonds was proclaimed.”

Tattha [P 6.0593] mahāpākāratoraṇanti mahantehi pākārehi ca toraṇehi ca samannāgataṃ. Naccagītehi cūbhayanti naccehi ca gītehi ca ubhayehi samannāgataṃ. Vittāti tuṭṭhā somanassappattā. Āgate dhanadāyaketi mahājanassa dhanadāyake mahāsatte āgate. Nandiṃ pavesīti “vessantarassa mahārājassa āṇā”ti nagare nandibherī cari. Bandhanā mokkho aghosathāti sabbasattānaṃ bandhanā mokkho ghosito. Antamaso biḷāraṃ upādāya vessantaramahārājā sabbasatte bandhanā vissajjāpesi.

There, ‘with its great ramparts and gateways’ means endowed with great walls and gateways. ‘And with both dance and song’ means endowed with both dancing and singing. ‘Joyful’ means delighted and having attained gladness. ‘When the giver of wealth arrived’ means when the great being, the giver of wealth to the people, had arrived. ‘Joy entered’ means the drum of joy circulated in the city, proclaiming, “By the command of the great King Vessantara.” ‘Release from bonds was proclaimed’ means the release from bondage for all beings was proclaimed. The great King Vessantara had all beings released from their bonds, even down to the cats.

So nagaraṃ paviṭṭhadivaseyeva paccūsakāle cintesi “ye vibhātāya rattiyā mama āgatabhāvaṃ sutvā yācakā āgamissanti, tesāhaṃ kiṃ dassāmī”ti? Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakkassa bhavanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. So āvajjento taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā tāvadeva rājanivesanassa purimavatthuñca pacchimavatthuñca kaṭippamāṇaṃ pūrento ghanamegho viya sattaratanavassaṃ vassāpesi, sakalanagare jāṇuppamāṇaṃ vassāpesi. Punadivase mahāsatto “tesaṃ tesaṃ kulānaṃ purimapacchimavatthūsu vuṭṭhadhanaṃ tesaṃ tesaññeva hotū”ti dāpetvā avasesaṃ āharāpetvā attano gehavatthusmiṃ saddhiṃ dhanena koṭṭhāgāresu okirāpetvā dānamukhe ṭhapesi. Tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā āha –

On the very day he entered the city, at dawn, he thought, “When the night is over, those beggars who have heard of my arrival will come—what shall I give them?” At that moment, Sakka's abode showed signs of heat. Sakka, reflecting and knowing the reason, immediately caused a rain of the seven kinds of precious jewels to fall like a dense cloud, filling the front and back courtyards of the royal residence to the height of a waist, and caused it to rain knee-deep throughout the rest of the city. The next day, the Great Being ordered, “Let the wealth that rained in the front and back courtyards of each household belong to those respective householders,” and had the rest collected. He then had it stored together with his own wealth in the treasuries and placed it at the disposal of his giving. The Teacher, revealing this meaning, said:

2439.

2439.

“Jātarūpamayaṃ vassaṃ, devo pāvassi tāvade;

Vessantare paviṭṭhamhi, sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhane.

“Then the deity rained down a shower of gold at once, when Vessantara, the prosperer of the Sivi kingdom, had entered.

2440.

2440.

“Tato vessantaro rājā, dānaṃ datvāna khattiyo;

Kāyassa bhedā sappañño, saggaṃ so upapajjathā”ti.

“Then King Vessantara, the wise noble, having given gifts, at the breaking up of the body, arose in heaven.”

Tattha [V 7.0381][M 7.0387] saggaṃ so upapajjathāti tato cuto dutiyacittena tusitapure uppajjīti.

In that context, ‘he arose in heaven’ means that having passed away from there, with the following thought-moment he was reborn in the Tusita heaven.

Nagarakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on the City is concluded.

Satthā imaṃ gāthāsahassappaṭimaṇḍitaṃ mahāvessantaradhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā jūjako devadatto ahosi, amittatāpanā ciñcamāṇavikā, cetaputto channo, accutatāpaso sāriputto, sakko anuruddho, sañcayanarindo suddhodanamahārājā, phussatī devī sirimahāmāyā, maddī devī rāhulamātā, jālikumāro rāhulo, kaṇhājinā uppalavaṇṇā, sesaparisā buddhaparisā, mahāvessantaro rājā pana ahameva sammāsambuddho ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse on the Great Vessantara, adorned with a thousand verses, connected the birth story: “At that time, Jūjaka was Devadatta; Amittatāpanā was Ciñcamāṇavikā; Cetaputta was Channa; the ascetic Accuta was Sāriputta; Sakka was Anuruddha; King Sañcaya was the great King Suddhodana; Queen Phussatī was Queen Sirimahāmāyā; Queen Maddī was Rāhula’s mother; Prince Jālika was Rāhula; Kaṇhājinā was Uppalavaṇṇā; the remaining assembly was the Buddha’s assembly; and King Mahāvessantara was I myself, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.”

Vessantarajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Vessantara Jātaka, the tenth.

Mahānipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Great Nipāta is concluded.

Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā samattā.

The Jātaka Commentary is complete.
